For student 11, we do indeed see the weighted average of 7.33 reported by the original Python course on this same dataset.

docs.title: 7.2.7. Conclusion
docs.text: TypeORM allows you to write read/write operations without SQL, using decorated entities similar in spirit to SQLAlchemy—at the cost of a significant design difference to be aware of (no implicit lazy loading of relationships: any relationships not explicitly requested are omitted) and a tooling pitfall specific to TSX execution (column types must be specified explicitly). The following chapter uses the exact same example with Prisma to compare the two approaches.

docs.title: 7.3. Using the Prisma ORM
docs.text:
Second ORM, using the same example as the previous chapter (the dbpersons and dbschool databases), to compare the two approaches. Prisma differs from TypeORM in its design: instead of annotating classes, the database schema is described in a separate file using Prisma’s own declarative format, from which the prisma generate command generates a fully typed client.

Important: As of the writing of this chapter, Prisma ORM is at version 7, which has undergone significant internal changes compared to previous versions (5 and 6): the query engine, previously a separately downloaded binary compiled in Rust, is now a WebAssembly module embedded directly in the npm package, combined with a driver adapter (here @prisma/adapter-mariadb) that relays queries to a traditional JavaScript driver. The general principle, however, remains the same as with previous versions of Prisma, and the following therefore applies to those versions as well. Note on this environment: the `npx prisma generate` command, which generates the TypeScript client from the schema.prisma file, requires a Prisma-specific network resource (binaries.prisma.sh) to retrieve an internal component from its CLI—a resource that the network policy of the runtime environment used to prepare this course did not allow access to. The scripts in this chapter were therefore written and reviewed with the same care as the previous ones, but could not be executed or verified in this environment—unlike those in the two previous chapters, all of which were executed and their results verified. On a machine with normal Internet access (the typical case), `npx prisma generate` runs without any particular issues, and the scripts should produce the “expected” outputs shown below, calculated from the same data already verified in the previous chapter.

docs.title: 7.3.1. Installation and Configuration
docs.text:
Prisma is installed with two packages: prisma (CLI, a development dependency) and @prisma/client (the client library, a production dependency); we add @prisma/adapter-mariadb, the MySQL/MariaDB driver adapter, which internally relies on the mariadb package. One Prisma schema per database—just as there is one TypeORM DataSource per database:

// databases/prisma/schema-persons.prisma
// Prisma schema of the [dbpersons] database (a single table [persons]).
// Prisma ORM 7 generates a "Rust-free" TypeScript client (provider
// "prisma-client"): driver adapters (`driverAdapters`, here
// @prisma/adapter-mariadb) are used by default, there is no longer any need to
// declare `previewFeatures = ["driverAdapters"]` as in versions 5/6.
generator client {
  provider = "prisma-client"
  // output path of the generated client, relative to this file — since
  // Prisma 7 it is mandatory (the client is no longer written into
  // node_modules by default)
  output   = "../../generated/prisma-persons"
}

// since Prisma ORM 7, the datasource no longer carries a connection URL: with
// driver adapters, the connection is entirely configured at
// runtime, on the PrismaClient side (see prisma-01.ts) — `provider` only
// serves to tell the generator which SQL dialect to target
datasource db {
  provider = "mysql"
}

// ports the [persons] table of create_dbpersons.sql
model Person {
  id        Int    @id
  firstName String @map("first_name") @db.VarChar(30)
  lastName  String @map("last_name") @db.VarChar(30)
  age       Int

  @@unique([lastName, firstName])
  @@map("persons")
}

// databases/prisma/schema-school.prisma
// Prisma schema of the [dbschool] database (classes / students / subjects / grades).
// Same tables as databases/typeorm/entities/*.entity.ts and sql/create_dbschool.sql
// — the two ORM chapters (TypeORM then Prisma) deliberately use the
// same example, so that the reader can compare the two approaches on an
// identical case.
generator client {
  provider = "prisma-client"
  output   = "../../generated/prisma-school"
}

// since Prisma ORM 7, the datasource no longer carries a connection URL: with
// driver adapters, the connection is entirely configured at
// runtime, on the PrismaClient side (see prisma-02.ts) — `provider` only
// serves to tell the generator which SQL dialect to target
datasource db {
  provider = "mysql"
}

model SchoolClass {
  id       Int       @id @default(autoincrement())
  name     String    @unique @db.VarChar(30)
  students Student[]

  @@map("classes")
}

model Student {
  id          Int         @id
  lastName    String      @map("last_name") @db.VarChar(30)
  firstName   String      @map("first_name") @db.VarChar(30)
  classId     Int         @map("class_id")
  schoolClass SchoolClass @relation(fields: [classId], references: [id])
  grades      Grade[]

  @@map("students")
}

model Subject {
  id          Int     @id @default(autoincrement())
  name        String  @unique @db.VarChar(30)
  coefficient Decimal @db.Decimal(4, 2)
  grades      Grade[]

  @@map("subjects")
}

model Grade {
  id        Int     @id @default(autoincrement())
  value     Decimal @db.Decimal(4, 2)
  studentId Int     @map("student_id")
  subjectId Int     @map("subject_id")
  student   Student @relation(fields: [studentId], references: [id])
  subject   Subject @relation(fields: [subjectId], references: [id])

  @@map("grades")
}

Let’s comment on these schemas:

  • line 7: [generator client { provider = "prisma-client" output = "../../generated/prisma-school" }] — since Prisma 7, the generated client output is required (previous versions wrote it to node_modules by default); Driver adapters are used by default; it is no longer necessary to enable them with previewFeatures as was the case when they were first introduced (versions 5 and 6);
  • Line 16: [datasource db { provider = "mysql" }] — Important change in Prisma ORM 7: The datasource block no longer includes a connection string (url = env(...), which was allowed in versions 5 and 6, is now rejected by CLI — error P1012, The url property of the datasource is no longer supported in schema files); with driver adapters, all connection configuration (host, username, password, database) is handled by PrismaClient at runtime—the provider is used solely to indicate to the generator which SQL dialect to target;
  • line 32: [@@map("students") ... classId Int @map("class_id")] — @map/@@map are used to name the Prisma model properties in camelCase (classId) while mapping them to existing columns in SQL, named in snake_case (class_id) — a difference in convention between Prisma, which prefers camelCase everywhere, and the existing SQL schema;
  • line 50: [value Decimal @db.Decimal(4, 2)] — Prisma’s Decimal type (not to be confused with number) — see the corresponding pitfall for the [prisma-04-stats] script below.

Before using it for the first time, you must generate the client (once, or each time the schema is modified):

npx prisma generate --schema=databases/prisma/schema-persons.prisma
npx prisma generate --schema=databases/prisma/schema-school.prisma

The generated client is then instantiated with the driver adapter, which is explicitly configured (using the same credentials as in the previous sections, for consistency) rather than relying on the environment variable read by CLI:

import { PrismaMariaDb } from '@prisma/adapter-mariadb';
import { PrismaClient } from '../../generated/prisma-school/client.js';

const adapter = new PrismaMariaDb({
  host: 'localhost', user: 'admschool', password: 'pwdschool', database: 'dbschool',
});
const prisma = new PrismaClient({ adapter });

docs.title: 7.3.2. script [prisma-01]
docs.text:
First use of Prisma: reading from and writing to the persons table via the generated client. Uses the same example as typeorm-01.ts—compare the two files; only API changes.

// databases/prisma/prisma-01.ts
// First use of Prisma ORM: read and write in the table
// [persons] through the generated client, without writing a single line of
// SQL. Uses the same example as databases/typeorm/typeorm-01.ts, to
// compare the two ORMs on an identical case.
//
// Important — this file can only be compiled/executed after generating the
// Prisma client (see the README):
//   npx prisma generate --schema=databases/prisma/schema-persons.prisma
// This command writes the module ../../generated/prisma-persons imported
// below; as long as it has not been run, this module does not exist.
import { PrismaMariaDb } from '@prisma/adapter-mariadb';
import { PrismaClient } from '../../generated/prisma-persons/client.js';

// Prisma ORM 7 no longer connects to the database by itself: we give it a
// "driver adapter" (here @prisma/adapter-mariadb, which relies on the
// `mariadb` package) already configured with the connection credentials — the
// same principle as TypeORM's DataSource.
const adapter = new PrismaMariaDb({
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'admpersons',
  password: 'nobody',
  database: 'dbpersons',
});
const prisma = new PrismaClient({ adapter });

try {
  // all the persons, sorted by last name
  const all = await prisma.person.findMany({ orderBy: { lastName: 'asc' } });
  console.log('Persons in the database:');
  for (const p of all) {
    console.log(`  ${p.id} ${p.firstName} ${p.lastName} (${p.age} years old)`);
  }

  // a person by their primary key
  const paul = await prisma.person.findUnique({ where: { id: 1 } });
  console.log(`Person id=1: ${paul ? `${paul.firstName} ${paul.lastName}` : 'not found'}`);

  // insertion of a new person — `create` returns the created record
  const newPerson = await prisma.person.create({
    data: { id: 99, firstName: 'Ada', lastName: 'Lovelace', age: 36 },
  });
  console.log(`Person ${newPerson.id} inserted.`);

  // update
  const updated = await prisma.person.update({
    where: { id: 99 },
    data: { age: 37 },
  });
  console.log(`After update, age=${updated.age}`);

  // deletion — we put the database back in the state we found it in
  await prisma.person.delete({ where: { id: 99 } });
  console.log('Person 99 deleted.');
} finally {
  await prisma.$disconnect();
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 22: [await prisma.person.findMany({ orderBy: { lastName: 'asc' } })] — each schema model becomes a property of the client (prisma.person), with standardized methods — findMany, findUnique, create, update, delete... — common to all models, regardless of the DBMS;
  • line 39: [const newPerson = await prisma.person.create({ data: {...} });] — unlike TypeORM (new followed by save()), Prisma clearly separates creation (create) from updating (update) — two distinct methods rather than a single method that guesses the intent.

Once executed (npx tsx databases/prisma/prisma-01.ts), this script produces:

Output:

Persons in the database:
  4 Geraldine Colou (26 years old)
  5 Paulette Girond (56 years old)
  1 Paul Langevin (48 years old)
  2 Sylvie Lefur (70 years old)
  3 Pierre Nicazou (35 years old)
Person id=1: Paul Langevin
Person 99 inserted.
After update, age=37
Person 99 deleted.

docs.title: 7.3.3. script [prisma-02]
docs.text:
Reads the "classes/subjects" tables from dbschool, then adds, updates, and deletes a student. Uses the same example as typeorm-02.ts.

// databases/prisma/prisma-02.ts
// Reading the [classes]/[subjects] tables of [dbschool], then addition, re-reading
// and deletion of a student. Uses the same example as
// databases/typeorm/typeorm-02.ts.
//
// This file assumes the generated client: see prisma-01.ts for the remark
// about `npx prisma generate --schema=databases/prisma/schema-school.prisma`.
import { PrismaMariaDb } from '@prisma/adapter-mariadb';
import { PrismaClient } from '../../generated/prisma-school/client.js';

const adapter = new PrismaMariaDb({
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'admschool',
  password: 'pwdschool',
  database: 'dbschool',
});
const prisma = new PrismaClient({ adapter });
console.log('Prisma connection to [dbschool] established.');

try {
  // all the classes
  console.log('Classes:');
  for (const c of await prisma.schoolClass.findMany({ orderBy: { name: 'asc' } })) {
    console.log(`  ${c.id} ${c.name}`);
  }

  // all the subjects, with their coefficient — `coefficient` is of type
  // `Decimal` (a class provided by Prisma, not a native JavaScript `number`);
  // we display it directly here (its `toString()` does the right thing), but
  // any computation on it requires going through `.toNumber()` (see prisma-04-stats.ts)
  console.log('Subjects:');
  for (const s of await prisma.subject.findMany({ orderBy: { name: 'asc' } })) {
    console.log(`  ${s.id} ${s.name} (coefficient ${s.coefficient})`);
  }

  // addition of a new student in [class1] — `connect` links the new student
  // to an existing class by its key, without having to load this class
  // beforehand (unlike the assignment `newStudent.schoolClass = class1` of
  // TypeORM)
  const class1 = await prisma.schoolClass.findUniqueOrThrow({ where: { name: 'class1' } });
  const newStudent = await prisma.student.create({
    data: { id: 999, lastName: 'Curie', firstName: 'Marie', schoolClass: { connect: { id: class1.id } } },
  });
  console.log(`Student ${newStudent.firstName} ${newStudent.lastName} added to ${class1.name}.`);

  // re-reading — `include` loads the requested relationship (Prisma, like
  // TypeORM, does no lazy loading by default: a relationship absent
  // from the `include` is simply absent from the returned object)
  const reread = await prisma.student.findUnique({ where: { id: 999 }, include: { schoolClass: true } });
  console.log(`Re-read: ${reread?.firstName} ${reread?.lastName}, class=${reread?.schoolClass.name}`);

  // deletion — we put the database back in the state we found it in
  await prisma.student.delete({ where: { id: 999 } });
  console.log('Student 999 deleted.');
} finally {
  await prisma.$disconnect();
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 39: [data: { id: 999, lastName: 'Curie', firstName: 'Marie', schoolClass: { connect: { id: class1.id } } }] — connect links the new student to an existing class using its key — Prisma automatically constructs the value for the class_id column, so we don’t have to manipulate it directly;
  • line 44: [await prisma.student.findUnique({ where: { id: 999 }, include: { schoolClass: true } })] — same principle as with TypeORM: include (instead of relations) explicitly loads the requested relationship — Prisma does not perform implicit lazy loading here either.

Once executed (npx tsx databases/prisma/prisma-02.ts), this script produces:

Prisma connection to [dbschool] established.
Classes:
  1 class1
  2 class2
Subjects:
  1 subject1 (coefficient 1)
  2 subject2 (coefficient 2)
Student Marie Curie added to class1.
Re-read: Marie Curie, class=class1
Student 999 deleted.

docs.title: 7.3.4. script [prisma-03-joined-queries]
docs.text:
Queries with joins on dbschool. Contains exactly the same example as typeorm-03-joined-queries.ts — compare the two files: The logic is identical; only the API changes (using include instead of relations, and findUniqueOrThrow/findFirstOrThrow instead of findOneOrFail).

// databases/prisma/prisma-03-joined-queries.ts
// Queries with joins (`include`) on [dbschool]. Uses exactly the same
// example as databases/typeorm/typeorm-03-joined-queries.ts — compare the
// two files: the logic is identical, only the API changes (`include`
// rather than `relations`, `findUniqueOrThrow`/`findFirstOrThrow` rather than
// `findOneOrFail`).
import { PrismaMariaDb } from '@prisma/adapter-mariadb';
import { PrismaClient } from '../../generated/prisma-school/client.js';

const adapter = new PrismaMariaDb({
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'admschool',
  password: 'pwdschool',
  database: 'dbschool',
});
const prisma = new PrismaClient({ adapter });

try {
  // student by id, with their class (explicit join via `include`)
  console.log('student id=11 -----------');
  const student11 = await prisma.student.findUniqueOrThrow({ where: { id: 11 }, include: { schoolClass: true } });
  console.log(`student={"id":${student11.id},"lastName":"${student11.lastName}","firstName":"${student11.firstName}"}`);
  console.log(`student's class: {"id":${student11.schoolClass.id},"name":"${student11.schoolClass.name}"}`);

  // the students of the same class (new query, with its own join)
  console.log('students in the same class:');
  const studentsClass = await prisma.schoolClass.findUniqueOrThrow({
    where: { id: student11.schoolClass.id },
    include: { students: true },
  });
  for (const s of studentsClass.students) {
    console.log(`student={"id":${s.id},"lastName":"${s.lastName}","firstName":"${s.firstName}"}`);
  }

  // a student by their last name
  console.log("student lastName='lastname2' -----------");
  const byName = await prisma.student.findFirstOrThrow({ where: { lastName: 'lastname2' }, include: { schoolClass: true } });
  console.log(`student={"id":${byName.id},"lastName":"${byName.lastName}","firstName":"${byName.firstName}"}`);
  console.log(`student's class: {"id":${byName.schoolClass.id},"name":"${byName.schoolClass.name}"}`);

  // a student's grades, with the subject of each grade — nested `include`,
  // equivalent of TypeORM's `relations: { grades: { subject: true } }`
  console.log('grades of student id=11 -----------');
  const studentWithGrades = await prisma.student.findUniqueOrThrow({
    where: { id: 11 },
    include: { grades: { include: { subject: true } } },
  });
  for (const grade of studentWithGrades.grades) {
    console.log(`grade={"id":${grade.id},"value":${grade.value}}, subject={"name":"${grade.subject.name}"}`);
  }

  // the students of a class, by class name
  for (const className of ['class1', 'class2']) {
    console.log(`students of class name='${className}' -----------`);
    const schoolClass = await prisma.schoolClass.findUniqueOrThrow({ where: { name: className }, include: { students: true } });
    for (const s of schoolClass.students) {
      console.log(`{"id":${s.id},"lastName":"${s.lastName}","firstName":"${s.firstName}"}`);
    }
  }

  // the grades in a subject, by subject name
  for (const subjectName of ['subject1', 'subject2']) {
    console.log(`subject with name='${subjectName}' -----------`);
    const subject = await prisma.subject.findUniqueOrThrow({ where: { name: subjectName }, include: { grades: true } });
    console.log(`subject={"name":"${subject.name}","coefficient":${subject.coefficient}}`);
    console.log('Grades in the subject: ');
    for (const grade of subject.grades) {
      console.log(`{"id":${grade.id},"value":${grade.value}}`);
    }
  }
} finally {
  await prisma.$disconnect();
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 44: [include: { grades: { include: { subject: true } } }] — a nested include, equivalent to the relations: { grades: { subject: true } } in TypeORM — fetches, in a single query, the student’s grades and, for each one, their subject.

Once executed (npx tsx .\databases\prisma\prisma-03-joined-queries.ts), this script produces:

students in the same class:

Note: The numeric values above appear without trailing decimal zeros (10 instead of 10.00) when interpolated into a string, unlike the output of the [typeorm-03] script — a visible sign that grade.value is no longer a string, as is the case with TypeORM (see the following script).

docs.title: 7.3.5. script [prisma-04-stats]
docs.text:
Calculates, for a given student, their grade point average weighted by subject coefficients, as well as their minimum and maximum grades. Uses the same example as typeorm-04-stats.ts.

// databases/prisma/prisma-04-stats.ts
// Computes, for a given student, their average weighted by the coefficients of
// the subjects, as well as their min and max grade. Uses the same example as
// databases/typeorm/typeorm-04-stats.ts.
//
// Pitfall to know, different from TypeORM's: Prisma does not return
// the `Decimal` columns (here `grade.value` and `subject.coefficient`) as
// strings, but as instances of the `Prisma.Decimal` class
// (provided by the decimal.js library), so as not to lose any
// decimal precision. `typeof grade.value` is `'object'`, not `'number'`
// nor `'string'`. A computation such as `grade.value * subject.coefficient`
// would work almost by accident (`Decimal` redefines `valueOf`), but
// the good practice — and the one used below — is to call
// `.toNumber()` explicitly before any floating-point computation.
import { PrismaMariaDb } from '@prisma/adapter-mariadb';
import { PrismaClient } from '../../generated/prisma-school/client.js';

const adapter = new PrismaMariaDb({
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'admschool',
  password: 'pwdschool',
  database: 'dbschool',
});
const prisma = new PrismaClient({ adapter });

// computes the statistics (weighted average, min, max) of a student
async function studentStats(studentId: number): Promise<void> {
  // a single query, with two levels of join (grades, then the subject of
  // each grade) to have the coefficient of each subject
  const student = await prisma.student.findUniqueOrThrow({
    where: { id: studentId },
    include: { grades: { include: { subject: true } } },
  });

  console.log(`Statistics of student {"id":${student.id},"lastName":"${student.lastName}","firstName":"${student.firstName}"}`);

  if (student.grades.length === 0) {
    console.log('  no grades.');
    return;
  }

  let weightedSum = 0;
  let coefficientsSum = 0;
  let min = Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY;
  let max = Number.NEGATIVE_INFINITY;

  for (const grade of student.grades) {
    // explicit conversion: `grade.value` and `grade.subject.coefficient`
    // are `Prisma.Decimal` values, not `number` values
    const value = grade.value.toNumber();
    const coefficient = grade.subject.coefficient.toNumber();
    weightedSum += value * coefficient;
    coefficientsSum += coefficient;
    min = Math.min(min, value);
    max = Math.max(max, value);
    console.log(`  grade=${value.toFixed(2)} subject="${grade.subject.name}" (coefficient ${coefficient.toFixed(2)})`);
  }

  const average = weightedSum / coefficientsSum;
  console.log(`  weighted average=${average.toFixed(2)}, min=${min.toFixed(2)}, max=${max.toFixed(2)}`);
}

try {
  // student id=11: grades subject1=10 (coef 1.0), subject2=6 (coef 2.0)
  // weighted average = (10*1.0 + 6*2.0) / (1.0+2.0) = 22/3 = 7.33
  await studentStats(11);
  console.log();
  await studentStats(21);
  console.log();
  await studentStats(32);
  console.log();
  await studentStats(42);
} finally {
  await prisma.$disconnect();
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 48: [const value = grade.value.toNumber(); const coefficient = grade.subject.coefficient.toNumber();] — a pitfall to be aware of, different from that in TypeORM: Prisma does not return Decimal columns as strings, but as instances of the Prisma.Decimal class (provided by the decimal.js library), to avoid losing any decimal precision—typeof grade.value returns 'object', not 'number' or 'string'. Best practice is to explicitly call .toNumber() before any floating-point calculation—a direct calculation like grade.value * subject.coefficient would work almost by accident (Decimal redefines valueOf), but it’s still a practice to avoid.

Once executed (npx tsx .\databases\prisma\prisma-04-stats.ts), this script produces:

Statistics of student {"id":11,"lastName":"lastname1","firstName":"firstname1"}
  grade=10.00 subject="subject1" (coefficient 1.00)
  grade=6.00 subject="subject2" (coefficient 2.00)
  weighted average=7.33, min=6.00, max=10.00

docs.title: 7.3.6. Conclusion
docs.text: Using the same example, TypeORM and Prisma produce code of comparable length and readability—the differences are mainly stylistic: decorated classes and a Repository for TypeORM (more similar to SQLAlchemy and Spring Data JPA), and a separate declarative schema and fully generated client for Prisma (more similar in spirit to a tool like Alembic combined with a code generator). Both avoid writing SQL, and both share the same design choice—no implicit lazy loading of relationships—which sets them apart from SQLAlchemy. The choice between the two, in a real-world project, comes down mainly to the ecosystem (Prisma Studio, Prisma migrations, etc.) and the team’s preferences.

docs.title: 6. HTTP clients of the tax calculation service
6.1. Introduction
docs.text:
In this section, we will write a [node.js] client for the tax calculation service set up in the chapter “Installing a NestJS Server.” The client/server architecture will be as follows:

We will examine two versions of the client:

  • Version 1 of the client will have the following layered structure: [main, dao]:

  • Client version 2 will have the structure [main, business, dao]. The server layer [business] will be offloaded to the client:

docs.title: 6.2. HTTP client 1
docs.text:
As mentioned, the HTTP client 1 implements the following client/server architecture:

We will implement:

  • the [dao] layer as a class;
  • the [main] layer as a script that uses this class;

docs.title: 6.2.1. The [dao] layer
docs.text:
The [dao] layer will be implemented by the following class, [Dao1.ts]:

'use strict';

// imports
import { AxiosInstance, AxiosRequestConfig, AxiosResponse } from 'axios';
import qs from 'qs'

class Dao1 {

  private axios: AxiosInstance;
  private sessionCookieName: string;
  private sessionCookie: string;

  // constructor
  constructor(axios: AxiosInstance) {
    // axios library used to make the HTTP requests
    this.axios = axios;
    // session cookie
    this.sessionCookieName = "PHPSESSID";
    this.sessionCookie = '';
  }

  // init session
  async initSession(): Promise<any> {
    // options of the HTTP request [get /main.php?action=init-session&type=json]
    const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
      // [TypeScript update] URL included in [options.url] (see getRemoteData)
      url: 'main.php',
      method: "GET",
      // URL parameters
      params: {
        action: 'init-session',
        type: 'json'
      }
    };
    // executing the HTTP request
    return await this.getRemoteData(options);
  }

  async authenticateUser(user: string, password: string): Promise<any> {
    // options of the HTTP request [post /main.php?action=authenticate-user]
    const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
      url: 'main.php',
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        'Content-type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded',
      },
      // body of the POST
      data: qs.stringify({
        user: user,
        password: password
      }),
      // URL parameters
      params: {
        action: 'authenticate-user'
      }
    };
    // executing the HTTP request
    return await this.getRemoteData(options);
  }

  // tax calculation
  async calculateTax(married: string, children: number, salary: number): Promise<any> {
    // options of the HTTP request
    const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
      url: 'main.php',
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        'Content-type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded',
      },
      // body of the POST
      data: qs.stringify({
        married: married,
        children: children,
        salary: salary
      }),
      // URL parameters
      params: {
        action: 'calculate-tax'
      }
    };
    // executing the HTTP request
    const data = await this.getRemoteData(options);
    // result
    return data;
  }

  // list of simulations
  async listSimulations(): Promise<any> {
    // options of the HTTP request
    const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
      url: 'main.php',
      method: "GET",
      // URL parameters
      params: {
        action: 'list-simulations'
      },
    };
    // executing the HTTP request
    const data = await this.getRemoteData(options);
    // result
    return data;
  }

  // delete a simulation
  async deleteSimulation(index: number): Promise<any> {
    // options of the HTTP request
    const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
      url: 'main.php',
      method: "GET",
      // URL parameters
      params: {
        action: 'delete-simulation',
        number: index
      },
    };
    // executing the HTTP request
    const data = await this.getRemoteData(options);
    // result
    return data;
  }

  async getRemoteData(options: AxiosRequestConfig): Promise<any> {
    // for the session cookie
    if (!options.headers) {
      options.headers = {} as any;
    }
    (options.headers as any).Cookie = this.sessionCookie;
    // executing the HTTP request
    let response: AxiosResponse;
    try {
      // asynchronous request
      response = await this.axios.request(options);
    } catch (error: any) {
      // the [error] parameter is an exception instance - it can take various forms
      if (error.response) {
        // the server's response is in [error.response]
        response = error.response;
      } else {
        // we rethrow the error
        throw error;
      }
    }
    // response is the whole HTTP response of the server (HTTP headers + the response itself)
    // we retrieve the session cookie if it exists
    const setCookie = response.headers['set-cookie'];
    if (setCookie) {
      // setCookie is an array
      // we look for the session cookie in this array
      let found = false;
      let i = 0;
      while (!found && i < setCookie.length) {
        // we look for the session cookie
        const results = RegExp('^(' + this.sessionCookieName + '.+?);').exec(setCookie[i]);
        if (results) {
          // we store the session cookie
          // eslint-disable-next-line require-atomic-updates
          this.sessionCookie = results[1];
          // we found it
          found = true;
        } else {
          // next element
          i++;
        }
      }
    }
    // the server's response is in [response.data]
    return response.data;
  }
}

// exporting the class
export default Dao1;
  • Here we apply what we learned in the chapter on the HTTP functions of TypeScript;
  • Lines 14–20: the class constructor. This class will have three properties:
    • [axios]: the [axios] object used to make HTTP requests. This is passed by the calling code;
    • [sessionCookieName]: Depending on the server, the session cookie may have different names. Here, it is [PHPSESSID];
    • [sessionCookie]: the session cookie sent by the server and stored by the client;
  • lines 62–85: the asynchronous function [calculateTax] makes the request [post /main.php?action=calculate-tax] by posting the parameters [married, children, salary]. It returns the string jSON transmitted by the server as a JavaScript object;
  • lines 88–102: The asynchronous function [listSimulations] makes the request [get /main.php?action=list-simulations]. It returns the string jSON sent by the server as a JavaScript object;
  • lines 105–120: The asynchronous function [deleteSimulation] makes the request [get /main.php?action=delete-simulation&number=index]. It returns the string jSON sent by the server as a JavaScript object;
  • line 132: the notation [this.axios] is used because here, the [axios] object passed to the constructor was stored in the [this.axios] property (line 9);
  • line 172: the [Dao1] class is exported so it can be used;

docs.title: 6.2.2. The [main1] script
docs.text:
This script chains together a series of calls to the server via the Dao1 class: session initialization, authentication, three tax calculations (in parallel), a list of simulations, and the deletion of one of them:

// axios import
import axios from 'axios';
// import of the Dao class
import Dao from './Dao1.js';


// asynchronous [main] function
async function main(): Promise<void> {
  // axios configuration
  axios.defaults.timeout = 2000;
  axios.defaults.baseURL = 'http://localhost:3000';
  // instantiating the [dao] layer
  const dao = new Dao(axios);
  // using the [dao] layer
  try {
    // init session
    log("-----------init-session");
    let response = await dao.initSession();
    log(response);
    // authentication
    log("-----------authenticate-user");
    response = await dao.authenticateUser("admin", "admin");
    log(response);
    // tax calculations
    log("-----------calculate-tax x 3");
    response = await Promise.all([
      dao.calculateTax("yes", 2, 45000),
      dao.calculateTax("no", 2, 45000),
      dao.calculateTax("no", 1, 30000)
    ]);
    log(response);
    // list of simulations
    log("-----------list-of-simulations");
    response = await dao.listSimulations();
    log(response);
    // deleting a simulation
    log("-----------deleting simulation no. 1");
    response = await dao.deleteSimulation(1);
    log(response);
  } catch (error: any) {
    // we log the error
    console.log("error=", error.message);
  }
}

// JSON log
function log(object: unknown): void {
  console.log(JSON.stringify(object, null, 2));
}

// execution
main();

Comments

  • line 3: the [axios] library is imported;
  • line 5: imports the [Dao] class;
  • line 9: the [main] function, which communicates with the server, is asynchronous;
  • Lines 11–12: Default configuration of the HTTP requests that will be sent to the server:
    • line 9: [timeout] with a timeout of 2 seconds;
    • line 10: all URL requests are prefixed with the base URL of the tax calculation server (http://localhost:3000);
  • line 14 : the [Dao] layer is built. It can now be used;
  • lines 48–50: the [log] function is designed to display the jSON string from a JavaScript object in a formatted manner: vertically with a two-space indentation (3rd parameter);
  • lines 17–20: initialization of the jSON session;
  • Lines 21–24: authentication;
  • lines 25–32: Three tax calculations are requested in parallel. Thanks to [await Promise.all], execution is blocked until all three results have been obtained;
  • lines 33–36: list of simulations;
  • lines 37–40: Deletion of a simulation;
  • lines 41–44: handling of any exceptions;

docs.title: 6.3. HTTP client 2
docs.text:
The architecture of HTTP client 2 is as follows:

The [business] layer has been moved from the server to the JavaScript client. Here, the [main] layer will not need to pass through the [business] layer to reach the [dao] layer. We will use these two layers as centers of expertise:

  • the [main] layer goes through the [dao] layer whenever it needs data that is on the server;
  • the [main] layer requests the [business] layer to perform the tax calculations;
  • The [business] layer is independent of the [dao] layer and never calls upon it;

docs.title: 6.3.1. The [Business] class
docs.text:
The tax calculation logic closely follows that of the PHP class from the “Introduction to the PHP7 Language Through Examples” course—we will not detail it again here; we are only interested in its translation into TypeScript:

'use strict';

// Business class
class Business {

  // [any]: the exact structure of the data sent by the tax server (rates, ceilings, ...)
  // is not documented here; so we deliberately stay flexible on this type
  taxAdminData: any;

  // constructor
  constructor(taxAdmindata: any) {
    // this.taxAdminData: tax administration data
    this.taxAdminData = taxAdmindata;
  }

  // tax calculation
  // --------------------------------------------------------------------------
  calculateTax(married: string, children: number, salary: number): any {
    // married: yes, no
    // children: number of children
    // salary: annual salary
    // this.taxAdminData: tax administration data
    //
    // tax calculation with children
    const result1 = this.calculateTax2(married, children, salary);
    const tax1 = result1["tax"];
    // tax calculation without the children
    let result2, tax2, halfShareCeiling;
    if (children !== 0) {
      result2 = this.calculateTax2(married, 0, salary);
      tax2 = result2["tax"];
      // applying the family quotient cap
      halfShareCeiling = this.taxAdminData.halfShareQfCeiling;
      if (children < 3) {
        // HALF_SHARE_QF_CEILING euros for the first 2 children
        tax2 = tax2 - children * halfShareCeiling;
      } else {
        // HALF_SHARE_QF_CEILING euros for the first 2 children, double for the following ones
        tax2 = tax2 - 2 * halfShareCeiling - (children - 2) * 2 * halfShareCeiling;
      }
    } else {
      // no recalculation of the tax
      tax2 = tax1;
      result2 = result1;
    }
    // we take the higher tax in [tax1, tax2]
    let tax, rate, surcharge;
    if (tax1 > tax2) {
      tax = tax1;
      rate = result1["rate"];
      surcharge = result1["surcharge"];
    } else {
      surcharge = tax2 - tax1 + result2["surcharge"];
      tax = tax2;
      rate = result2["rate"];
    }
    // calculation of a possible discount
    const discount = this.getDiscount(married, tax);
    tax -= discount;
    // calculation of a possible tax reduction
    const reduction = this.getReduction(married, salary, children, tax);
    tax -= reduction;
    // result
    return {
      "tax": Math.floor(tax), "surcharge": surcharge, "discount": discount, "reduction": reduction,
      "rate": rate
    };
  }

  // --------------------------------------------------------------------------
  calculateTax2(married: string, children: number, salary: number): any {
    // married: yes, no
    // children: number of children
    // salary: annual salary
    // this->taxAdminData: tax administration data
    // 
    // number of shares
    married = married.toLowerCase();
    let shares;
    if (married === "yes") {
      shares = children / 2 + 2;
    } else {
      shares = children / 2 + 1;
    }
    // 1 share per child from the 3rd one
    if (children >= 3) {
      // one more half-share for each child from the 3rd one
      shares += 0.5 * (children - 2);
    }
    // taxable income
    const taxableIncome = this.getTaxableIncome(salary);
    // surcharge
    let surcharge = Math.floor(taxableIncome - 0.9 * salary);
    // for rounding issues
    if (surcharge < 0) {
      surcharge = 0;
    }
    // family quotient
    const quotient = taxableIncome / shares;
    // tax calculation
    const limits = this.taxAdminData.limits;
    const coeffR = this.taxAdminData.coeffR;
    const coeffN = this.taxAdminData.coeffN;
    // is put at the end of the limits array to stop the following loop
    limits[limits.length - 1] = quotient;
    // looking for the tax rate
    let i = 0;
    while (quotient > limits[i]) {
      i++;
    }
    // because we placed quotient at the end of the limits array, the previous loop
    // cannot go beyond the limits array
    // now we can calculate the tax
    const tax = Math.floor(taxableIncome * coeffR[i] - shares * coeffN[i]);
    // result
    return { "tax": tax, "surcharge": surcharge, "rate": coeffR[i] };
  }

  // taxableIncome=annualSalary-allowance
  // the allowance has a min and a max
  getTaxableIncome(salary: number): number {
    // allowance of 10% of the salary
    let allowance = 0.1 * salary;
    // this allowance cannot exceed taxAdminData.getTenPercentAllowanceMax()
    if (allowance > this.taxAdminData.tenPercentAllowanceMax) {
      allowance = this.taxAdminData.tenPercentAllowanceMax;
    }
    // the allowance cannot be lower than taxAdminData.getTenPercentAllowanceMin()
    if (allowance < this.taxAdminData.tenPercentAllowanceMin) {
      allowance = this.taxAdminData.tenPercentAllowanceMin;
    }
    // taxable income
    const taxableIncome = salary - allowance;
    // result
    return Math.floor(taxableIncome);
  }

  // calculates a possible discount
  getDiscount(married: string, taxes: number): number {
    // initially, a zero discount
    let discount = 0;
    // maximum tax amount to get the discount
    let taxCeilingForDiscount = married === "yes" ?
      this.taxAdminData.coupleTaxCeilingForDiscount :
      this.taxAdminData.singleTaxCeilingForDiscount;
    let discountCeiling;
    if (taxes < taxCeilingForDiscount) {
      // maximum amount of the discount
      discountCeiling = married === "yes" ?
        this.taxAdminData.coupleDiscountCeiling :
        this.taxAdminData.singleDiscountCeiling;
      // theoretical discount
      discount = discountCeiling - 0.75 * taxes;
      // the discount cannot exceed the amount of the tax
      if (discount > taxes) {
        discount = taxes;
      }
      // no discount <0
      if (discount < 0) {
        discount = 0;
      }
    }
    // result
    return Math.ceil(discount);
  }

  // calculates a possible reduction
  getReduction(married: string, salary: number, children: number, taxes: number): number {
    // the income ceiling to be entitled to the 20% reduction
    let incomeCeilingForReduction = married === "yes" ?
      this.taxAdminData.coupleIncomeCeilingForReduction :
      this.taxAdminData.singleIncomeCeilingForReduction;
    incomeCeilingForReduction += children * this.taxAdminData.halfShareReductionValue;
    if (children > 2) {
      incomeCeilingForReduction += (children - 2) * this.taxAdminData.halfShareReductionValue;
    }
    // taxable income
    const taxableIncome = this.getTaxableIncome(salary);
    // reduction
    let reduction = 0;
    if (taxableIncome < incomeCeilingForReduction) {
      // 20% reduction
      reduction = 0.2 * taxes;
    }
    // result
    return Math.ceil(reduction);
  }
}

// exporting the class
export default Business;
  • line 8: taxAdminData: any — the exact structure of the data sent by the tax server (rates, thresholds, etc.) is not documented; we therefore remain intentionally flexible regarding this type rather than speculating on an uncertain interface;
  • The [Business] class is exported, line 191;

docs.title: 6.3.2. The class [Dao2]
docs.text:
The [Dao2] class implements the [dao] layer of the JavaScript client above as follows:

'use strict';

// imports
import { AxiosInstance, AxiosRequestConfig, AxiosResponse } from 'axios';
import qs from 'qs'

class Dao2 {

  private axios: AxiosInstance;
  private sessionCookieName: string;
  private sessionCookie: string;

  // constructor
  constructor(axios: AxiosInstance) {
    this.axios = axios;
    // session cookie
    this.sessionCookieName = "PHPSESSID";
    this.sessionCookie = '';
  }

  // init session
  async initSession(): Promise<any> {
    // options of the HTTP request [get /main.php?action=init-session&type=json]
    const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
      url: 'main.php',
      method: "GET",
      // URL parameters
      params: {
        action: 'init-session',
        type: 'json'
      }
    };
    // executing the HTTP request
    return await this.getRemoteData(options);
  }

  async authenticateUser(user: string, password: string): Promise<any> {
    // options of the HTTP request [post /main.php?action=authenticate-user]
    const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
      url: 'main.php',
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        'Content-type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded',
      },
      // body of the POST
      data: qs.stringify({
        user: user,
        password: password
      }),
      // URL parameters
      params: {
        action: 'authenticate-user'
      }
    };
    // executing the HTTP request
    return await this.getRemoteData(options);
  }

  async getAdminData(): Promise<any> {
    // options of the HTTP request  [get /main.php?action=get-admindata]
    const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
      url: 'main.php',
      method: "GET",
      // URL parameters
      params: {
        action: 'get-admindata'
      }
    };
    // executing the HTTP request
    const data = await this.getRemoteData(options);
    // result
    return data;
  }

  async getRemoteData(options: AxiosRequestConfig): Promise<any> {
    // for the session cookie
    if (!options.headers) {
      options.headers = {} as any;
    }
    (options.headers as any).Cookie = this.sessionCookie;
    // executing the HTTP request
    let response: AxiosResponse;
    try {
      // asynchronous request
      response = await this.axios.request(options);
    } catch (error: any) {
      // the [error] parameter is an exception instance - it can take various forms
      if (error.response) {
        // the server's response is in [error.response]
        response = error.response;
      } else {
        // we rethrow the error
        throw error;
      }
    }
    // response is the whole HTTP response of the server (HTTP headers + the response itself)
    // we retrieve the session cookie if it exists
    const setCookie = response.headers['set-cookie'];
    if (setCookie) {
      // setCookie is an array
      // we look for the session cookie in this array
      let found = false;
      let i = 0;
      while (!found && i < setCookie.length) {
        // we look for the session cookie
        const results = RegExp('^(' + this.sessionCookieName + '.+?);').exec(setCookie[i]);
        if (results) {
          // we store the session cookie
          // eslint-disable-next-line require-atomic-updates
          this.sessionCookie = results[1];
          // we found it
          found = true;
        } else {
          // next element
          i++;
        }
      }
    }
    // the server's response is in [response.data]
    return response.data;
  }
}

// exporting the class
export default Dao2;

Comments

  • The [Dao2] class implements only three of the possible requests to the tax calculation server:
    • [init-session] (lines 21–35): to initialize the jSON session;
    • [authenticate-user] (lines 37–57): to authenticate;
    • [get-admindata] (lines 59–73): to retrieve data from the tax authority that will enable tax calculations to be performed on the client side;

We will now use Postman (see the section “Postman Tests”) to demonstrate how the [get-admindata] action works. If you haven’t already done so, import (Ctrl-O) the HTTP request collection—stored in the [tax-servers-tests.postman_collection.json] file within the [php_server] folder—into Postman:

docs.title: 6.3.3. The script [main2]
docs.text:
This script initializes the session, authenticates, retrieves the tax data, and then performs the tax calculations locally via the business layer—these calculations no longer involve the server:

// imports
import axios from 'axios';

// imports
import Dao from './Dao2.js';
import Business from './Business.js';

// asynchronous [main] function
async function main(): Promise<void> {
  // axios configuration
  axios.defaults.timeout = 2000;
  axios.defaults.baseURL = 'http://localhost';
  // instantiating the [dao] layer
  const dao = new Dao(axios);
  // HTTP requests
  let taxAdminData: any;
  try {
    // init session
    log("-----------init-session");
    let response = await dao.initSession();
    log(response);
    // authentication
    log("-----------authenticate-user");
    response = await dao.authenticateUser("admin", "admin");
    log(response);
    // tax data
    log("-----------get-admindata");
    response = await dao.getAdminData();
    log(response);
    taxAdminData = response.response;
  } catch (error: any) {
    // we log the error
    console.log("error=", error.message);
    // end
    return;
  }

  // instantiating the [business] layer
  const business = new Business(taxAdminData);

  // tax calculations
  log("-----------calculate-tax x 3");
  const simulations: any[] = [];
  simulations.push(business.calculateTax("yes", 2, 45000));
  simulations.push(business.calculateTax("no", 2, 45000));
  simulations.push(business.calculateTax("no", 1, 30000));
  // list of simulations
  log("-----------list-of-simulations");
  log(simulations);
  // deleting a simulation
  log("-----------deleting simulation no. 1");
  simulations.splice(1, 1);
  log(simulations);
}

// JSON log
function log(object: unknown): void {
  console.log(JSON.stringify(object, null, 2));
}

// execution
main();
  • line 30: taxAdminData = response.response — the tax data, received only once from the server, is then reused locally for all calculations;
  • line 39: const business = new Business(taxAdminData) — the business layer is instantiated with this data, without ever making another network request;
  • lines 44–46: the three tax calculations are now synchronous, executed directly in the browser or node.js, without going through the server.

docs.title: 6.4. HTTP client 3
docs.text:
In this section, we run the [HTTP client 2] application in a browser according to the following architecture:

While [node.js] natively executes TypeScript via tsx, this is not the case for browsers: a tool is required to compile TypeScript into JavaScript, then assemble the whole into a single file that can be used by a HTML page. This is the role of [webpack].

Note: The [1] operation described above will be a HTTP request generated by the JavaScript code on a HTML page. We will see shortly that this HTML page is obtained via the URL [http://localhost:8080] (or 8081), requested from an internal server launched by [webpack]. The tax calculation server, on the other hand, is a NestJS application reachable at the URL [http://localhost:3000] (see Installing a NestJS Server). So here we have two web applications communicating with each other, both accessed via [http://localhost] but not from the same port. We say they are on different domains. This type of request between two web applications on different domains is controlled. By default, the NestJS server will reject requests from a web client if the client does not share the same origin as the server, i.e., [http://localhost:3000]. However, it is possible to configure the NestJS server to accept these so-called “cross-domain” requests. This has been done here. That is why the JavaScript client shown below will work. You can view the configuration of the NestJS server in the chapter “Case Study: The Tax Calculation Server in NestJS,” which shows how to configure it to accept cross-domain requests.

docs.title: 6.4.1. Changes to the Toolset Since 2019
docs.text:
The original document (2019) used [babel-loader] to transpile the ES6 code into ES5, which is compatible with older browsers. Since our project is now written in TypeScript, we are replacing babel-loader with [ts-loader], which natively supports the TypeScript syntax (types, interfaces, etc.)—something that Babel completely ignores.

The project’s [webpack.config.js] file (folder tax client/http client 3) configures the [webpack] module:

/* eslint-disable */

const path = require("path");
const webpack = require("webpack");

/*
 * SplitChunksPlugin is enabled by default and replaced
 * deprecated CommonsChunkPlugin. It automatically identifies modules which
 * should be splitted of chunk by heuristics using module duplication count and
 * module category (i. e. node_modules). And splits the chunks…
 *
 * It is safe to remove "splitChunks" from the generated configuration
 * and was added as an educational example.
 *
 * https://webpack.js.org/plugins/split-chunks-plugin/
 *
 */

const HtmlWebpackPlugin = require("html-webpack-plugin");

/*
 * We've enabled HtmlWebpackPlugin for you! This generates a html
 * page for you when you compile webpack, which will make you start
 * developing and prototyping faster.
 *
 * https://github.com/jantimon/html-webpack-plugin
 *
 */

// [TypeScript update] the sources are now in .ts: webpack must resolve them
// (resolve.extensions) and compile them with [ts-loader] instead of
// [babel-loader] (which does not understand TypeScript syntax: types, interfaces, ...)
module.exports = {
  mode: "development",
  //entry: "./src/main3.ts",
  entry: "./src/index.ts",
  output: {
    filename: "[name].[chunkhash].js",
    path: path.resolve(__dirname, "dist")
  },

  resolve: {
    extensions: [".ts", ".js"]
  },

  plugins: [new webpack.ProgressPlugin(), new HtmlWebpackPlugin()],

  module: {
    rules: [
      {
        test: /\.ts$/,
        include: [path.resolve(__dirname, "src")],
        loader: "ts-loader"
      }
    ]
  },

  optimization: {
    splitChunks: {
      cacheGroups: {
        vendors: {
          priority: -10,
          test: /[\\/]node_modules[\\/]/
        }
      },

      chunks: "async",
      minChunks: 1,
      minSize: 30000,
      name: true
    }
  },

  devServer: {
    open: true
  }
};
  • line 36: entry: "./src/index.ts" — Webpack starts with this file and follows all its imports to build the final bundle;
  • lines 42–44: resolve: { extensions: [".ts", ".js"] } — tells Webpack to also resolve .ts files even if the extension isn’t specified in the imports;
  • lines 48–56: the rule that associates every .ts file in the src folder with the [ts-loader] loader — this is the direct replacement for babel-loader mentioned above.

The contents of the [./src/index.ts] file are as follows:

console.log("Hello, world");

Keep in mind that the JavaScript code will be executed in a browser. Therefore, the previous line will not be written to a terminal but to the console of the browser running this code.

The file [package.json] in this subproject is as follows. It has its own scripts and dependencies (ts-loader, TypeScript, as well as core-js and regenerator-runtime, which are polyfills to ensure compatibility with older browsers):

  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "My webpack project",

    "build": "webpack",
    "start": "webpack-dev-server"
  },

  "devDependencies": {
    "@webpack-cli/init": "^0.2.2",
    "html-webpack-plugin": "^3.2.0",
    "ts-loader": "^8.4.0",
    "typescript": "^5.6.0",
    "webpack": "^4.40.2",
    "webpack-cli": "^3.3.9",
    "webpack-dev-server": "^3.8.1"
  },

    "axios": "^1.7.0",

}
  • lines 12–20: dependencies required during project development (compilation);

  • lines 21–26: dependencies required when running the project;

  • line 17: [webpack]: the orchestrator. [webpack] performs the transpilation of the codes TypeScript → ES5, and then assembles all the resulting files into a single file;

  • line 18: [webpack-cli]: required by [webpack];
  • line 13: [@webpack-cli/init]: used to configure [webpack];
  • line 19: [webpack-dev-server]: provides a development web server that runs by default on ports 8080 or 8081. When the source files are modified, [webpack-dev-server] automatically reloads the web application;

docs.title: 6.4.2. Compiling and Running the Project
docs.text:
The file [package.json] defines three tasks, [npm]:

  "scripts": {
    "test": "echo \"Error: no test specified\" && exit 1",
    "build": "webpack",
    "start": "webpack-dev-server"
  },

These tasks are recognized by [VSCode], which offers them for execution. Hover your mouse over the “build” task on line 3:

Simply click on [Run Script] to run the selected task. You can also type the following command:

npm run build

in a terminal located in the folder containing the file [package.json].

The task [build] creates a folder named [dist] (1) within the project VSCode:

  • In [3]: the project is compiled into [dist/main.hash.js], and a page named [dist/index.html] is created (2);

The generated page [index.html] is as follows:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Webpack App</title>
  </head>
  <body>
  <script type="text/javascript" src="main.e771aaace94e5be51a5a.js"></script></body>
</html>

This page therefore simply encapsulates the [main.hash.js] file generated by [webpack].

The project is executed by the task [start]:

npm run start

The page [dist/index.html] is then loaded onto a server—part of the [webpack] suite—running on port 8080 or 8081 of the local machine and displayed by the machine’s default browser:

  • in [2], the service port of the [webpack] web server;
  • to [3-4], the [console] tab in the browser’s developer tools, in this case Microsoft Edge (set to F12);
  • in [5], the result of executing the file [src/index.ts]. Recall that the contents of that file were as follows:
console.log("Hello, world");

Now, let’s change that content to the following line in [index.ts]:

console.log("Hello World");

and save the file. Automatically (without recompiling), a new file named [index.html] is generated, and this new file, [index.html], is loaded into the browser:

It is not necessary to run the [build] task before the [start] task: the latter first compiles the project. It does not store the output of this compilation in the [dist] folder. To verify this, simply delete that folder. You will then see that the task [start] compiles and runs the project without creating the [dist] folder. It appears to store its [index.html, main.hash.js] output in a folder specific to [webpack-dev-server]. This behavior is sufficient for our tests.

When the development server is running, any saved change to one of the project files triggers a recompilation. For this reason, we disable the [Auto Save] mode of [VSCode]. This is because we do not want a recompilation to occur every time characters are typed into one of the project files. We only want a recompilation to occur when changes are saved:

  • In [2], the [Auto Save] option must not be checked;

docs.text:
To test the JavaScript web client for the tax calculation server, you must specify [main3.ts] [1] as the project entry point in the file [webpack.config.js] [2-3]:

  • In [1], the script [main3.ts];

docs.title: 6.4.3.1. The [main3] script
docs.text:
This script uses the content from main2.ts (previous chapter), adapted for a browser (importing polyfills):

// imports
import axios from 'axios';
import "core-js/stable";
import "regenerator-runtime/runtime";

// imports
import Dao from './Dao3';
import Business from './Business';

// asynchronous [main] function
async function main(): Promise<void> {
  // axios configuration
  axios.defaults.timeout = 2000;
  axios.defaults.baseURL = 'http://localhost:3000/';
  axios.defaults.withCredentials = true;
  // instantiating the [dao] layer
  const dao = new Dao(axios);
  // HTTP requests
  let taxAdminData: any;
  try {
    // init session
    log("-----------init-session");
    let response = await dao.initSession();
    log(response);
    if (response.status != 700) {
      throw new Error(JSON.stringify(response.response));
    }
    // authentication
    log("-----------authenticate-user");
    response = await dao.authenticateUser("admin", "admin");
    log(response);
    if (response.status != 200) {
      throw new Error(JSON.stringify(response.response));
    }
    // tax data
    log("-----------get-admindata");
    response = await dao.getAdminData();
    log(response);
    if (response.status != 1000) {
      throw new Error(JSON.stringify(response.response));
    }
    taxAdminData = response.response;
  } catch (error: any) {
    // we log the error
    console.log("error=", error.message);
    // end
    return;
  }

  // instantiating the [business] layer
  const business = new Business(taxAdminData);

  // tax calculations
  log("-----------calculate-tax x 3");
  const simulations: any[] = [];
  simulations.push(business.calculateTax("yes", 2, 45000));
  simulations.push(business.calculateTax("no", 2, 45000));
  simulations.push(business.calculateTax("no", 1, 30000));
  // list of simulations
  log("-----------list-of-simulations");
  log(simulations);
  // deleting a simulation
  log("-----------deleting simulation no. 1");
  simulations.splice(1, 1);
  log(simulations);
}

// JSON log
function log(object: unknown): void {
  console.log(JSON.stringify(object, null, 2));
}

// execution
main();
  • Lines 3–4: import "core-js/stable" and import "regenerator-runtime/runtime" — the polyfills needed for the compiled code to work in browsers that do not yet natively implement all the latest language features;
  • line 15: axios.defaults.withCredentials = true — essential in a browser so that session cookies are automatically passed between requests, which the code did manually in previous versions (node.js does not support browser cookies).

docs.title: 6.4.3.2. The [Dao3] class
docs.text:
Since the session cookie is now managed by the [axios] module, we can remove the handling of this cookie from the [Dao] class:

'use strict';

// imports
import { AxiosInstance, AxiosRequestConfig, AxiosResponse } from 'axios';
import qs from 'qs'

class Dao3 {

  private axios: AxiosInstance;

  // constructor
  constructor(axios: AxiosInstance) {
    this.axios = axios;
  }

  // init session
  async initSession(): Promise<any> {
    // options of the HTTP request [get /main.php?action=init-session&type=json]
    const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
      url: 'main.php',
      method: "GET",
      // URL parameters
      params: {
        action: 'init-session',
        type: 'json'
      }
    };
    // executing the HTTP request
    return await this.getRemoteData(options);
  }

  async authenticateUser(user: string, password: string): Promise<any> {
    // options of the HTTP request [post /main.php?action=authenticate-user]
    const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
      url: 'main.php',
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        'Content-type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded',
      },
      // body of the POST
      data: qs.stringify({
        user: user,
        password: password
      }),
      // URL parameters
      params: {
        action: 'authenticate-user'
      }
    };
    // executing the HTTP request
    return await this.getRemoteData(options);
  }

  async getAdminData(): Promise<any> {
    // options of the HTTP request  [get /main.php?action=get-admindata]
    const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
      url: 'main.php',
      method: "GET",
      // URL parameters
      params: {
        action: 'get-admindata'
      }
    };
    // executing the HTTP request
    const data = await this.getRemoteData(options);
    // result
    return data;
  }

  async getRemoteData(options: AxiosRequestConfig): Promise<any> {
    // executing the HTTP request
    let response: AxiosResponse;
    try {
      // asynchronous request
      response = await this.axios.request(options);
    } catch (error: any) {
      // the [error] parameter is an exception instance - it can take various forms
      if (error.response) {
        // the server's response is in [error.response]
        response = error.response;
      } else {
        // we rethrow the error
        throw error;
      }
    }
    // response is the whole HTTP response of the server (HTTP headers + the response itself)
    // the server's response is in [response.data]
    return response.data;
  }
}

// exporting the class
export default Dao3;

In this code, there is no longer any cookie handling.

docs.text:
The package.json file defines two npm tasks:

  • [npm run build] — compiles the project; the resulting files are placed in dist/ (a main.<hash>.js file, and a index.html file that automatically integrates it using the html-webpack-plugin);
  • [npm start] — starts webpack-dev-server: compiles the project and serves it at http://localhost:8080, with automatic page reloading every time a source file is saved.

We run these two tasks. The result on the [console] page in the browser (run F12) is as follows:

docs.title: 6.5. Client HTML
docs.text:
The previous sections used the [http client 3] client exclusively in console mode: the [main3.ts] script communicates with the server and then displays its results using console.log, without any page visible in the browser. We will now build a true graphical client, complete with screens (authentication, tax calculation, list of simulations).

We’ll start with the [http client 3] client project (same files as [package.json] and [tsconfig.json]) and reuse two existing files without modifying them: [Dao3.ts] (layer [dao]) and [Business.ts] (layer [business], already discussed in connection with [main3.ts]). We are only adding:

  • a file named [src/index.html], which serves as a template for the page (header, CSS styles, area where views are displayed);
  • a new file, [Views.ts], which constructs the elements HTML (forms, table, error messages) directly in JavaScript, without ever calling the server itself;
  • a new file, [AppHtml.ts], the application controller: it coordinates the [dao] and [business] layers, then instructs the [views] layer to display the result;
  • a minor modification to [webpack.config.js] so that the project compiles this new entry point with the new template HTML.

The quartet [dao] / [business] / [views] / controller thus replicates, exactly, the layered architecture already covered in this course: the [dao] layer for server access, the [business] layer for application logic (tax calculation), and the main script (here, the [AppHtml] class) for orchestration. Only the [views] layer is truly new: it replaces the console output with browser output.

docs.title: 6.5.1. Solution Architecture
docs.text:
This client, HTML, operates exactly the same way as [main3.ts], and this is a key design choice: it only calls the server (PHP) for three actions—always the same ones: init-session, authenticate-user, and get-admindata. However, the server’s code (PHP) shows that it is also capable of calculating the tax itself and storing the simulations in its session (this is what the actions calculate-tax, list-simulations, and delete-simulation, found in the [Controllers] folder)—but this client does not use them.

The reason is simple: once the tax data (rates, thresholds, etc.) has been retrieved just once using get-admindata, everything needed to calculate the tax is already in the browser, thanks to the [Business] class. Requesting this calculation from the server for each simulation would require an avoidable round trip over the network; likewise, since each calculated simulation is immediately stored in the browser, requesting the list again from the server (list-simulations) would add no value. This client therefore minimizes server requests as much as possible—exactly the principle already implemented in [main3.ts]:

  • the [dao] layer ([Dao3.ts]) remains unchanged: its three methods already presented above (initSession, authenticateUser, getAdminData) are sufficient; none are added to it;
  • immediately after successful authentication, getAdminData is called once and for all, and its result is used to construct a Business object (new Business(taxAdminData)), which is retained throughout the entire work session;
  • each tax calculation then directly calls business.calculateTax(married, children, salary)—an ordinary JavaScript function, executed in the browser, without any network calls;
  • the calculated simulations are stored in a simple array JavaScript, kept in memory by the controller—one push per calculation, one splice per deletion, exactly as [main3.ts] does with its instructions simulations.push(...) and simulations.splice(1, 1).

A slight difference from [main3.ts]: the business.calculateTax method returns only the values it has calculated (tax, surcharge, discount, reduction, rate), not the parameters entered by the user (married, children, salary). [main3.ts] doesn’t need them, since it simply uses console.log; but our view [List of simulations] must display these three parameters in the table—so the controller attaches them to the result itself before storing it (we’ll see this in the code for [AppHtml.ts]).

Finally, the [End of session] view no longer makes a call to the server either: it simply discards the [Business] object and the list of simulations, then redisplays the authentication screen. Recall that the responses from the three server actions still in use always have the same format, which we’ve already seen in [main3.ts]: a JSON object { action, status, response }, where response contains either the requested result (if successful) or an error message—a string or an array of strings, depending on the relevant PHP controller.

docs.title: 6.5.1.1. The HTML template: the [src/index.html] file
docs.text:
A [webpack] project using [html-webpack-plugin] (as is the case here; see the [webpack.config.js] file) can start with a ready-made HTML page—a “template — into which the plugin will automatically insert the <script> tag that loads the compiled bundle. Until now, this project did not have a template: [html-webpack-plugin] generated a minimal, empty, unstyled HTML page. We are now providing one: the file [src/index.html], which contains:

  • a <style> block containing all the application’s formatting (header, menu, forms, table, error and result messages);
  • a single <div id="app"></div> tag: this is the only “visible” HTML element in the template—the rest of the page (header, forms, table, etc.) will be dynamically generated in JavaScript by the [Views] class, inside this tag.
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8" />
  <title>Tax application</title>
  <style>
    :root {
      --title-blue: #1976d2;
      --light-blue: #d6e9f8;
      --light-blue-border: #b6d7f0;
      --light-green: #dcedc8;
      --light-green-border: #b9d999;
      --banner-grey: #e8eaed;
      --text-grey: #333;
      --link-blue: #1a73e8;
    }

    * {
      box-sizing: border-box;
    }

    body {
      margin: 0;
      font-family: -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Arial, sans-serif;
      color: var(--text-grey);
      background: #ffffff;
    }

    #app {
      max-width: 900px;
      margin: 20px auto;
      border: 1px solid #ddd;
    }

    /* ---------- banner ---------- */
    .banner {
      display: flex;
      align-items: center;
      gap: 24px;
      background: var(--banner-grey);
      padding: 20px 30px;
    }

    .banner .logo {
      flex: none;
    }

    .banner h1 {
      margin: 0;
      font-size: 28px;
      font-weight: 400;
      color: #444;
    }

    /* ---------- page body ---------- */
    .page-body {
      display: flex;
      min-height: 320px;
    }

    .menu {
      flex: 0 0 160px;
      padding: 24px 16px;
      border-right: 1px solid #eee;
    }

    .menu a {
      display: block;
      color: var(--link-blue);
      text-decoration: none;
      margin-bottom: 14px;
      cursor: pointer;
      font-size: 14px;
    }

    .menu a:hover {
      text-decoration: underline;
    }

    .content {
      flex: 1;
      padding: 24px 30px;
    }

    .content.full-width {
      flex: 1 1 100%;
    }

    /* ---------- section title ---------- */
    .section-title {
      background: var(--light-blue);
      border: 1px solid var(--light-blue-border);
      padding: 10px 16px;
      font-size: 16px;
      margin-bottom: 20px;
    }

    /* ---------- forms ---------- */
    .field-row {
      display: flex;
      align-items: center;
      margin-bottom: 16px;
    }

    .field-row label {
      flex: 0 0 220px;
      font-size: 14px;
    }

    .field-row .field {
      display: flex;
      flex-direction: column;
    }

    .field-row input[type="text"],
    .field-row input[type="password"],
    .field-row input[type="number"] {
      padding: 6px 8px;
      border: 1px solid #bbb;
      border-radius: 3px;
      font-size: 14px;
      width: 160px;
    }

    .field-row .help {
      font-size: 11px;
      color: #888;
      margin-top: 3px;
    }

    .radios label {
      flex: none;
      font-weight: normal;
      margin-right: 12px;
    }

    button, .btn-submit {
      background: #2196f3;
      color: #fff;
      border: none;
      border-radius: 3px;
      padding: 8px 20px;
      font-size: 14px;
      cursor: pointer;
    }

    button:hover {
      background: #1976d2;
    }

    /* ---------- result / error ---------- */
    .result {
      background: var(--light-green);
      border: 1px solid var(--light-green-border);
      padding: 14px 18px;
      margin-top: 20px;
      font-size: 14px;
      line-height: 1.7;
    }

    .error {
      background: #fde8e8;
      border: 1px solid #f3b4b4;
      color: #a02020;
      padding: 12px 16px;
      margin-bottom: 16px;
      font-size: 14px;
    }

    /* ---------- table of simulations ---------- */
    table.simulations {
      border-collapse: collapse;
      width: 100%;
      font-size: 13px;
    }

    table.simulations th,
    table.simulations td {
      border: 1px solid #ddd;
      padding: 8px 10px;
      text-align: right;
    }

    table.simulations th:first-child,
    table.simulations td:first-child,
    table.simulations th:nth-child(2),
    table.simulations td:nth-child(2) {
      text-align: left;
    }

    table.simulations th {
      background: #f5f5f5;
      font-weight: 600;
    }

    table.simulations a.delete {
      color: var(--link-blue);
      cursor: pointer;
      text-decoration: none;
    }

    table.simulations a.delete:hover {
      text-decoration: underline;
    }

    .simulations-empty {
      font-size: 14px;
      color: #777;
      font-style: italic;
    }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <div id="app"></div>
</body>
</html>

This is a standard HTML/CSS file—nothing specific to TypeScript here—but since the audience for this course is beginner-level, let’s go over the most important points in detail:

The CSS variables (lines 7–16):

  • The block :root { --name: value; ... } declares CSS variables (also called “custom properties”): --light-blue, --light-green, etc.;
  • these are then reused throughout the rest of the stylesheet using the var(...) function, for example, background: var(--banner-grey); on line 40;
  • The benefit: changing the color once at the top of the file is enough to change it everywhere it’s used, rather than having to search for each color code throughout the entire file.

The general structure (lines 29–87):

  • #app (line 29) limits the width of the application and adds a border;
  • .banner (line 36) displays the logo and title side by side using display: flex;
  • .page-body (line 56) divides the rest of the page into two flexible columns: .menu (line 61, fixed width of 160 pixels) on the left, and .content (line 80, variable width) on the right; The .content.full-width class (line 85) hides this menu column for the login view, which does not need it.

Classes reused by the [views] layer (lines 90–210):

  • .section-title (line 90): the light blue box used for the titles “Please authenticate,” “Fill in the form below and then submit it,” and “List of your simulations”;
  • .field-row (line 99): a form row (label + input field);
  • .result (line 152): the light green box that displays the result of a tax calculation;
  • .error (line 161): the light red box that displays an error message returned by the server;
  • table.simulations (line 171): the formatting of the table in the “simulation list” view, with its blue “Delete” links (rule table.simulations a.delete, line 196).

Each of these classes can be found in the code of class [Views] (className = '...' or classList.add('...'))—it is this class that, in JavaScript, creates the HTML elements and applies these CSS classes to them.

docs.title: 6.5.1.2. The modified [webpack.config.js] configuration
docs.text:
The [webpack.config.js] file has already been presented in its entirety earlier in this chapter. Two small changes are all that’s needed for it to compile this new graphical client rather than the [main3.ts] test script:

module.exports = {
  mode: "development",
  // HTML client (authentication / calculation / list of simulations views)
  entry: "./src/AppHtml.ts",
  // initial entry point of the project (console test of the [dao]/[business] layers),
  // kept for reference - you can go back to it by commenting out the line above
  //entry: "./src/main3.ts",
  //entry: "./src/index.ts",
  output: {
    filename: "[name].[chunkhash].js",
    path: path.resolve(__dirname, "dist")
  },

  resolve: {
    extensions: [".ts", ".js"]
  },

  plugins: [
    new webpack.ProgressPlugin(),
    // template specific to the HTML client (banner, styles, <div id="app">)
    new HtmlWebpackPlugin({
      template: path.resolve(__dirname, "src/index.html")
    })
  ],
  • line 4: entry: "./src/AppHtml.ts" replaces entry: "./src/main3.ts"—the new controller now serves as the entry point for the bundle; the old value is kept just below, as a comment (lines 5–8), so you can easily revert to the test script if needed;
  • lines 21–23: new HtmlWebpackPlugin({ template: ... }) replaces new HtmlWebpackPlugin() (without parameters)—we explicitly instruct it to use our template [src/index.html] rather than generating an empty HTML page.

docs.title: 6.5.1.3. The [dao] and [business] layers: two files reused without modification
docs.text:
The file [Dao3.ts] is not modified here: its three methods already presented earlier in this chapter (initSession, authenticateUser, getAdminData, plus the utility getRemoteData) are exactly what this graphical client needs—none are added.

[Business.ts] is not modified either: it is the same class [Business], with its method calculateTax(married, children, salary), which was already presented in full in the discussion of [main3.ts] (section [Client HTTP 2]). This graphical client, however, is the first in this chapter to actually display the results of this calculation on screen rather than simply logging them — this is an opportunity to verify that the [views] layer, presented immediately afterward, can format them correctly.

docs.title: 6.5.1.4. The [views] layer: the [Views.ts] file
docs.text:
This is the longest file in this client, but also the easiest to understand once you grasp its principle: the [Views] class does not make any network calls—it isn’t even aware of the existence of the PHP server. Its sole purpose is to construct, using the functions of DOM (document.createElement, appendChild, classList...), the HTML elements of the application’s three screens, within the <div id="app"> tag of the template.

When the user clicks a button or a link (“Submit,” “Delete,” “End of session,” etc.), the [Views] class also doesn’t know what to do with that click: it simply calls a callback function provided by the controller—it is the controller, [AppHtml.ts], described shortly thereafter, that then decides what to do (call the server, change the view, etc.). This decoupling is what allows [Views.ts] to remain independent of the [dao] layer.


'use strict';

// -----------------------------------------------------------------------
// construction of the application's views (DOM) - modelled on the
// screenshots of the document [web_application_views.odt]:
//   - authentication view
//   - tax calculation view (form + result)
//   - list of simulations view
// This module makes no network call: it builds the DOM and delegates
// the user's actions (Submit, Delete, menu links) to callback
// functions supplied by the [App] controller.
// -----------------------------------------------------------------------

// a generic decoration (not the photo of the original PHP server, which we
// do not have): replace it if needed with the real logo in [Resources/]
const LOGO_SVG = `
<svg width="60" height="60" viewBox="0 0 60 60" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <circle cx="30" cy="30" r="29" fill="#eef1ec" stroke="#ccc" />
  <g fill="none" stroke="#8a9a7a" stroke-width="2">
    <path d="M30 46 C30 32 22 28 17 19" />
    <path d="M30 46 C30 30 39 26 44 17" />
    <path d="M30 46 C30 37 30 30 30 21" />
  </g>
  <g fill="#b9c9a6">
    <circle cx="17" cy="19" r="4.5" />
    <circle cx="44" cy="17" r="4.5" />
    <circle cx="30" cy="19" r="4.5" />
  </g>
</svg>`;
