docs.title: 3.2.5. script [arr-05]
docs.text:
[NEW since 2019] This script demonstrates the new array methods introduced between 2022 and 2023:

'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW since 2019] new array methods
// ========================================================================

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 1) at(index)  (ECMAScript 2022)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// before, to access the last element of an array, we wrote arr[arr.length - 1]
const arr: number[] = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50];
console.log("arr[arr.length - 1] =", arr[arr.length - 1]); // old way
console.log("arr.at(-1) =", arr.at(-1)); // -> last element, more readable
console.log("arr.at(-2) =", arr.at(-2)); // -> second-to-last element
console.log("arr.at(0)  =", arr.at(0));  // -> equivalent to arr[0]
// .at also works on character strings
console.log("'hello'.at(-1) =", "hello".at(-1));

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 2) findLast() and findLastIndex()  (ECMAScript 2023)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// symmetrical to find() / findIndex()
const numbers: number[] = [5, 12, 8, 21, 3, 17];
const lastEven = numbers.findLast(n => n % 2 === 0);
console.log("last even number =", lastEven); // -> 8 
const lastEvenIndex = numbers.findLastIndex(n => n % 2 === 0);
console.log("index of the last even number =", lastEvenIndex);

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 3) the "immutable" methods  (ECMAScript 2023)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// sort(), reverse(), splice() modify the original array (side effect) - cf arr-04.js
// their "to..." equivalents return a NEW array and leave the original intact
// [(number | string)[]] because toSpliced() inserts strings into this array further down
const original: (number | string)[] = [4, 5, 4, 2];

// toSorted: like sort(), but without modifying the original
const sorted = original.toSorted();
console.log("original =", original, " (unchanged)");
console.log("sorted =", sorted);

// toReversed: like reverse(), but without modifying the original
const reversed = original.toReversed();
console.log("reversed =", reversed, ", original still =", original);

// toSpliced: like splice(), but without modifying the original
// toSpliced(startIndex, countToDelete, ...elements to insert)
const modified: (number | string)[] = original.toSpliced(1, 2, "a", "b", "c");
console.log("modified =", modified, ", original still =", original);

// with(index, value): returns a copy of the array with a single element replaced
const replaced = original.with(0, 999);
console.log("replaced =", replaced, ", original still =", original);

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// why it is useful: these methods avoid side effects, which is
// particularly appreciated in front-end frameworks (React, Angular, Vue...)
// where we often have to produce a new state without modifying the old one.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  • [at(index)] (ES2022): secure and readable access, including with negative indices (at(-1) = last element) — more readable than arr[arr.length - 1];
  • [findLast]/[findLastIndex] (ES2023): same as find/findIndex, but returns the last element that satisfies the condition;
  • [toSorted], [toReversed], [toSpliced], [with] (ES2023): the immutable equivalents of sort, reverse, splice, and indexed assignment—they return a new array without modifying the original, unlike the methods in the arr-03 script. Very useful in front-end frameworks (React, Vue...) where you need to produce a new state without modifying the old one.

docs.title: 3.2.6. Conclusion
docs.text: The key takeaway from this chapter is that an array is an object referenced by a pointer, with no fixed size, and equipped with a rich set of methods—some of which modify the array in place (push, sort…), while others, more recent ones, consistently return a new array (toSorted, with…). The next chapter covers literal objects.

docs.title: 3.3. Literal Objects
docs.text: Here, we refer to “literal objects” as objects defined directly in the code, as opposed to instances of [class] (discussed in the chapter “Classes”). The scripts for this chapter are located in the [objects] folder of the project:

docs.title: 3.3.1. script [obj-01]
docs.text:
As with arrays, an object is accessed via a pointer. In TypeScript, you must also define the object's structure using an interface before you can dynamically add properties to it.

'use strict';
// an empty object
// interface: we announce in advance the properties we are going to add dynamically,
// because TypeScript (unlike JavaScript) requires knowing the shape of an object
interface Obj1 {
  prop1?: string;
  prop2?: number[];
  prop3?: boolean;
  [key: string]: unknown;
}
const obj1: Obj1 = {};
// the properties of the object can be created dynamically
obj1.prop1 = "abcd";
console.log('obj1=', obj1);
// another property
obj1.prop2 = [1, 2, 3];
console.log("obj1=", obj1);
// another property with a different notation
obj1['prop3'] = true;
console.log("obj1=", obj1);
// obj1 is a reference to the object (pointer), not the object itself
const obj2: Obj1 = obj1;
// obj2 and obj1 point to the same object
obj2.prop1 = "xyzt";
console.log("obj1=", obj1);
console.log("obj2=", obj2);
// the properties can be variables
const var1: string = 'prop1';
console.log('prop1=', obj1[var1]);
  • Lines 5–9: [interface] Obj1 declares in advance the properties that will be added (prop1, prop2, prop3, all optional with ?). The line [key: string]: unknown is an index signature: it also allows the addition of any other property not specified in advance;
  • line 19: obj1.prop3 can also be written as obj1['prop3']—this notation is essential when the property name is actually the value of a variable (lines 28–29);
  • lines 22–25: const obj2: Obj1 = obj1 is a reference copy, not a copy of the object—therefore, modifying obj2 also modifies what is seen through obj1, just as with arrays.
npx tsx objects/obj-01.ts

Execution result:

obj1= { prop1: 'abcd' }
obj1= { prop1: 'abcd', prop2: [ 1, 2, 3 ] }
obj1= { prop1: 'abcd', prop2: [ 1, 2, 3 ], prop3: true }
obj1= { prop1: 'xyzt', prop2: [ 1, 2, 3 ], prop3: true }
obj2= { prop1: 'xyzt', prop2: [ 1, 2, 3 ], prop3: true }
prop1= xyzt

docs.title: 3.3.2. script [obj-02]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates a multi-level object and introduces the global object [JSON], which converts an object to a string and vice versa.

'use strict';
// a multi-level object
interface PersonWithFamily {
  firstName: string;
  age: number;
  father: { firstName: string; age: number };
  mother: { firstName: string; age: number };
}
const person: PersonWithFamily = {
  firstName: "martin",
  age: 12,
  father: {
    firstName: "paul",
    age: 45
  },
  mother: {
    firstName: "micheline",
    age: 42
  }
}
// accessing the properties
console.log("person first name=", person.firstName);
console.log("mother first name=", person.mother.firstName);
person.mother.age = 40;
console.log("mother age=", person.mother.age);
// console.log can display objects
console.log("person=", person);
console.log("mother=", person.mother);
// we can also display the jSON string of the object
let json: string = JSON.stringify(person);
console.log("jSON=", json);
// we can read the jSON back
let person2: PersonWithFamily = JSON.parse(json);
console.log("father=", person2.father);
  • Lines 3–8: A [interface] can itself contain nested object types (father, mother);
  • line 30: [JSON.stringify] converts a TypeScript object into a JSON string;
  • line 33: [JSON.parse] does the reverse—note that the result is of type PersonWithFamily, which implies that the JSON string does indeed conform to this format (TypeScript does not check this at runtime, only at compile time).

mother first name= micheline

  firstName: 'martin',
  age: 12,
  father: { firstName: 'paul', age: 45 },
  mother: { firstName: 'micheline', age: 40 }
}
mother= { firstName: 'micheline', age: 40 }
jSON= {"firstName":"martin","age":12,"father":{"firstName":"paul","age":45},"mother":{"firstName":"micheline","age":40}}

docs.title: 3.3.3. script [obj-03]
docs.text:
This script introduces the concept of getters and setters for an object’s property:

'use strict';
// getters and setters of an object
interface PersonWithName {
  _name?: string;
  name: string;
}
const person: PersonWithName = {
  // getter
  get name() {
    console.log("name getter");
    return this._name as string;
  },
  // setter
  set name(aName: string) {
    console.log("name setter");
    this._name = aName;
  }
};
// setter
person.name = "Hercule";
// getter
console.log(person.name);
// the object itself
console.log("person=", person);
// this does not prevent accessing the [_name] property directly
person._name = "xyz";
console.log("person=", person);
  • Lines 3–6: the [interface] PersonWithName declares _name as an optional property (prefixed with an underscore by convention, to indicate that it is a “private” property, even though TypeScript does not prevent access to it—see true encapsulation with #field in the chapter “Classes”);
  • lines 8–11: [getter]—using the get keyword rather than a function—returns the value of _name;
  • lines 13–16: [setter]—using the set keyword—receives the assigned value and can validate it before storing it;
  • line 20: person.name = "Hercule" implicitly calls the setter;
  • line 22: person.name implicitly calls the getter;
  • line 26: nothing prevents direct access to _name—encapsulation by convention depends on the developer’s discipline.
npx tsx objects/obj-03.ts

Execution result:

name setter
name getter
Hercule
person= { name: [Getter/Setter], _name: 'Hercule' }
person= { name: [Getter/Setter], _name: 'xyz' }

Note that [console.log] displays [Getter/Setter] to indicate that "name" is managed by accessors rather than being a direct value.

docs.title: 3.3.4. script [obj-04]
docs.text:
Three ways to write a property name, two ways to access it, and a shorthand notation:

'use strict';
// the names of the properties of an object  can be literal [name], surrounded by apostrophes ['name']
// or by quotation marks ["name"]

interface FullName {
  lastName: string;
  firstName: string;
}

// literal
const obj1: FullName = {
  lastName: "martin",
  firstName: "jean"
};
console.log("firstName=", obj1.firstName);

// surrounded by apostrophes
const obj2: FullName = {
  'lastName': "martin",
  'firstName': "jean"
};
console.log("lastName=", obj2.lastName);

// surrounded by quotation marks
const obj3: FullName = {
  "lastName": "martin",
  "firstName": "jean"
};

// two possible syntaxes to access the [lastName] property
console.log("lastName=", obj3.lastName);
console.log("lastName=", obj3['lastName']);

// shorthand notation equivalent to {obj1:obj1, obj2:obj2}
const obj4 = {
  obj1, obj2
}

console.log("obj4=", obj4)
  • Property names can be written literally (name:), enclosed in single quotes ('name':), or enclosed in double quotes ("name":)—all three are equivalent;
  • Line 31: obj3.lastName and obj3['lastName'] access the same property;
  • Lines 34–36: const obj4 = { obj1, obj2 } is the shorthand notation for { obj1: obj1, obj2: obj2 }—widely used when grouping existing variables into an object.

docs.title: 3.3.5. script [obj-05]
docs.text:
An object literal can have properties of type function—this brings us closer to the concept of a class (properties + methods):

'use strict';

// an object can have properties of type [function]
interface PersonWithToString {
  firstName: string;
  age: number;
  father: { firstName: string; age: number };
  mother: { firstName: string; age: number };
  toString: () => string;
}
const person: PersonWithToString = {
  // properties
  firstName: "martin",
  age: 12,
  father: {
    firstName: "paul",
    age: 45
  },
  mother: {
    firstName: "micheline",
    age: 42
  },
  // method
  toString: function () {
    return JSON.stringify(this);
  }
}

// usage
console.log("person=", person);
console.log("person.toString=", person.toString());
  • line 4: [interface] declares toString: () => string—the type of a method is declared as that of a function property;
  • line 25: inside the method, [this] refers to the object itself—this.firstName is the “firstName” property of that object.

  firstName: 'martin',
  age: 12,
  father: { firstName: 'paul', age: 45 },
  mother: { firstName: 'micheline', age: 42 },
  toString: [Function: toString]
}
person.toString= {"firstName":"martin","age":12,"father":{"firstName":"paul","age":45},"mother":{"firstName":"micheline","age":42}}

docs.title: 3.3.6. script [obj-06]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates how to iterate through an object’s properties without knowing their names in advance:

'use strict';

// an object can have properties of type [function]
interface PersonWithToString {
  firstName: string;
  age: number;
  father: { firstName: string; age: number };
  mother: { firstName: string; age: number };
  toString: () => string;
  // index signature needed to allow the dynamic for..in traversal below
  [key: string]: unknown;
}
let person: PersonWithToString = {
  // properties
  firstName: "martin",
  age: 12,
  father: {
    firstName: "paul",
    age: 45
  },
  mother: {
    firstName: "micheline",
    age: 42
  },
  // method
  toString: function () {
    return JSON.stringify(this);
  }
}

// usage
console.log(person);
// properties
console.log("-----------------------");
for (const key in person) {
  // eslint-disable-next-line no-prototype-builtins
  if (person.hasOwnProperty(key)) {
    const element = person[key];
    console.log(key, "=", element);
  }
}
// to escape the eslint warning (1)
console.log("-----------------------");
for (const key in person) {
  if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(person, key)) {
    const element = person[key];
    console.log(key, "=", element);
  }
}
// to escape the eslint warning (2)
console.log("-----------------------");
for (const key in person) {
  // eslint-disable-next-line no-prototype-builtins
  if (person.hasOwnProperty(key)) {
    const element = person[key];
    console.log(key, "=", element);
  }
}
  • Line 11: The index signature [key: string]: unknown is required here so that TypeScript allows dynamic access to person[key] from the loop for...in;
  • Lines 35–41: for (const key in person) iterates through the property names. The hasOwnProperty test filters out any inherited properties (not present in this script, but a good practice to follow systematically);
  • this script offers three equivalent ways to write this test—the second (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(...)) is the most robust, while the third simply suppresses the corresponding ESLint warning. Since 2022, the Object.hasOwn() method (script obj-09, below) has made this choice unnecessary.

docs.title: 3.3.7. [obj-07] script
docs.text:
This script demonstrates object destructuring—a syntax that directly extracts properties into variables:

'use strict';
// destructuring

interface FullName {
  lastName: string;
  firstName: string;
}

// literal
const obj1: FullName = {
  lastName: "martin",
  firstName: "jean"
};

// destructuring obj1 into variables [n,p]
const { lastName: n, firstName: p } = obj1;
console.log("n=", n, "p=", p);

// destructuring obj1 into variables [n2,p2]
function f({ lastName: n2, firstName: p2 }: FullName): void {
  console.log("f-n2=", n2, "f-p2=", p2);
}
f(obj1);

// destructuring obj1 into variables [lastName,firstName]
function g({ lastName: lastName, firstName: firstName }: FullName): void {
  console.log("g-lastName=", lastName, "g-firstName=", firstName);
}
g(obj1);

// destructuring obj1 into variables [lastName,firstName]
// with shorthand notation equivalent to h({lastName:lastName,firstName:firstName})
function h({ lastName, firstName }: FullName): void {
  console.log("h-lastName=", lastName, "h-firstName=", firstName);
}
h(obj1);
  • line 16: const { lastName: n, firstName: p } = obj1 creates two variables n and p, equivalent to const n = obj1.lastName; const p = obj1.firstName;
  • lines 19–22, 24–27, 30–33: destructuring also works directly on function parameters—very common in TypeScript/React for extracting properties from a configuration object or props;
  • line 33: function h({ lastName, firstName }: FullName) is a shorthand for { lastName: lastName, firstName: firstName }—when the name of the created variable is identical to the property name, it can be omitted.

g-lastName= martin g-firstName= jean
h-lastName= martin h-firstName= jean

docs.title: 3.3.8. script [obj-08]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates how to create a shallow copy of an object using the spread operator ... :

'use strict'

// cloning objects
interface FullName {
  lastName: string;
  firstName: string;
}
const obj1: FullName = {
  lastName: "martin",
  firstName: "jean"
};

// clone of obj1 with the spread operator
const obj2: FullName = { ...obj1 }

// checks
// obj2 points to a copy of obj1
console.log("obj2===obj1 :", obj1 === obj2)
console.log("obj2=", obj2)

npx tsx objects/obj-08.ts

Execution result:

obj2===obj1 : false
obj2= { lastName: 'martin', firstName: 'jean' }
  • obj2===obj1 evaluates to false: the two references do not point to the same object;
  • obj2 does indeed contain a copy of obj1's properties—but be careful, as we'll see in the next script, it's only a shallow copy.

docs.title: 3.3.9. script [obj-09]
docs.text:
[NEW since 2019] This script demonstrates three useful additions introduced since 2020: [Object.hasOwn], [structuredClone], and the combination of optional chaining with null coalescing on nested objects.

'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW since 2019] object manipulation: some handy additions
// ========================================================================

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 1) Object.hasOwn(object, property)  (ECMAScript 2022)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// before, to know whether a property belongs directly to an object (and is not
// inherited through the prototype chain), we wrote:
//   object.hasOwnProperty(property)               -> can crash if the object redefines hasOwnProperty
//   Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(object, property)  -> correct but verbose (cf. objects/obj-06.js)
// [Object.hasOwn] does this job simply and without risk
interface FullName {
  lastName: string;
  firstName: string;
  [key: string]: unknown;
}
const person: FullName = { lastName: "Dupont", firstName: "Jean" };

console.log("Object.hasOwn(person, 'lastName') =", Object.hasOwn(person, "lastName"));
console.log("Object.hasOwn(person, 'age') =", Object.hasOwn(person, "age"));

// typical use in a traversal of properties
console.log("-----------------------");
for (const key in person) {
  if (Object.hasOwn(person, key)) {
    console.log(key, "=", person[key]);
  }
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 2) structuredClone(object)  (global API available since node 17)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// obj-08.js shows shallow cloning with the spread operator [...obj]
// but a spread only clones the 1st level: the sub-objects remain shared!
interface PersonWithAddress {
  lastName: string;
  address: { city: string; postalCode: string };
}
const original: PersonWithAddress = {
  lastName: "Dupont",
  address: { city: "Nantes", postalCode: "44000" }
};

// shallow cloning with spread
const shallowCopy: PersonWithAddress = { ...original };
shallowCopy.address.city = "Angers"; // also modifies the address of [original]!
console.log("shallow copy modified the original :", original.address.city === "Angers");

// reset for the next test
original.address.city = "Nantes";

// [structuredClone] does a deep clone: all the sub-objects are copied
const deepCopy: PersonWithAddress = structuredClone(original);
deepCopy.address.city = "Angers";
console.log("deep copy did not modify the original :", original.address.city === "Nantes");
console.log("original =", original);
console.log("deepCopy =", deepCopy);

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 3) optional chaining + nullish on nested object methods
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// very frequent combination in practice to read a partial configuration
interface AppearanceConfiguration {
  appearance?: { theme?: string };
}
function displayTheme(configuration?: AppearanceConfiguration): void {
  // if configuration, configuration.appearance or configuration.appearance.theme is missing,
  // we fall back on "light" without ever crashing
  const theme = configuration?.appearance?.theme ?? "light";
  console.log("theme =", theme);
}
displayTheme({ appearance: { theme: "dark" } });
displayTheme({ appearance: {} });
displayTheme({});
displayTheme(undefined);
  • [Object.hasOwn(object, property)] (ES2022) is a better replacement for object.hasOwnProperty(...) (see script obj-06): easier to read, and never encounters issues if the object itself redefines hasOwnProperty;
  • [structuredClone(object)] (available natively since Node 17) performs a deep clone: unlike the spread { ...obj } in the obj-08 script, which copies only the first level, structuredClone also copies the subobjects—modifying the copy never modifies the original, at any level;
  • the function displayTheme combines ?. and ?? to read a multi-level, potentially incomplete configuration without ever crashing and with a clear fallback value.

docs.title: 3.3.10. Conclusion
docs.text: The scripts in this chapter have shown that the TypeScript literal object is similar to a class instance: you can define properties, methods, and getters/setters—with the added benefit of a [interface] that precisely describes its form at compile time. It is a dynamic object, comparable to a dictionary, whose elements can be of any type, including functions.

docs.title: 3.4. Strings
docs.text: The scripts for this chapter are located in the [strings] folder of the project:

docs.title: 3.4.1. script [str-01]
docs.text:
The first thing to understand is that once a string is created, it can no longer be modified (it is immutable). There are many methods available to create a new string from the original one, but the original string always remains unchanged.

'use strict';

// character strings are read-only (they cannot be modified)

// a string
const string1: string = "abcd ";
// type
console.log("typeof(string1)=", typeof (string1));
// character no. 2
console.log("string1[2]=", string1[2]);
// causes an error
// [TypeScript update] TypeScript detects the error at compile time:
// a string only has read access by index
// @ts-expect-error : a character string is read-only
string1[2] = "0";
  • Line 10: string1[2] reads the third character of the string (index 0);
  • line 15: string1[2] = "0" attempts a write operation, which TypeScript rejects at compile time, thanks to @ts-expect-error—the comment above confirms that this error is expected and is intended precisely to demonstrate it.

Type checking:

npx tsc --noEmit

Execution result:

strings/str-01.ts(15,1): error TS2540: Cannot assign to '2' because it is a read-only property.

Execution with tsx (without prior type checking):

npx tsx strings/str-01.ts

Execution result:

typeof(string1)= string
string1[2]= c
TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property '2' of string 'abcd '
    at strings/str-01.ts:15:10

docs.title: 3.4.2. script [str-02]
docs.text:
A character string can be one of two types: [string] (literal string) or [object] (instance of the [String] class):

'use strict';

// character strings can be of two types

// a literal string
const string1: string = "abcd ";
// type
console.log("typeof(string1)=", typeof (string1));
// instance of String
// eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/ban-types -- here [String] (object) is the exact type wanted, not [string] (primitive): that is precisely the subject of the demo
const string2: String = new String("xyzt");
// type
console.log("typeof(string2)=", typeof (string2));
// other syntax (without new)
const string3: string = String("12 34");
// type
console.log("typeof(string3)=", typeof (string3));
// the [string] type and the [object] type offer the same methods, those of the String class
console.log("string1.length=", string1.length);
console.log("string2.length=", string2.length);
  • Line 6: The standard way to define a string—string1 will be of type string;
  • Line 11: new String(...) creates a string object—string2 will be of type object. Here, the declared TypeScript type is String (with a capital S), the *wrapper object* type, which is different from the primitive type string (lowercase);
  • Both types offer the same methods—those of the String class.
npx tsx strings/str-02.ts

Execution result:

typeof(string1)= string
typeof(string2)= object
typeof(string3)= string
string1.length= 5
string2.length= 4

docs.title: 3.4.3. script [str-03]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates variable interpolation in a string:

'use strict';

// string
const string: string = "Introduction to Javascript by example";
// string with variable interpolation
const str: string = `[${string}].substr(3, 2)=` + string.substr(3, 2)
console.log(str);
  • Line 6: A string enclosed in backticks (*backticks*, AltGr-7 on a French keyboard) can contain ${variable} expressions, which are replaced by the variable’s value—this is called a template string.
npx tsx strings/str-03.ts

Result of execution:

[Introduction to Javascript by example].substr(3, 2)=ro

docs.title: 3.4.4. script [str-04]
docs.text:
The template string alone is insufficient for precise formatting (width, alignment, decimal precision, etc.). For this purpose, we use an external package, [sprintf-js], which replicates the printf/sprintf functions familiar from other languages. It is installed with npm install sprintf-js and can be easily imported:

'use strict';
// using an external package to have the sprintf function
import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';
// string
const string: string = "Introduction to Javascript by example";
// method
console.log(sprintf("[%s].substr(3,2)=[%s]", string, string.substr(3, 2)));
Background: In 2019, the `import` statement caused issues with Node.js (which did not yet natively support ECMAScript modules) and required an intermediate package called `esm`. This is no longer the case since Node 12+: our project, with "type": "module" in package.json, uses import/export natively, without any additional configuration. 
npx tsx strings/str-04.ts

Execution result:

[Introduction to Javascript by example].substr(3,2)=[ro]

docs.title: 3.4.5. script [str-05]
docs.text:
The [sprintf] function accepts, as in C, "formats" introduced by %: %s (string), %d (integer), %f (floating-point), %j (JSON), %T (type), %t (boolean), along with width and alignment modifiers (%20s, %-20s, %04d...):

'use strict';
// using an external package to have the sprintf function
import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';
// string
const string: string = "Javascript";
// character strings
console.log(sprintf("[%s, %%s]=>[%s]", string, string));
console.log(sprintf("[%s, %%20s]=>[%20s]", string, string));
console.log(sprintf("[%s, %%-20s]=>[%-20s]", string, string));
// integers
console.log(sprintf("[%d, %%d]=>[%d]", 10, 10));
console.log(sprintf("[%d, %%4d]=>[%4d]", 10, 10));
console.log(sprintf("[%d, %%-4d]=>[%-4d]", 10, 10));
console.log(sprintf("[%d, %%04d]=>[%04d]", 10, 10));
// reals
console.log(sprintf("[%f, %%f]=>[%f]", -10.5, -10.5));
console.log(sprintf("[%f, %%10.2f]=>[%10.2f]", -10.5, -10.5));
console.log(sprintf("[%f, %%-10.2f]=>[%-10.2f]", -10.5, -10.5));
console.log(sprintf("[%f, %%010.3f]=>[%010.3f]", -10.5, -10.5));
// json
console.log(sprintf("person (%%j)=%j", { name: "mathieu", age: 34 }));
// type
console.log(sprintf("person type (%%T)=%T", { name: "mathieu", age: 34 }));
// boolean
console.log(sprintf("boolean (%%t)=%t", 4 === 4));

docs.title: 3.4.6. [str-06] script
docs.text:
This script lists the most common methods of the [String] class:

'use strict';
// using an external package to have the sprintf function
import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';
// string
const string: string = "  Introduction to Javascript ";
// some methods
// substr(10,2): 2 characters starting from no. 10
console.log(sprintf("[%s].substr(10,2)=[%s]", string, string.substr(10, 2)));
// trim: removal of the blanks at the start and end of the string (blank=\b \t \r \n \f)
console.log(sprintf("[%s].trim()=[%s]", string, string.trim()));
// toLowerCase: conversion to lowercase
console.log(sprintf("[%s].toLowerCase=[%s]", string, string.toLowerCase()));
// toUpperCase: conversion to uppercase
console.log(sprintf("[%s].toUpperCase=[%s]", string, string.toUpperCase()));
// indexOf: position of a searched string in the string, -1 if the substring does not exist
console.log(sprintf("[%s].indexOf('Java')=[%s]", string, string.indexOf('Java')));
console.log(sprintf("[%s].trim().indexOf('abcd')=[%s]", string, string.indexOf('abcd')));
// includes: true if the searched string is in the string
console.log(sprintf("[%s].includes('Java')=[%s]", string, string.includes('Java')));
// length: length of the string - it is not a method but a property
console.log(sprintf("[%s].length=[%s]", string, string.length));
// slice (7,10): string of characters no. 7 to 9
console.log(sprintf("[%s].slice(7,10)=[%s]", string, string.slice(7, 10)));
// match: looks for an expression in the string - this expression can be a regular expression
// /intro/i: regular expression designating the string [intro] in uppercase or lowercase
// returns the string found
console.log(sprintf("[%s].match(/intro/i)=[%s]", string, string.match(/intro/i)));
// replace: replaces string1 with string2 in string
// replaces the 1st occurrence of i with x
console.log(sprintf("[%s].replace('i','x')=[%s]", string, string.replace('i', 'x')));
// replaces all the occurrences of i with x
// /i/g is a regular expression designating all (g) the occurrences of i
console.log(sprintf("[%s].replace(/i/g,'x')=[%s]", string, string.replace(/i/g, 'x')));
// split: divides the string into words separated by the split parameter
// returns the array of these words
// /\s*/: words separated by 0 or more spaces
console.log(sprintf("[%s].split(/\\s*/)=[%s]", string, string.split(/\s*/)));
// /\s+/: words separated by one or more spaces
console.log(sprintf("[%s].split(/\\s+/)=[%s]", string, string.split(/\s+/)));
  • [trim] removes leading and trailing whitespace; [toLowerCase]/[toUpperCase] change case;
  • [indexOf] returns the position of a substring (-1 if absent); [includes] returns a Boolean;
  • [slice] extracts a substring by position; [match] matches the string against a regular expression (see the next chapter);
  • [replace] replaces the first occurrence found (or all occurrences, using a /g regex); [split] splits the string into an array of words.

docs.title: 3.4.7. script [str-07]
docs.text:
[NEW since 2019] Three new features introduced between 2020 and 2024: [replaceAll], [matchAll], and the detection/correction of “malformed” strings:

'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW since 2019] new methods of character strings
// ========================================================================

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 1) replaceAll(search, replace)  (ECMAScript 2021)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// str-06.js shows that replace() with a string only replaces the 1st occurrence
// and that a regular expression /i/g had to be used to replace everything
const string: string = "one cat, two cats, three cats";
console.log("replace (only 1 occurrence) :", string.replace("cat", "dog"));
console.log("replaceAll (all the occurrences) :", string.replaceAll("cat", "dog"));
// replaceAll also accepts a regular expression, but it must then have the [g] flag
console.log("replaceAll with regexp :", string.replaceAll(/cat/g, "dog"));

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 2) matchAll(regexp)  (ECMAScript 2020)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// match() with the [g] flag only returns the strings found, without their position or their groups
// matchAll() returns an iterator giving, for each occurrence, all the info (like exec())
const text: string = "Jean is 30 years old, Marie is 25 years old, Paul is 40 years old";
const pattern: RegExp = /(\w+) is (\d+) years old/g;

// with match (g flag): we lose the detail of the captured groups
console.log("match =", text.match(pattern));

// with matchAll: we keep the detail (captured name, captured age, position...)
console.log("-----------------------");
for (const result of text.matchAll(pattern)) {
  console.log("name =", result[1], ", age =", result[2], ", position =", result.index);
}

// we can also turn the iterator into an array thanks to the spread operator
const allResults = [...text.matchAll(pattern)];
console.log("number of matches =", allResults.length);

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 3) isWellFormed() / toWellFormed()  (ECMAScript 2024)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// a JavaScript string can contain an invalid isolated "unicode half-character"
// (for example when a string has been badly cut). This can make
// some functions crash (encodeURIComponent, ...)
const validString: string = "café ☕";
const malformedString: string = "abc\uD800def"; // \uD800 is an isolated "half-character", invalid on its own

console.log("validString.isWellFormed() =", validString.isWellFormed());
console.log("malformedString.isWellFormed() =", malformedString.isWellFormed());

// toWellFormed() replaces the invalid characters with the replacement character �
console.log("malformedString.toWellFormed() =", malformedString.toWellFormed());
  • [replaceAll] (ES2021) replaces all occurrences of a string without requiring a /g regular expression, as in the str-06 script;
  • [matchAll] (ES2020) returns an iterator of all results found, each with its captured groups and position (index)—whereas a match with the g flag returns only the found strings, without this detail;
  • [isWellFormed]/[toWellFormed] (ES2024) detects and corrects strings containing an isolated “half Unicode character” (often caused by incorrect string splitting), which can cause certain functions—such as encodeURIComponent—to crash.

docs.title: 3.5. Regular Expressions
docs.text: The scripts in this chapter are located in the [regexp] folder of the project. In both TypeScript and JavaScript, a regular expression is not a string but an object in its own right, of type RegExp—therefore, you do not enclose a regular expression in quotes.

docs.title: 3.5.1. script [regexp-01]
docs.text:
This script matches several strings against different patterns (a sequence of digits, a dd/mm/yy date, a decimal number) and retrieves the matched groups:

'use strict';

/// regular expressions in javascript
// retrieving the various fields of a string
// the pattern: a sequence of digits surrounded by any characters
// we only want to retrieve the sequence of digits
let pattern: RegExp = /(\d+)/;
console.log("type of a regular expression : ", typeof (pattern));
// we match the string against the pattern
comparePatternToString(pattern, "xyz1234abcd");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "12 34");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "abcd");

// the pattern: a sequence of digits surrounded by any characters
// we want the sequence of digits as well as the fields that follow and precede it
pattern = /^(.*?)(\d+)(.*?)$/;
// we match the string against the pattern
comparePatternToString(pattern, "xyz1234abcd");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "12 34");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "abcd");

// the pattern - a date in the dd/mm/yy format
pattern = /^\s*(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\/(\d\d)\s*$/;
comparePatternToString(pattern, "10/05/97");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "  04/04/01  ");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "5/1/01");

// the pattern - a decimal number
pattern = /^\s*([+|-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*$/;
comparePatternToString(pattern, "187.8");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "-0.6");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "4");
comparePatternToString(pattern, ".6");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "4.");
comparePatternToString(pattern, " + 4");

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
function comparePatternToString(pattern: RegExp, str: string): void {
  // compares the string [str] to the pattern [pattern]
  console.log(`----------- string=${str}, pattern=${pattern}`)
  // we match the string against the pattern
  const result1 = pattern.exec(str);
  console.log(`comparison with exec=`, result1);
  // another way of doing it
  const result2 = str.match(pattern);
  console.log(`comparison with match=`, result2);
}
  • line 7: let pattern: RegExp = /(\d+)/ — the type RegExp is explicit here, but TypeScript would have deduced it automatically from the /.../ syntax anyway;
  • The methods [pattern.exec(str)] and [str.match(pattern)] return the same result: either null (no match) or an array where:
    • the element [0] is the entire string that matches the pattern;
    • the elements [1], [2]... correspond to the groups captured in parentheses, in order;
    • the .index property returns the position of the match within the string;
    • the .input property returns the original string.

docs.title: 3.5.2. script [regexp-02]
docs.text:
Sometimes, you don’t want to extract elements from the tested string but only want to know if it matches the pattern. In that case, use [RegExp.test] instead of exec/match, and you can remove the capture parentheses, which are no longer needed:

'use strict';

/// regular expressions in javascript
// retrieving the various fields of a string
// the pattern: a sequence of digits surrounded by any characters
// we only want to retrieve the sequence of digits
let pattern: RegExp = /\d+/;
console.log("type of a regular expression : ", typeof (pattern));
// we match the string against the pattern
comparePatternToString(pattern, "xyz1234abcd");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "12 34");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "abcd");

// the pattern: a sequence of digits surrounded by any characters
// we want the sequence of digits as well as the fields that follow and precede it
pattern = /^.*?\d+.*?$/;
// we match the string against the pattern
comparePatternToString(pattern, "xyz1234abcd");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "12 34");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "abcd");

// the pattern - a date in the dd/mm/yy format
pattern = /^\s*\d\d\/\d\d\/\d\d\s*$/;
comparePatternToString(pattern, "10/05/97");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "  04/04/01  ");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "5/1/01");

// the pattern - a decimal number
pattern = /^\s*[+|-]?\s*\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+\s*$/;
comparePatternToString(pattern, "187.8");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "-0.6");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "4");
comparePatternToString(pattern, ".6");
comparePatternToString(pattern, "4.");
comparePatternToString(pattern, " + 4");

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
function comparePatternToString(pattern: RegExp, str: string): void {
  // test
  const matches = pattern.test(str);
  // compares the string [str] to the pattern [pattern]
  console.log(`----------- string=${str}, pattern=${pattern}, matches=${matches}`);
}

docs.title: 3.6. The Functions
docs.text: The scripts in this chapter are located in the [functions] folder of the project:

docs.title: 3.6.1. script [func-01]
docs.text:
This script focuses on how parameters are passed to a function: by value for numbers, strings, and booleans; by reference for arrays, literal objects, and functions.

'use strict';
// how function parameters are passed
// -----------------------number - pass by value
function doSomethingWithNumber(param: number): void {
  param++;
  console.log("[param inside function]=", param, "[type]=", typeof (param), "[pass by reference]=", param === count);
}
// calling code
let count: number = 10;
doSomethingWithNumber(count);
console.log("[count outside function]=", count);

// --------------------- string - pass by value
function doSomethingWithString(param: string): void {
  param += " xyz"
  console.log("[param inside function]=", param, "[type]=", typeof (param), "[pass by reference]=", param === text);
}
// calling code
let text: string = "abcd";
doSomethingWithString(text);
console.log("[text outside function]=", text);

// --------------------- boolean - pass by value
function doSomethingWithBoolean(param: boolean): void {
  param = !param;
  console.log("[param inside function]=", param, "[type]=", typeof (param), "[pass by reference]=", param === bool);
}
// calling code
let bool: boolean = true;
doSomethingWithBoolean(bool);
console.log("bool [outside function]=", bool);

// --------------------- array - pass by reference
function doSomethingWithArray(param: number[]): void {
  param.push(1000);
  console.log("[param inside function]=", param, "[type]=", typeof (param), "[pass by reference]=", param === arr);
}
// calling code
const arr: number[] = [10, 20, 30];
doSomethingWithArray(arr);
console.log("[arr outside function]=", arr);

// --------------------- object - pass by reference
// [any] to be able to dynamically add [aNewProperty], as in JS
function doSomethingWithObject(param: any): void {
  param.aNewProperty = "xyz";
  console.log("[param inside function]=", param, "[type]=", typeof (param), "[pass by reference]=", param === obj);
}
// calling code
const obj: any = [10, 20, 30];
doSomethingWithObject(obj);
console.log("[obj outside function]=", obj);

// --------------------- function - pass by reference
// [any] because we dynamically assign a property to the function itself (see below)
function doSomethingWithFunction(param: any): void {
  // a rather strange thing that nevertheless works
  param.aNewProperty = "xyz";
  console.log("[param inside function]=", param, "[type]=", typeof (param), "[pass by reference]=", param === f);
}
// calling code
const f: any = (x: number) => x + 4;
doSomethingWithFunction(f);
console.log("[f outside function]=", f, f.aNewProperty, typeof (f));
  • Primitive types (number, string, boolean) are passed by value: modifying param inside the function never changes the original variable (pass-by-reference = false in each case);
  • arrays, objects, and functions are passed by reference: param === arr (or obj, or f) evaluates to true, and a modification made inside the function is clearly visible outside;
  • line 45: function doSomethingWithObject(param: any) — typed as any because a property (aNewProperty) not provided for in the original type of the obj array is dynamically added;
  • line 58: same thing for doSomethingWithFunction — a property is added to the function itself; this behavior (JavaScript) is a bit confusing but perfectly valid (a function is also an object).
npx tsx functions/func-01.ts

Execution result:

[count outside function]= 10
[param inside function]= abcd xyz [type]= string [pass by reference]= false
[text outside function]= abcd
[param inside function]= false [type]= boolean [pass by reference]= false
bool [outside function]= true
[param inside function]= [ 10, 20, 30, 1000 ] [type]= object [pass by reference]= true
[arr outside function]= [ 10, 20, 30, 1000 ]
[param inside function]= [ 10, 20, 30, aNewProperty: 'xyz' ] [type]= object [pass by reference]= true
[obj outside function]= [ 10, 20, 30, aNewProperty: 'xyz' ]
[param inside function]= [Function: f] { aNewProperty: 'xyz' } [type]= function [pass by reference]= true
[f outside function]= [Function: f] { aNewProperty: 'xyz' } xyz function

docs.title: 3.6.2. script [func-02]
docs.text:
This script shows that [function] is a data type like any other: a variable can have this type, and there are two ways to define a function—using the function keyword or the arrow notation =>.

'use strict';
// a function can be assigned to a variable
const variable1: (a: number, b: number) => number = function (a, b) {
  return a + b;
};
console.log("typeof(variable1)=", typeof (variable1));
// the variable can then be used like a function
console.log("variable1(10,12)=", variable1(10, 12));
// the function can be defined with the => notation
const variable2: (a: number, b: number, c: number) => number = (a, b, c) => {
  return a - b + c;
};
console.log("variable2(10,12,14)=", variable2(10, 12, 14));
// the braces can be omitted if there is only one expression in the function's code
// this expression is then the return value of the function
const variable3 = (a: number, b: number, c: number): number => a + b + c;
console.log("variable3(10,12,14)=", variable3(10, 12, 14));
  • line 3: const variable1: (a: number, b: number) => number = function (a, b) {...} — the type of a function variable is declared as a signature (parameters) => returnType;
  • lines 10–12: the same thing using arrow notation (a, b, c) => { ... };
  • line 16: without curly braces, the function body is reduced to a single expression, which automatically becomes the return value — (a, b, c): number => a + b + c.
npx tsx functions/func-02.ts

Execution result:

typeof(variable1)= function
variable1(10,12)= 22
variable2(10,12,14)= 12
variable3(10,12,14)= 36

docs.title: 3.6.3. script [func-03]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates that a function can be passed as an argument to another function—a technique widely used in the TypeScript/JavaScript frameworks (callbacks, map/filter/reduce from the “Arrays” chapter...):

'use strict';
// the parameters of a function can be of type [function]

// function f1
function f1(param1: number, param2: number): number {
  return param1 + param2 + 10;
}
// function f2
function f2(param1: number, param2: number): number {
  return param1 + param2 + 20;
}
// function g with a function f as parameter
function g(param1: number, param2: number, f: (a: number, b: number) => number): number {
  return f(param1, param2) + 100;
}
// uses of g
console.log(g(0, 10, f1));
console.log(g(0, 10, f2));
// the actual function-type parameter can be passed directly - form 1
console.log(g(0, 10, (param1, param2) => {
  return param1 + param2 + 30;
}));
// the actual function-type parameter can be passed directly - form 2
console.log(g(0, 10, function (param1, param2) {
  return param1 + param2 + 40;
}));
  • line 13: function g(param1: number, param2: number, f: (a: number, b: number) => number): number — the third parameter, f, is itself typed as a function;
  • lines 20–22 and 24–26: the actual function-type parameter can be passed directly, either as an arrow function or a regular function, without first being stored in a variable.
npx tsx functions/func-03.ts

130
140

docs.title: 3.6.4. script [func-04]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates that a function can behave like a class—a mechanism that predates ES6 but is still valid, although it has now been replaced by the class keyword (see the chapter “Classes”):

'use strict';
// a function can be used as an object

// an empty shell
// [any]: the type of [this] is deliberately loose here, because we assign
// properties to the function itself AFTER its definition (see below) -
// a pattern that TypeScript cannot infer on its own
function f(this: any): void {

}
// to which we assign properties from the outside
(f as any).prop1 = "val1";
(f as any).show = function (this: any) {
  console.log(this.prop1);
};
// using f
(f as any).show();

// a function g working like a class
function g(this: any): void {
  this.prop2 = "val2";
  this.show = function (this: any) {
    console.log(this.prop2);
  };
}
// instantiation of the function with [new]
new (g as any)().show();
  • lines 5–10: f is an “empty shell” function, typed as this: any—this special annotation on the first parameter tells TypeScript the type of this inside the function, which is necessary here because properties are added to it from the outside, a pattern that TypeScript cannot deduce on its own;
  • lines 12–15: properties are assigned to f from the outside — (f as any).prop1 = ...;
  • Line 17: We call f.show(), not f()—this is indeed the notation for using an object, not a standard function call;
  • Lines 20–25: g defines this.prop2 and this.show within itself, just as a class constructor would;
  • line 27: new (g as any)() **instantiates **g as a class.
npx tsx functions/func-04.ts

Execution result:

val1
val2
Note: ES6 introduced the `class` keyword (see the chapter “Classes”), which allows you to achieve this result directly without using this functional workaround.

docs.title: 3.6.5. script [func-05]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates the use of [rest operator] (...), which collects all remaining arguments from a call into an array:

'use strict';
// rest operator
function f(arg1: number, ...otherArgs: unknown[]): void {
  // 1st argument
  console.log("arg1=", arg1);
  // the other arguments
  let i = 0;
  otherArgs.forEach(element => {
    console.log("otherArguments[", i, "]=", element);
    i++;
  });
}

// call
f(1, "two", "three", { x: 2, y: 3 })
  • line 3: function f(arg1: number, ...otherArgs: unknown[]): void — otherArgs collects all arguments passed after arg1, regardless of their number. The unknown[] type is appropriate here because otherArgs intentionally mixes different types (strings and objects, in the call on line 15).
npx tsx functions/func-05.ts

Execution result:

arg1= 1
otherArguments[ 0 ]= two
otherArguments[ 1 ]= three
otherArguments[ 2 ]= { x: 2, y: 3 }

docs.title: 3.7. Errors and Exceptions
docs.text: TypeScript inherits the exception handling system from JavaScript, which is rather basic: the [throw] statement signals an error, and the [try / catch / finally] structure catches it. The scripts in this chapter are located in the [exceptions] folder of the project.

docs.title: 3.7.1. [excep-01] script
docs.text:
This script displays the current time in the format hours:minutes:seconds:milliseconds using the [moment.js] library (npm install moment), then demonstrates how try/catch/finally works by triggering an error based on the parity of the current milliseconds:

'use strict';

// moment package
import moment from 'moment';

// principle of try / catch / finally
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  // date - time of the current moment
  const now = Date.now();
  // time formatting to get the milliseconds
  const time = moment(now).format("HH:mm:ss:SSS");
  // the milliseconds
  const milli = Number(time.substr(time.length - 3));
  // display
  console.log("--------------------iteration no. ", i, "at", time);
  try {
    // random number
    const nbr = milli % 2;
    if (nbr === 0) {
      // throw an error msg
      throw "error";
    }
    // if we get here it means there was no error
    console.log("no error");
  } catch (error) {
    // if we get here, it means there was an error
    console.log("error1=", error);
  } finally {
    // executed in all cases, error or not
    console.log("finally")
  }
}
  • line 4: import moment from 'moment' — imports a third-party library, just like sprintf-js in the “Strings” chapter;
  • on each loop iteration, if the current number of milliseconds is even, an error is thrown (line 21) and caught by the catch block; otherwise, the message “no error” is displayed;
  • The [finally] clause is executed systematically, regardless of whether an error occurred or not.

This script depends on the exact execution time: the result below (obtained from an actual run) will therefore differ each time it is run—only the principle (the finally block is always executed) is guaranteed:

docs.title: 3.7.2. script [excep-02]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates that [throw] can throw any type of data—string, array, object, or Error instance—and that this data is fully captured by the catch clause:

'use strict';

// we can "throw" just about anything to signal an error
let i = 0;
console.log("--------------------attempt no. ", i);
// throw a character string
try {
  throw "error msg";
} catch (error) {
  // there was an error
  console.log("error=[", error, "], type=", typeof (error));
}
// throw a literal object
i++;
console.log("--------------------attempt no. ", i);
try {
  throw [1, 2, 3]
} catch (error) {
  // there was an error
  console.log("error=[", error, "], type=", typeof (error));
}
// throw an object
i++;
console.log("--------------------attempt no. ", i);
try {
  throw { name: "hercule", country: "ancient greece" }
} catch (error) {
  // there was an error
  console.log("error=[", error, "], type=", typeof (error));
}
// throw an Error type
i++;
console.log("--------------------attempt no. ", i);
try {
  throw new Error("network connection error");
} catch (error) {
  // there was an error
  console.log("error=[", error, "], type=", typeof (error));
}
// throw an Error type
i++;
console.log("--------------------attempt no. ", i);
try {
  throw new Error("network connection error");
} catch (error: any) {
  // there was an error - the message is in [error.message]
  // [any] because TypeScript types catch variables as [unknown] by default (see the other
  // try/catch blocks above, where it is enough to display [error] without accessing a property)
  console.log("error.message=[", error.message, "], type(error)=", typeof (error));
}
  • [Error] is a built-in class whose constructor accepts an error message as its first parameter, which can be retrieved in error.message;
  • TypeScript sets the catch variable to "unknown" by default (see the note on line 47): accessing a property such as .message then requires either a type check (instanceof, see the following script) or an explicit catch annotation (error: any) as shown on line 47 here;
  • There are other classes besides Error that can be used to signal an error: EvalError, RangeError, ReferenceError, SyntaxError, TypeError, URIError.

docs.title: 3.7.3. script [excep-03]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates how to distinguish, within a catch block, the specific type of error that was caught, using the [instanceof] operator:

'use strict';

// moment package
import moment from 'moment';

// differentiating the Error instance received in a [catch]
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  // date - time of the current moment
  const now = Date.now();
  // time formatting to get the milliseconds
  const time = moment(now).format("HH:mm:ss:SSS");
  // the milliseconds
  const milli = Number(time.substr(time.length - 3));
  console.log("--------------------iteration no. ", i);
  try {
    // random number
    const nbr = milli % 3;
    switch (nbr) {
      case 0:
        throw new ReferenceError("error 1");
      case 1:
        throw new RangeError("error 2");
      default:
        throw new EvalError("error 3");
    }
  } catch (error) {
    // there was an error
    if (error instanceof ReferenceError) {
      console.log("ReferenceError :", error.message);
    } else {
      if (error instanceof RangeError) {
        console.log("RangeError :", error.message);
      }
      else {
        if (error instanceof EvalError) {
          console.log("EvalError :", error.message);
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: 3.7.4. script [excep-04]
docs.text:
[NEW since 2019] This script includes two important additions introduced with ECMAScript 2022: the [cause] option for Error, and custom error classes.

'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW since 2019] the [cause] property of an error  (ECMAScript 2022)
// ========================================================================

// it is common to catch a technical (low-level) error and to
// rethrow it as a more explicit (high-level) error, so that
// the calling code better understands the business context.
// BEFORE 2022, we lost the trace of the original error by doing this.

function readConfiguration(): void {
  // simulates a low-level technical error (e.g.: file not found)
  throw new Error("ENOENT: file 'config.json' not found");
}

function startApplication(): void {
  try {
    readConfiguration();
  } catch (technicalError) {
    // the 2nd parameter { cause } makes it possible to attach the original error
    // to the new error, without losing the information
    throw new Error("unable to start the application", { cause: technicalError });
  }
}

try {
  startApplication();
} catch (error: any) {
  console.log("error=", error.message);
  // error.cause gives access to the original error, very useful for debugging
  console.log("cause=", error.cause?.message);
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// custom error classes (already possible since ECMAScript 2015,
// but very often used with [cause] since 2022, hence reviewed here)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// we can create our own error types by extending [Error], which then makes it possible
// to distinguish them with [instanceof], as for ReferenceError or RangeError
// (cf. exceptions/excep-03.js)
class ValidationError extends Error {

  fieldInError: string;

  constructor(message: string, fieldInError: string, options?: ErrorOptions) {
    // we pass the message and the [options] (including a possible cause) to the parent [Error]
    super(message, options);
    // the default name would be "Error"; we customize it
    this.name = "ValidationError";
    // we can add business information specific to this type of error
    this.fieldInError = fieldInError;
  }
}

function validate(age: unknown): boolean {
  if (typeof (age) !== "number") {
    throw new ValidationError("the age must be a number", "age");
  }
  if (age < 0 || age > 130) {
    throw new ValidationError("the age must be between 0 and 130", "age");
  }
  return true;
}

// some attempts with different values
for (const value of [25, -5, "thirty", 200]) {
  try {
    validate(value);
    console.log(`value [${value}] : validation OK`);
  } catch (error) {
    // we can distinguish our business errors from the other errors thanks to instanceof
    if (error instanceof ValidationError) {
      console.log(`value [${value}] : validation error on [${error.fieldInError}] - ${error.message}`);
    } else {
      // an unexpected error, not anticipated by our code
      throw error;
    }
  }
}
  • lines 17–22: When catching a low-level technical error to rethrow it in a more explicit form, the second parameter {cause} of new Error(...) allows you to preserve the trace of the original error, which would otherwise be lost (pre-2022 behavior);
  • line 31: error.cause?.message retrieves the message from the original error, which is very useful for debugging;
  • lines 41–53: A custom error class (ValidationError extends Error) allows you to create your own business error types, which can then be distinguished using instanceof (line 72), just like ReferenceError or RangeError in the previous script.
npx tsx exceptions/excep-04.ts

cause= ENOENT: file 'config.json' not found
value [25] : validation OK
value [-5] : validation error on [age] - the age must be between 0 and 130
value [thirty] : validation error on [age] - the age must be a number
value [200] : validation error on [age] - the age must be between 0 and 130

docs.title: 3.8. Modules
docs.text: The ECMAScript modules allow you to build applications structured into independent, reusable files, each of which exports what it wants to make available to the others. The scripts in this chapter are located in the [modules] folder of the project.

docs.title: 3.8.1. [import-01, export-01] scripts
docs.text:
The [import-01] script uses the [export-01] module:

// default export of an unnamed object
export default {
  data: 2,
  do() {
    console.log(this.data);
  }
};
  • [export default] exports an unnamed object—only one default export is allowed per module.
'use strict';
// import of an object exported by default
import export01 from './export-01.js';
// using this object
export01.do();
// a default export can be imported under any name
import data from './export-01.js';
console.log(data.data);
  • Lines 3 and 7 import the module’s default export under two different names (export01, then data)—the name given to the import is arbitrary; it does not need to correspond to anything in the source module;
  • Once imported, the object can be used as if it had been defined locally.
npx tsx modules/import-01.ts

Execution result:

2
2

docs.title: 3.8.2. [import-02, export-02] scripts
docs.text:
These scripts show that exporting a named object (previously stored in a variable) works exactly the same way:

// default export of a named object
const data = {
  data: 2,
  do() {
    console.log(this.data);
  }
};
// export
export default data;

'use strict';
// import of an object exported by default
import module1 from './export-02.js';
// using this object
module1.do();
// a default export can be imported under any name
import module2 from './export-02.js';
console.log(module2.data);

npx tsx modules/import-02.ts

Execution result:

2
2

docs.title: 3.8.3. [import-03, export-03] scripts
docs.text:
A module can export multiple elements using the syntax export { element }:

// multi-exports
// object export
const data = {
  data: 2,
  do() {
    console.log(this.data);
  }
};
// function export
export { data };
function doSomething(): void {
  console.log("doSomething");
}
export { doSomething };

'use strict';
// import of a module [export03]
import {data, doSomething} from './export-03.js';
// using the imports
data.do();
doSomething();
// other syntax
import * as module from './export-03.js';
// using the import
console.log(module.data);
module.doSomething();
  • Line 3: Named imports use the exact names of the exported elements, enclosed in curly braces;
  • line 8: import \* as module from '...' imports all exported elements, grouped into a named object (here, module).
npx tsx modules/import-03.ts

Execution result:

2
doSomething
{ data: 2, do: [Function: do] }
doSomething

docs.title: 3.8.4. [import-04, remote-config] scripts — top-level await
docs.text:
[NEW since 2019] ECMAScript Version 2022 introduced top-level await: the ability to use await directly at the top level of a module, without wrapping it in an async function. Previously, you had to create an async “main” function and call it immediately (see the next chapter, script async-06).

The [remote-config] module simulates the loading of a remote configuration and uses top-level await:

// module simulating the reading of a remote configuration (e.g.: network call)
// used by modules/import-04.js to illustrate top-level await

interface Configuration {
  applicationName: string;
  version: string;
}

// a function that simulates an asynchronous call (e.g.: fetch of a configuration file)
function loadFromNetwork(): Promise<Configuration> {
  return new Promise(resolve => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      resolve({ applicationName: "ECMAScript course", version: "2026" });
    }, 300);
  });
}

// [NEW since 2022] top-level await: we can use [await] directly
// at the top level of a module, without wrapping it in an async function.
// the WHOLE module (and any module that imports it) waits for this line to finish
// before continuing: this is very handy to initialize a configuration
// only once, when the module is loaded.
console.log("[remote-config] loading the configuration...");
const configuration: Configuration = await loadFromNetwork();
console.log("[remote-config] configuration loaded");

// we export the result, already resolved (and not a promise to await again)
export default configuration;

The script [import-04] imports this module:

'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW since 2019] top-level await  (ECMAScript 2022)
// ========================================================================

// before ECMAScript 2022, it was impossible to use [await] outside
// an [async] function: at the top level of a script, you had to create
// an async "main" function and call it immediately (cf. async/async-06.js)

// note on the execution order: with ES modules, the [import]s are always
// evaluated BEFORE the code of the importing module, even if written on the 1st line.
// this is why the logs of [remote-config.js] are displayed before this one,
// although the following line is textually placed before the import in this file.
console.log("[import-04] before importing the remote-config module");

// thanks to the top-level await used IN remote-config.js, the import below
// only completes when the configuration has finished loading: no need
// to call .then() or to create an async function here
import configuration from './remote-config.js';

console.log("[import-04] after the import: the configuration is already available");
console.log("configuration =", configuration);

// we can also use [await] directly here, in this module, at the top level
console.log("[import-04] waiting 200ms with top-level await...");
await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 200));
console.log("[import-04] finished");
  • Line 19: Thanks to the top-level await used **in **remote-config.ts, the import on line 19 completes only after the configuration has finished loading—no need for .then() or an async function here;
  • ES modules are always evaluated before the code in the module that imports them, even if the import statement isn’t on the first line of the file: this is why the messages from remote-config.ts are displayed before those from import-04.ts, even though the latter is literally placed before the import in the file;
  • line 26: You can also use await directly within import-04.ts itself, at its own top level.
