docs.title: 3.9. Event-Driven Programming and Asynchronous Functions
docs.text:
An asynchronous function is a function whose execution is initiated but whose result is not immediately awaited. When execution is complete, the asynchronous function signals its result—via an event, or via a **[Promise]**, as we will see later.

This mode of operation is well-suited for execution in a browser, where the application constantly responds to events (clicks, keystrokes, network responses, etc.). The scripts in this chapter are executed by [node.js], which also uses an event loop:

  • execution of the script’s main code is the first event processed;
  • if this code has initiated asynchronous tasks, script execution continues until they are complete—they emit an event once finished, which is queued in the event loop;
  • the main script must subscribe to these events to retrieve their results;
  • the script does not terminate until all the events it has emitted have been processed.

The scripts in this chapter are located in the [async] folder of the project.

docs.title: 3.9.1. script [async-01]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates the behavior of a script containing an asynchronous action, using the native function [setTimeout]:

'use strict';

// imports
import moment from 'moment';
import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';

// start
const scriptStart = moment(Date.now());
console.log("[start of the script],", time());

// setTimeout arms a 1000 ms timer (2nd parameter) and immediately returns the number of this timer
// when the timer has used up the 1000 ms it emits an event that is queued in the runtime's queue
// when the event is processed by the runtime, the function (1st parameter) is executed
setTimeout(function () {
  // this code will be executed when the timer has reached the value 0
  console.log("[end of the asynchronous action setTimeout],", time(scriptStart));
}, 1000)

// will be displayed before the msg of the timer's inner function
console.log("[end of the main code of the script],", time(scriptStart));

// utility displaying time and duration
function time(start?: moment.Moment): string {
  // time of the current moment
  const now = moment(Date.now());
  // time formatting
  let result = "time=" + now.format("HH:mm:ss:SSS");
  // should a duration be calculated?
  if (start) {
    const duration = now.valueOf() - start.valueOf();
    const milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    const seconds = Math.floor(duration / 1000);
    // time + duration formatting
    result = result + sprintf(", duration= %s second(s) and %s milliseconds", seconds, milliseconds);
  }
  // result
  return result;
}
  • Lines 14–17: [setTimeout] takes two parameters: a function to execute and a delay in milliseconds. It executes instantly: it starts a timer and immediately returns control, without waiting for the delay to elapse;
  • line 20: This message therefore appears before the one on line 16, even though it is written later in the code;
  • line 23: function time(start?: moment.Moment): string — the start parameter is optional (?), of type moment.Moment; if provided, the function calculates and adds the elapsed time.
npx tsx async/async-01.ts

Execution result:

[start of the script], time=07:41:36:456
[end of the main code of the script], time=07:41:36:457, duration= 0 second(s) and 2 milliseconds
[end of the asynchronous action setTimeout], time=07:41:37:458, duration= 1 second(s) and 3 milliseconds

We can see that the asynchronous action setTimeout completes approximately 1 second after the main code finishes—which is exactly the programmed delay. The overall script, however, does not complete until this asynchronous task is finished.

Note: We’ll use setTimeout to simulate asynchronous tasks throughout this chapter. A real asynchronous task (network request, file read, etc.) behaves in the same way: it yields control immediately and then reports its result later—usually via two possible events, one for success and one for failure.

docs.title: 3.9.2. script [async-02]
docs.text:
This script demonstrates how an asynchronous function can communicate its result by emitting events, using the native class EventEmitter (node:events module):

'use strict';

// asynchronous functions can return a result by emitting an event
// the main code can retrieve these results by subscribing to the emitted events

// imports
import moment from 'moment';
import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';
import EventEmitter from 'events';

// start
const scriptStart = moment(Date.now());
console.log("[start of the script],", time());
// an event emitter
const eventEmitter = new EventEmitter();

// setTimeout arms a 1000 ms timer (2nd parameter) and immediately returns the number of this timer
// when the timer has used up the 1000 ms it emits an event that is queued in the runtime's queue
// when the event is processed by the runtime, the function (1st parameter) is executed
setTimeout(function () {
  // this code will be executed when the timer has reached the value 0
  console.log("[setTimeout, end of the 1 s timer],", time(scriptStart));
  // we emit an event to say that a result is available
  eventEmitter.emit("timer1Success", { success: 4 });
  // we emit another event to say that another result is available
  eventEmitter.emit("timer1Failure", { failure: 6 });
}, 1000)

// we subscribe to the [timer1Success] evt
eventEmitter.on('timer1Success', (result) => {
  console.log(sprintf("the timer's asynchronous function returned the result [%j], %s, via the [timer1Success] event", result, time(scriptStart)));
});

// we subscribe to the [timer1Failure] evt
eventEmitter.on('timer1Failure', (result) => {
  console.log(sprintf("the timer's asynchronous function returned the result [%j], %s, via the [timer1Failure] event", result, time(scriptStart)));
});

// will be displayed before the msgs of the evts emitted by the function associated with [timer1]
console.log("[end of the main code of the script],", time(scriptStart));

// utility displaying time and duration
function time(start?: moment.Moment): string {
  // time of the current moment
  const now = moment(Date.now());
  // time formatting
  let result = "time=" + now.format("HH:mm:ss:SSS");
  // should a duration be calculated?
  if (start) {
    const duration = now.valueOf() - start.valueOf();
    const milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    const seconds = Math.floor(duration / 1000);
    // time + duration formatting
    result = result + sprintf(", duration= %s second(s) and %s milliseconds", seconds, milliseconds);
  }
  // result
  return result;
}
  • line 9: import EventEmitter from 'events' — imports the class that allows events to be emitted and listened to;
  • line 15: const eventEmitter = new EventEmitter() — an event emitter is instantiated using new;
  • lines 24 and 26: the function encapsulated in setTimeout emits two events, timer1Success and timer1Failure, each with its own associated data (here, for demonstration purposes only—normally, a single task would emit only one or the other);
  • lines 29–37: the main code subscribes to these two events using eventEmitter.on(eventName, callback)—the callback will not execute until the event is actually emitted, not at the time of subscription;
  • line 40: the main code ends here, but the global script does not end until the asynchronous task (and the subscribed callbacks) have finished executing.
npx tsx async/async-02.ts

Execution result:

[start of the script], time=07:41:38:163
[end of the main code of the script], time=07:41:38:170, duration= 0 second(s) and 7 milliseconds
[setTimeout, end of the 1 s timer], time=07:41:39:173, duration= 1 second(s) and 10 milliseconds
the timer's asynchronous function returned the result [{"success":4}], time=07:41:39:173, duration= 1 second(s) and 10 milliseconds, via the [timer1Success] event
the timer's asynchronous function returned the result [{"failure":6}], time=07:41:39:173, duration= 1 second(s) and 10 milliseconds, via the [timer1Failure] event

docs.title: 3.9.3. script [async-03]
docs.text:
The event loop in node.js executes only one event at a time: the next event is processed only after the previous one has finished. Synchronous code that ties up the processor for a long time therefore delays the processing of all pending events—including those that have already been issued. This script (identical to async-02, with an intensive loop added) demonstrates this:

'use strict';

// asynchronous functions can return a result by emitting an event
// the main code can retrieve these results by subscribing to the emitted events

// imports
import moment from 'moment';
import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';
import EventEmitter from 'events';

// start
const scriptStart = moment(Date.now());
console.log("[start of the script],", time());
// an event emitter
const eventEmitter = new EventEmitter();

// setTimeout arms a 1000 ms timer (2nd parameter) and immediately returns the number of this timer
// when the timer has used up the 1000 ms it emits an event that is queued in the runtime's queue
// when the event is processed by the runtime, the function (1st parameter) is executed
setTimeout(function () {
  // this code will be executed when the timer has reached the value 0
  console.log("[setTimeout, end of the 1 s timer],", time(scriptStart));
  // we emit an event to say that a result is available
  eventEmitter.emit("timer1Success", { success: 4 });
  // we emit another event to say that another result is available
  eventEmitter.emit("timer1Failure", { failure: 6 });
}, 1000)

// we subscribe to the [timer1Success] evt
eventEmitter.on('timer1Success', (result) => {
  console.log(sprintf("the timer's asynchronous function returned the result [%j], %s, via the [timer1Success] event", result, time(scriptStart)));
});

// we subscribe to the [timer1Failure] evt
eventEmitter.on('timer1Failure', (result) => {
  console.log(sprintf("the timer's asynchronous function returned the result [%j], %s, via the [timer1Failure] event", result, time(scriptStart)));
});

// somewhat intensive synchronous code that prevented the main code from finishing before the end of [timer1]
for (let i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) {
  for (let j = 0; j < 10000; j++) {
    i + i ^ 2 + i ^ 3;
  }
}

// will be displayed before the msgs of the evts emitted by the function associated with [timer1]
console.log("[end of the main code of the script],", time(scriptStart));

// utility displaying time and duration
function time(start?: moment.Moment): string {
  // time of the current moment
  const now = moment(Date.now());
  // time formatting
  let result = "time=" + now.format("HH:mm:ss:SSS");
  // should a duration be calculated?
  if (start) {
    const duration = now.valueOf() - start.valueOf();
    const milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    const seconds = Math.floor(duration / 1000);
    // time + duration formatting
    result = result + sprintf(", duration= %s second(s) and %s milliseconds", seconds, milliseconds);
  }
  // result
  return result;
}
  • lines 40–44: a purely synchronous double loop, unrelated to the asynchronous task, but which occupies the processor for several seconds;
  • the 1-second timer has finished its countdown well before the end of this loop—but the event it emitted must wait for the synchronous code to yield control back to the event loop before it can finally be processed.
npx tsx async/async-03.ts

Execution result:

[start of the script], time=07:41:39:891
[end of the main code of the script], time=07:41:45:623, duration= 5 second(s) and 732 milliseconds
[setTimeout, end of the 1 s timer], time=07:41:45:625, duration= 5 second(s) and 734 milliseconds
the timer's asynchronous function returned the result [{"success":4}], time=07:41:45:625, duration= 5 second(s) and 734 milliseconds, via the [timer1Success] event
the timer's asynchronous function returned the result [{"failure":6}], time=07:41:45:625, duration= 5 second(s) and 734 milliseconds, via the [timer1Failure] event

The main code took approximately 5.7 seconds to execute (duration varies by machine), even though the timer had long since completed its one-second countdown: the associated event had to wait for the synchronous loop to finish. It’s important to note that long-running synchronous code should, whenever possible, be broken down into shorter asynchronous tasks.

docs.title: 3.9.4. The Promise Mechanism
docs.text:
The type [Promise] is a class that avoids explicitly managing events: this is done implicitly, but understanding the underlying events helps provide a better grasp of how it works. Its constructor takes an asynchronous function as a parameter, to which it passes two functions, traditionally named [resolve] and [reject]:

const promise = new Promise(function (resolve, reject) {
  // an asynchronous task is started
  // ...
  // if successful: call resolve(result) where [result] is the result of the task
  // if failed: call reject(error) where [error] encapsulates the error encountered
});

A Promise object can be in one of four states:

  • [pending]: the asynchronous task is not yet complete;
  • [fulfilled]: it has completed successfully;
  • [rejected]: it has failed;
  • [settled]: it has completed (regardless of whether it succeeded or failed).

You subscribe to the results of a Promise using the syntax promise.then(f1).catch(f2).finally(f3): f1 executes on success (it receives the result passed by resolve), f2 runs in case of failure (it receives the error returned by reject), and f3 runs in all cases, without any parameters.

docs.title: 3.9.5. script [async-04]
docs.text:
This script creates two independent Promises, each encapsulating a setTimeout, and subscribes to their results:

'use strict';

// it is possible to get the results (success, failure) of an asynchronous function
// without explicitly using events thanks to the [Promise] class
// this class implicitly uses events but they are not visible in the code

// imports
import moment from 'moment';
import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';

// start
const scriptStart = moment(Date.now());
console.log("[start of the script],", time(scriptStart));

// definition of an asynchronous task using a [Promise]
// the asynchronous task is the parameter of the [Promise] constructor
const promise1Start = moment(Date.now());
const promise1 = new Promise<string>(function (resolve) {
  // log
  console.log("[start of the asynchronous function of promise1],", time(promise1Start));
  // asynchronous code
  setTimeout(function () {
    // this code is executed after a 1 second delay (2nd parameter)
    console.log("[end of the asynchronous function of promise1],", time(promise1Start));
    // the asynchronous task returns a result with the [resolve] function
    // the promise is then successful
    resolve('[success]');
  }, 1000)
});

// we can know the result of the promise [promise1]
// when it has been resolved (resolve) or rejected (reject)
// the following instruction is a subscription to the [resolved] evt via the [then] method
// and to the [rejected] evt via the [catch] method
// the [finally] method is executed whether after a then or a catch
promise1.then(result => {
  // case where the promise succeeds  [evt resolved]
  console.log(sprintf("[promise1.then], %s, result=%s", time(promise1Start), result));
}).catch(result => {
  // error case  [evt rejected]
  console.log(sprintf("[promise1.catch], %s, result=%s", time(promise1Start), result));
}).finally(() => {
  // executed in all cases
  console.log("[promise1.finally]", time(promise1Start));
});

// definition of an asynchronous task using a [Promise]
const promise2Start = moment(Date.now());
const promise2 = new Promise<string>(function (resolve, reject) {
  // log
  console.log("[start of the asynchronous function of promise2],", time(promise2Start));
  // asynchronous task
  setTimeout(function () {
    console.log("[end of the asynchronous function of promise2],", time(promise2Start));
    // the asynchronous task returns a result with the [reject] function
    // the promise has then failed
    reject('[failure]');
  }, 2000)
});

// we can know the result of the promise [promise2]
// when it has been resolved (resolve) or rejected (reject)
promise2.then(result => {
  // case where the promise succeeds [evt resolved]
  console.log(sprintf("[promise2.then], %s, result=%s", time(promise2Start), result));
}).catch(result => {
  // error case [evt rejected]
  console.log(sprintf("[promise2.catch], %s, result=%s", time(promise2Start), result));
}).finally(() => {
  // executed in all cases
  console.log(sprintf("[promise2.finally], %s", time(promise2Start)));
});

// will be displayed before the msgs of the asynchronous functions and those of the associated evts
console.log("[end of the main code of the script],", time(scriptStart));

// utility
function time(start?: moment.Moment): string {
  // time of the current moment
  const now = moment(Date.now());
  // time formatting
  let result = "time=" + now.format("HH:mm:ss:SSS");
  if (start) {
    const duration = now.valueOf() - start.valueOf();
    const milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    const seconds = Math.floor(duration / 1000);
    // duration formatting
    result = result + sprintf(", duration= %s second(s) and %s milliseconds", seconds, milliseconds);
  }
  // result
  return result;
}
  • line 18: new Promise<string>(function (resolve) {...}) — TypeScript allows you to specify, via the generic parameter <string>, the type of value that resolve will return; without it, the type would be inferred as unknown;
  • promise1 resolves successfully after 1 second (resolve('[success]')); promise2 fails after 2 seconds (reject('[failure]'));
  • the main code (line 75) finishes well before both promises have a result—the global script, however, continues until both are settled.
npx tsx async/async-04.ts

Execution result:

[start of the script], time=07:42:29:437, duration= 0 second(s) and 0 milliseconds
[start of the asynchronous function of promise1], time=07:42:29:443, duration= 0 second(s) and 0 milliseconds
[start of the asynchronous function of promise2], time=07:42:29:444, duration= 0 second(s) and 0 milliseconds
[end of the main code of the script], time=07:42:29:444, duration= 0 second(s) and 7 milliseconds
[end of the asynchronous function of promise1], time=07:42:30:445, duration= 1 second(s) and 2 milliseconds
[promise1.then], time=07:42:30:446, duration= 1 second(s) and 3 milliseconds, result=[success]
[promise1.finally] time=07:42:30:447, duration= 1 second(s) and 4 milliseconds
[end of the asynchronous function of promise2], time=07:42:31:445, duration= 2 second(s) and 1 milliseconds
[promise2.catch], time=07:42:31:446, duration= 2 second(s) and 2 milliseconds, result=[failure]
[promise2.finally], time=07:42:31:446, duration= 2 second(s) and 2 milliseconds

docs.title: 3.9.6. script [async-05]
docs.text:
It is most common to define an asynchronous function that returns a Promise, rather than creating the Promise object directly—which is useful when the function needs parameters. This script defines two asynchronous functions and waits for both of them to complete with [Promise.all]:

'use strict';

// we can define asynchronous functions that return a [Promise] type
// they can then be tagged with the [async] keyword
// here again
// imports
import moment from 'moment';
import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';

// start
const scriptStart = moment(Date.now());
console.log("[start of the script],", time());

// shape of the result returned by async01 and async02
interface AsyncResult {
  prop1: number[];
  prop2: string;
  prop3: number;
}

// an asynchronous function can return a [Promise]
// and then have the [async] attribute
async function async01(p1: number): Promise<AsyncResult> {
  return new Promise<AsyncResult>(resolve => {
    console.log("[start of the asynchronous task async01]");
    // the asynchronous task
    const async01Start = moment(Date.now());
    setTimeout(function () {
      // this code is executed after a 1 second delay (2nd parameter)
      console.log("[end of the asynchronous task async01],", time(async01Start));
      // the asynchronous task can return a complex result
      resolve({
        prop1: [10, 20, 30],
        prop2: "abcd",
        prop3: p1,
      });
    }, 1000)
  });
}

// a function can return a [Promise]
// and can then have the [async] attribute
async function async02(p1: number, p2: number): Promise<AsyncResult> {
  return new Promise<AsyncResult>(resolve => {
    console.log("[start of the asynchronous task async02]");
    // asynchronous task
    const async02Start = moment(Date.now());
    setTimeout(function () {
      // the following code is executed after a 2 second delay (2nd parameter)
      console.log("[end of the asynchronous task async02],", time(async02Start));
      // the asynchronous task can return a complex result
      resolve({
        prop1: [11, 21, 31],
        prop2: "xyzt",
        prop3: p1 + p2
      });
    }, 2000)
  })
}

// we launch the two asynchronous functions in parallel
// and we wait until both of them have finished
// the then will only execute if both functions have emitted the [resolved] evt
// the catch will execute as soon as one of the two functions emits the [rejected] evt
Promise.all([async01(10), async02(10, 20)])
  // the result is an array [result1, result2] where [result1] is the result emitted by a [resolve] of [async01]
  // and [result2] the result emitted by a [resolve] of [async02]
  .then(result => {
    console.log(sprintf("[promise-all success], %s, result=%j", time(scriptStart), result));
  })
  // error is the result emitted by the first [reject] of one of the two asynchronous functions
  .catch(error => {
    console.log(sprintf("[promise-all error], %s, error=%j", time(scriptStart), error));
  })
  // finally is executed after the then or the catch
  .finally(() => {
    console.log(sprintf("[promise-all finally], %s", time(scriptStart)));
  });

// will be displayed before the msgs of the asynchronous functions and of the associated evts
console.log("[end of the main code of the script],", time(scriptStart));

// utility
function time(start?: moment.Moment): string {
  // time of the current moment
  const now = moment(Date.now());
  // time formatting
  let result = "time=" + now.format("HH:mm:ss:SSS");
  if (start) {
    const duration = now.valueOf() - start.valueOf();
    const milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    const seconds = Math.floor(duration / 1000);
    // duration formatting
    result = result + sprintf(", duration= %s second(s) and %s milliseconds", seconds, milliseconds);
  }
  // result
  return result;
}
  • lines 23 and 43: the asynchronous functions are typed as Promise<AsyncResult> thanks to the AsyncResult interface defined above;
  • line 65: [Promise.all([...])] waits for all promises in the array to resolve before executing its then—as soon as one fails, its catch executes immediately, without waiting for the others;
  • the two tasks run in parallel (their respective waiting periods overlap): the total duration (~2s) corresponds to the longer of the two, not to their sum (~3s).
npx tsx async/async-05.ts

Execution result:

[start of the script], time=07:42:32:179
[start of the asynchronous task async01]
[start of the asynchronous task async02]
[end of the main code of the script], time=07:42:32:180, duration= 0 second(s) and 6 milliseconds
[end of the asynchronous task async01], time=07:42:33:181, duration= 1 second(s) and 1 milliseconds
[end of the asynchronous task async02], time=07:42:34:182, duration= 2 second(s) and 2 milliseconds
[promise-all success], time=07:42:34:183, duration= 2 second(s) and 9 milliseconds, result=[{"prop1":[10,20,30],"prop2":"abcd","prop3":10},{"prop1":[11,21,31],"prop2":"xyzt","prop3":30}]
[promise-all finally], time=07:42:34:183, duration= 2 second(s) and 9 milliseconds

docs.title: 3.9.7. script [async-06] — async / await
docs.text:
The keywords [async]/[await] allow you to write asynchronous code that looks like synchronous code: the underlying event handling is completely hidden, which makes the code much easier to read. This script defines three asynchronous functions—the third one fails intentionally—and executes them first sequentially, then in parallel:

'use strict';

// parallel or sequential execution of several asynchronous tasks
// with the async / await keywords

// imports
import moment from 'moment';
import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';

// start
const scriptStart = moment(Date.now());
console.log("[start of the main code of the script],", time());

// shape of the result returned by async01/async02/async03
interface AsyncResult {
  prop1: number[];
  prop2: string;
}

// an asynchronous function returning a [Promise]
async function async01(async01Start: moment.Moment): Promise<AsyncResult> {
  return new Promise(function (resolve) {
    console.log("[start of the asynchronous function async01],", time());
    // asynchronous function
    setTimeout(function () {
      console.log("[end of the asynchronous function async01],", time(async01Start));
      // the asynchronous action can return a complex result
      // here success
      resolve({
        prop1: [11, 21, 31],
        prop2: "abcd"
      });
    }, 1000)
  });
}

// an asynchronous function returning a [Promise]
async function async02(async02Start: moment.Moment): Promise<AsyncResult> {
  console.log("[start of the asynchronous function async02],", time());
  return new Promise(function (resolve) {
    // asynchronous function
    setTimeout(function () {
      console.log("[end of the asynchronous function async02],", time(async02Start));
      // the asynchronous action can return a complex result
      // here success
      resolve({
        prop1: [12, 22, 32],
        prop2: "xyzt"
      });
    }, 2000)
  })
}

// an asynchronous function returning a [Promise]
async function async03(async03Start: moment.Moment): Promise<AsyncResult> {
  console.log("[start of the asynchronous function async03],", time());
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    // asynchronous function
    setTimeout(function () {
      console.log("[end of the asynchronous function async03],", time(async03Start));
      // the asynchronous action can return a complex result
      // here failure
      reject({
        prop1: [13, 23, 33],
        prop2: "failure"
      });
    }, 3000)
  })
}

// asynchronous function - using async / await
async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const sequentialStart = moment(Date.now());
  // sequential execution of the asynchronous tasks
  console.log("------------ sequential execution of the asynchronous tasks started ------------------------")
  try {
    // execution with wait of [async01]
    const async01Start = moment(Date.now());
    const result1 = await async01(async01Start);
    console.log("[async01 result]=", result1);
    // execution with wait of [async02]
    const async02Start = moment(Date.now());
    console.log("start async02-------------", time());
    const result2 = await async02(async02Start);
    console.log("[async02 result]=", result2);
    // execution with wait of [async03]
    const async03Start = moment(Date.now());
    console.log("start async03-------------", time());
    const result3 = await async03(async03Start);
    console.log("[async03 result]=", result3);
  } catch (error) {
    // one of the asynchronous actions failed
    console.log(sprintf("[sequential error]= %j, %s", error, time(sequentialStart)));
  } finally {
    // finished
    console.log("[end of the sequential execution of the asynchronous tasks],", time(sequentialStart));
  }

  const parallelStart = moment(Date.now());
  // parallel execution of the asynchronous tasks
  console.log("------------ parallel execution of the asynchronous tasks started ------------------------");
  try {
    const result = await Promise.all([async01(parallelStart), async02(parallelStart), async03(parallelStart)]);
    console.log(sprintf("[parallel success], %s, result=%j", time(parallelStart), result));
  } catch (error) {
    // one of the asynchronous actions failed
    console.log(sprintf("[parallel error], %s, error=%j", time(parallelStart), error));
  } finally {
    // finished
    console.log(sprintf("[end of the parallel execution of the asynchronous tasks],%s", time(parallelStart)));
  }

  // finished
  console.log("[end of the main function],", time(sequentialStart));
}
// execution of the asynchronous main function
main();

// will be displayed before the various msgs of the asynchronous functions and of their evts
console.log("[end of the main code of the script],", time(scriptStart));

// utility
function time(start?: moment.Moment): string {
  // time of the current moment
  const now = moment(Date.now());
  // time formatting
  let result = "time=" + now.format("HH:mm:ss:SSS");
  if (start) {
    const duration = now.valueOf() - start.valueOf();
    const milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    const seconds = Math.floor(duration / 1000);
    // duration formatting
    result = result + sprintf(", duration= %s second(s) and %s milliseconds", seconds, milliseconds);
  }
  // result
  return result;
}
  • line 72: async function main(): Promise<void> — a function tagged with async always returns a Promise, even if its body does not explicitly indicate it;
  • line 79: await async01(async01Start) suspends the execution of main until the promise is resolved, without blocking the rest of the program (the await keyword can only be used inside an async function or at the top level of a module—see the “Modules” chapter, script import-04);
  • lines 76–90: sequential execution—each await waits for the previous task to finish before starting the next one; the total duration is the sum of the three wait times (~6s);
  • lines 102–111: parallel execution, with await Promise.all([...])—the total duration is that of the longest task (~3s);
  • A standard try/catch block is sufficient to handle the failure of an awaited promise—there’s no longer a need for chained .catch() calls as in the previous scripts.

docs.title: 3.9.8. [async-07] script — Promise extensions
docs.text:
[NEW since 2019] This script presents four extensions introduced between 2020 and 2024, which are now widely used in modern TypeScript:

'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW since 2019] additions to the Promise class
// ========================================================================

// small utility function: returns a promise that succeeds or fails after [delay] ms
function task(name: string, delay: number, succeeds: boolean): Promise<string> {
  return new Promise<string>((resolve, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      if (succeeds) {
        resolve(`result of ${name}`);
      } else {
        reject(`failure of ${name}`);
      }
    }, delay);
  });
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 1) Promise.allSettled()  (ECMAScript 2020)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// async-05.js shows Promise.all(): if ONE of the promises fails, the catch is triggered
// and we lose the result of the other promises which, for their part, had succeeded
// Promise.allSettled() ALWAYS waits until all the promises are finished
// (successful or failed) and returns the detail of each one, without ever rejecting
async function demoAllSettled(): Promise<void> {
  console.log("--- Promise.allSettled ---");
  const results = await Promise.allSettled([
    task("task1", 300, true),
    task("task2", 200, false),
    task("task3", 100, true)
  ]);
  // each element has the shape { status: "fulfilled", value: ... } or { status: "rejected", reason: ... }
  results.forEach((result, index) => {
    if (result.status === "fulfilled") {
      console.log(`task${index + 1} succeeded :`, result.value);
    } else {
      console.log(`task${index + 1} failed :`, result.reason);
    }
  });
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 2) Promise.any()  (ECMAScript 2021)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// returns the result of the FIRST promise that succeeds (the others are ignored)
// rejects only if ALL the promises fail (with an AggregateError grouping the errors)
async function demoAny(): Promise<void> {
  console.log("--- Promise.any ---");
  try {
    const result = await Promise.any([
      task("slow-mirror", 500, true),
      task("fast-mirror", 100, true),
      task("broken-mirror", 50, false)
    ]);
    console.log("first available mirror :", result);
  } catch (globalError: any) {
    // globalError.errors contains the list of all the individual errors
    console.log("all the mirrors failed :", globalError.errors);
  }
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 3) Promise.withResolvers()  (ECMAScript 2024)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// before, to "take out" the resolve/reject functions from the Promise constructor
// (e.g. to call them much later, elsewhere in the code), you needed
// a somewhat artificial intermediate variable:
//   let externalResolve;
//   const promise = new Promise(resolve => { externalResolve = resolve; });
// Promise.withResolvers() does this directly, in a single expression
function demoWithResolvers(): Promise<string> {
  console.log("--- Promise.withResolvers ---");
  const { promise, resolve } = Promise.withResolvers<string>();

  // we can resolve the promise from anywhere, for example in another callback
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("[external callback] we trigger the resolution of the promise");
    resolve("value passed from an external callback");
  }, 200);

  return promise;
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 4) cancelling an asynchronous operation with AbortController
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// AbortController makes it possible to cancel an ongoing asynchronous operation (fetch, timers, ...)
// it is the standard mechanism used by [fetch] for timeouts (cf http/fetch-01.js)
function cancellableTask(delay: number, signal: AbortSignal): Promise<string> {
  return new Promise<string>((resolve, reject) => {
    const timer = setTimeout(() => resolve("finished normally"), delay);
    // if the cancellation signal is triggered, we stop everything and reject
    signal.addEventListener("abort", () => {
      clearTimeout(timer);
      reject(new Error("operation cancelled : " + signal.reason));
    });
  });
}

async function demoAbortController(): Promise<void> {
  console.log("--- AbortController ---");
  const controller = new AbortController();
  // we schedule the cancellation in 100 ms, before the normal end of the task (500 ms)
  setTimeout(() => controller.abort("timeout exceeded on the user side"), 100);
  try {
    const result = await cancellableTask(500, controller.signal);
    console.log("result =", result);
  } catch (error: any) {
    console.log("error :", error.message);
  }
}

// successive execution of the demonstrations
async function main(): Promise<void> {
  await demoAllSettled();
  await demoAny();
  console.log("--- Promise.withResolvers, result ---", await demoWithResolvers());
  await demoAbortController();
}

main();
  • [Promise.allSettled] (ES2020): unlike Promise.all (async-05 script), it always waits for all promises to complete—whether they succeed or fail—and returns the details of each one—useful when you never want to lose the results of tasks that succeeded, even if another one failed;
  • [Promise.any] (ES2021): returns the result of the first promise that succeeds, ignoring the others—it only rejects if all of them fail;
  • [Promise.withResolvers] (ES2024): extracts resolve and reject from the Promise constructor into a single expression, which is useful for resolving a promise later from another part of the code;
  • [AbortController]: allows you to cancel a pending asynchronous operation—this is the standard mechanism used by fetch for timeouts (see the chapter “The HTTP Functions”).
npx tsx async/async-07.ts

Execution result:

--- Promise.allSettled ---
task1 succeeded : result of task1
task2 failed : failure of task2
task3 succeeded : result of task3
--- Promise.any ---
first available mirror : result of fast-mirror
--- Promise.withResolvers ---
[external callback] we trigger the resolution of the promise
--- Promise.withResolvers, result --- value passed from an external callback
--- AbortController ---
error : operation cancelled : timeout exceeded on the user side

docs.title: 3.10. The classes
docs.text:
Here we introduce the ECMAScript classes, as typed in TypeScript. Before presenting them, let’s recall (script class-00, previously covered in the chapter “Functions” under the name func-04) that functions can already behave like classes—it is this historical mechanism that the keyword [class] simplifies.

The scripts for this chapter are located in the [classes] folder of the project.

docs.title: 3.10.1. script [class-00]
docs.text:
Reminder of the historical mechanism (functions used as classes):

'use strict';
// a function can be used as an object

// an empty shell
// [any]: the type of [this] is deliberately loose here, because we assign
// properties to the function itself AFTER its definition (see below) -
// a pattern that TypeScript cannot infer on its own
function f(this: any): void {

}
// to which we assign properties from the outside
(f as any).prop1 = "val1";
(f as any).show = function (this: any) {
  console.log(this.prop1);
};
// using f
(f as any).show();

// a function g working like a class
function g(this: any): void {
  this.prop2 = "val2";
  this.show = function (this: any) {
    console.log(this.prop2);
  };
}
// instantiation of the function with [new]
new (g as any)().show();

npx tsx classes/class-00.ts

Execution result:

val1
val2
Note: ES6 introduced the `class` keyword, which allows you to achieve the same result in a much more readable and reliable way, without resorting to this functional workaround—as demonstrated by the following scripts.

docs.title: 3.10.2. script [class-01]
docs.text:
This script defines a class named [Person], with a constructor, getters/setters, and the method toString:

// class
class Person {

  private _lastName!: string;
  private _firstName!: string;
  private _age!: number;

  // constructor
  constructor(lastName: string, firstName: string, age: number) {
    this.lastName = lastName;
    this.firstName = firstName;
    this.age = age;
  }

  // getters and setters
  get lastName(): string {
    return this._lastName;
  }
  set lastName(value: string) {
    this._lastName = value;
  }

  get firstName(): string {
    return this._firstName;
  }
  set firstName(value: string) {
    this._firstName = value;
  }

  get age(): number {
    return this._age;
  }
  set age(value: number) {
    this._age = value;
  }

  // toString in JSON
  toString(): string {
    return JSON.stringify(this);
  }
}

// using the class
function main(): void {
  const person = new Person("Poirot", "Hercule", 66);
  console.log("person=", person.toString(), typeof (person), person instanceof (Person));
}

// call to main
main();
  • line 2: [class] introduces the class;
  • line 9: [constructor] is its constructor—there can only be one per class;
  • lines 4–6: The fields _lastName, _firstName, and _age are declared with the modifier [private]—making them accessible only from within the class, as opposed to a simple naming convention. The ! (*definite assignment assertion*) tells TypeScript that these fields will indeed be assigned before any read operation, even if this is not directly visible in their declaration (the constructor, via the setters, handles this);
  • lines 16–35: getters and setters — syntax identical to that seen for object literals (chapter “Literal Objects,” script obj-03), but integrated into the class;
  • line 46: person instanceof (Person)—you can determine the exact type of a class instance, unlike with literal objects.
npx tsx classes/class-01.ts

Execution result:

person= {"_lastName":"Poirot","_firstName":"Hercule","_age":66} object true

docs.title: 3.10.3. script [class-02] — inheritance
docs.text:
This script demonstrates inheritance using the keyword [extends]. The Person class is first isolated in its own file, Person.ts:

// class
class Person {

  // private properties (accessed via the getters/setters below)
  // [!]: we assert to TypeScript that they will be assigned before being read
  // (here, via the constructor which calls the setters)
  private _lastName!: string;
  private _firstName!: string;
  private _age!: number;

  // constructor
  constructor(lastName: string, firstName: string, age: number) {
    this.lastName = lastName;
    this.firstName = firstName;
    this.age = age;
  }

  // getters and setters
  get lastName(): string {
    return this._lastName;
  }
  set lastName(value: string) {
    this._lastName = value;
  }

  get firstName(): string {
    return this._firstName;
  }
  set firstName(value: string) {
    this._firstName = value;
  }

  get age(): number {
    return this._age;
  }
  set age(value: number) {
    this._age = value;
  }

  // toString in JSON
  toString(): string {
    return JSON.stringify(this);
  }
}
// class export
export default Person;

The script [class-02] creates a class [Teacher] derived from Person:

// imports
// [2026 update] with node's native ESM, the .js extension is mandatory
// in relative paths (it was optional with the [esm] loader used in 2019)
import Person from './Person.js';

// class
class Teacher extends Person {

  private _subject!: string;

  // constructor
  constructor(lastName: string, firstName: string, age: number, subject: string) {
    super(lastName, firstName, age);
    this.subject = subject;
  }

  // getters and setters
  get subject(): string {
    return this._subject;
  }
  set subject(value: string) {
    this._subject = value;
  }

}

// using the class
function main(): void {
  const teacher = new Teacher("Poirot", "Hercule", 66, "detective");
  console.log("teacher=", teacher.toString(), typeof (teacher), teacher instanceof Teacher);
}

// call to main
main();
  • line 5: import Person from './Person.js' — the class is imported from its module. The .js extension (not .ts) is required with Node.js’s modern module resolution, even if the source file is a .ts file (see the “Installation” chapter);
  • line 8: class Teacher extends Person — Teacher inherits all members from Person and adds a property _subject with its getter/setter;
  • line 14: super(lastName, firstName, age) calls the parent class’s constructor, which initializes _lastName, _firstName, and _age;
  • line 31: teacher instanceof Teacher — TypeScript/JavaScript knows the exact type of the instance, even after inheritance.
npx tsx classes/class-02.ts

Execution result:

teacher= {"_lastName":"Poirot","_firstName":"Hercule","_age":66,"_subject":"detective"} object true

docs.title: 3.10.4. script [class-03] — method override
docs.text:
This script demonstrates that a child class can override a method of its parent class—in this case, toString:

// imports
// [2026 update] with node's native ESM, the .js extension is mandatory
// in relative paths (it was optional with the [esm] loader used in 2019)
import Person from './Person.js';

// class
class Teacher extends Person {

  private _subject!: string;

  // constructor
  constructor(lastName: string, firstName: string, age: number, subject: string) {
    super(lastName, firstName, age);
    this.subject = subject;
  }

  // getters and setters
  get subject(): string {
    return this._subject;
  }
  set subject(value: string) {
    this._subject = value;
  }

  // redefinition of toString
  toString(): string {
    return "[Teacher]" + JSON.stringify(this);
  }
}

// using the class
function main(): void {
  const teacher = new Teacher("Poirot", "Hercule", 66, "detective");
  console.log("teacher=", teacher.toString(), typeof (teacher), teacher instanceof Teacher);
}

// call to main
main();

Execution result:

teacher= [Teacher]{"_lastName":"Poirot","_firstName":"Hercule","_age":66,"_subject":"detective"} object true

docs.title: 3.10.5. script [class-04] — polymorphism
docs.text:
This script demonstrates polymorphism in action: where a function expects a parameter of type Person, we can pass a derived type such as Teacher, since it possesses all the attributes of Person. First, we isolate Teacher in its own module, Teacher.ts:

// imports
// [2026 update] with node's native ESM, the .js extension is mandatory
// in relative paths (it was optional with the [esm] loader used in 2019)
import Person from './Person.js';

// class
class Teacher extends Person {

  // private property (accessed via the getter/setter below)
  private _subject!: string;

  // constructor
  constructor(lastName: string, firstName: string, age: number, subject: string) {
    super(lastName, firstName, age);
    this.subject = subject;
  }

  // getters and setters
  get subject(): string {
    return this._subject;
  }
  set subject(value: string) {
    this._subject = value;
  }

}

// class export
export default Teacher;

The script [class-04] uses this type polymorphically:

// imports
// [2026 update] with node's native ESM, the .js extension is mandatory
// in relative paths (it was optional with the [esm] loader used in 2019)
import Teacher from './Teacher.js';
import Person from './Person.js';

// function accepting a person as parameter
function show(person: Person): void {
  // in all cases
  console.log("parameter=", person.toString(), typeof (person));
  // instance of Person
  if (person instanceof Person) {
    console.log("person=", person.toString());
  }
  // instance of Teacher
  if (person instanceof Teacher) {
    console.log("teacher=", person.toString());
  }
}

// call of show with a teacher
show(new Teacher("Poirot", "Hercule", 66, "detective"));
show(new Person("Marple", "Miss", 70));
  • line 8: function show(person: Person): void — the function expects a parameter of type Person, but accepts any derived type (Teacher) — this is the principle of substitution, which is fundamental to object-oriented programming;
  • lines 11 –18: instanceof allows the behavior to be adapted to the actual type of the received object, beyond its declared type.
npx tsx classes/class-04.ts

Execution result:

parameter= {"_lastName":"Poirot","_firstName":"Hercule","_age":66,"_subject":"detective"} object
person= {"_lastName":"Poirot","_firstName":"Hercule","_age":66,"_subject":"detective"}
teacher= {"_lastName":"Poirot","_firstName":"Hercule","_age":66,"_subject":"detective"}
parameter= {"_lastName":"Marple","_firstName":"Miss","_age":70} object
person= {"_lastName":"Marple","_firstName":"Miss","_age":70}

docs.title: 3.10.6. [class-05] script — native private fields
docs.text:
[NEW since 2019] The previous scripts use the private modifier (TypeScript, _lastName, _firstName...), a protection mechanism that exists only at compile time—at runtime, in pure JavaScript, these fields remain simply normal properties. Since ECMAScript 2022, there have been true private fields, prefixed with #, which are invisible and inaccessible even at runtime:

'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW since 2019] private fields and static blocks  (ECMAScript 2022)
// ========================================================================

// in class-01.js, encapsulation was simulated by convention: a property
// named [_name] (with an underscore) that was accessed via a [name] getter/setter.
// BUT nothing really prevented writing person._name = "xyz" from the outside!
// since ECMAScript 2022, we can declare TRUE private fields with a [#]
// in front of their name: they are only accessible from inside the class.

class BankAccount {

  // private field: exists and is visible ONLY in the methods of this class
  #balance: number;

  // private field with default value
  #history: string[] = [];

  // normal public field (no #): accessible from the outside, as before
  holder: string;

  constructor(holder: string, initialBalance: number = 0) {
    this.holder = holder;
    this.#balance = initialBalance;
  }

  // public method giving controlled access to the private field
  get balance(): number {
    return this.#balance;
  }

  deposit(amount: number): void {
    this.#balance += amount;
    // #addToHistory is a private method, callable only from here
    this.#addToHistory(`deposit of ${amount}`);
  }

  withdraw(amount: number): void {
    if (amount > this.#balance) {
      throw new Error("insufficient balance");
    }
    this.#balance -= amount;
    this.#addToHistory(`withdrawal of ${amount}`);
  }

  // private method: the [#] also works on methods
  #addToHistory(operation: string): void {
    this.#history.push(operation);
  }

  displayHistory(): void {
    console.log(`history of ${this.holder} :`, this.#history);
  }
}

// normal use
const account = new BankAccount("Dupont", 100);
account.deposit(50);
account.withdraw(30);
console.log("balance =", account.balance); // via the public getter
account.displayHistory();

// we cannot access the private field directly from the outside
console.log("direct account.#balance : impossible, causes a syntax error if we try");
// console.log(account.#balance); // uncommenting this line causes a TypeScript compilation error

// nor can we read it with the [ ] notation as for a normal property
console.log("account['#balance'] =", (account as any)["#balance"]); // -> undefined, it is not the same thing

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// private STATIC fields and methods also exist
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
class IdGenerator {
  // private static field: shared by all instances, invisible from the outside
  static #lastId: number = 0;

  // static initialization block: executed only once, when the class is loaded
  // useful for a complex initialization that a simple "= value" does not allow
  static {
    console.log("[static block] initialization of IdGenerator");
    IdGenerator.#lastId = 1000; // custom starting value
  }

  // public static method giving controlled access to the private static field
  static nextId(): number {
    IdGenerator.#lastId++;
    return IdGenerator.#lastId;
  }
}

console.log("nextId() =", IdGenerator.nextId());
console.log("nextId() =", IdGenerator.nextId());
console.log("nextId() =", IdGenerator.nextId());
  • [#balance] (line 15), [#history] (line 18): true private fields—unlike _lastName in the class-01 script, it is impossible to access them from outside the class, even via account['#balance'] (line 69), which returns undefined rather than the actual value;
  • [#addToHistory] (line 48): a private method, callable only from within the class;
  • [static { ... }] (lines 80–83): a static initialization block (ES2022), executed only once when the class is loaded—useful for initialization that is more complex than a simple assignment;
  • [static #lastId] (line 76): a private static field, shared by all instances but invisible from the outside.
npx tsx classes/class-05.ts

Execution result:

balance = 120
history of Dupont : [ 'deposit of 50', 'withdrawal of 30' ]
direct account.#balance : impossible, causes a syntax error if we try
account['#balance'] = undefined
[static block] initialization of IdGenerator
nextId() = 1001
nextId() = 1002
nextId() = 1003

docs.title: 3.11. New ECMAScript Features 2020–2024
docs.text:
The previous chapters have already covered, as we went along, most of the language’s new features introduced since 2019—optional chaining and null coalescing (basics-09), Object.hasOwn and structuredClone (obj-09), new array methods (arr-05), replaceAll/matchAll (str-07), native private fields (class-05), Error with cause (excep-04), top-level await (import-04), and Promise extensions (async-07).

This chapter brings together the last two new features from ECMAScript 2024 that did not fit into any existing chapter: [Object.groupBy]/[Map.groupBy], and [Array.fromAsync]. The script is located in the [whats-new] folder of the project.
