docs.text:
'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW since 2019] Object.groupBy, Map.groupBy, Array.fromAsync (ECMAScript 2024)
// ========================================================================

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 1) Object.groupBy(array, groupingFunction)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// before, to group the elements of an array according to a criterion, you had to
// write a loop with reduce() yourself (cf. arrays/arr-04.js for reduce)
interface Student {
  name: string;
  grade: number;
}
const students: Student[] = [
  { name: "Ana", grade: 15 },
  { name: "Léo", grade: 8 },
  { name: "Nora", grade: 12 },
  { name: "Théo", grade: 6 },
  { name: "Zoé", grade: 17 }
];

// old way, with reduce()
const groupsWithReduce = students.reduce((accumulator: Record<string, Student[]>, student) => {
  const category = student.grade >= 10 ? "passed" : "failed";
  // if there is no array yet for this category, we create it
  (accumulator[category] ??= []).push(student);
  return accumulator;
}, {});
console.log("with reduce :", groupsWithReduce);

// new way, much more readable, with Object.groupBy
const groups = Object.groupBy(students, student => (student.grade >= 10 ? "passed" : "failed"));
console.log("with Object.groupBy :", groups);
console.log("passed =", groups.passed);
console.log("failed =", groups.failed);

// Map.groupBy works the same way, but returns a [Map] rather than a literal object
// useful when the grouping keys are not strings (e.g.: objects, numbers)
const groupsInMap = Map.groupBy(students, student => student.grade >= 10);
console.log("with Map.groupBy, key [true] (passed) =", groupsInMap.get(true));
console.log("with Map.groupBy, key [false] (failed) =", groupsInMap.get(false));

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 2) Array.fromAsync(asyncIterable)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Array.from() (ES2015) can build an array from a synchronous iterable
// Array.fromAsync() can do the same thing from an ASYNCHRONOUS iterable,
// that is, a source that produces its elements one by one, over time
// (for example: reading a network stream page by page)

// an asynchronous generator that produces 3 values, with a small delay between each one
async function* pageGenerator(): AsyncGenerator<string> {
  for (let i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    // we simulate a network wait before each page
    await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 100));
    yield `page ${i}`;
  }
}

async function demoFromAsync(): Promise<void> {
  console.log("--- Array.fromAsync ---");
  // without Array.fromAsync, a manual "for await...of" loop would have been needed
  const pages = await Array.fromAsync(pageGenerator());
  console.log("pages =", pages);
}

demoFromAsync();
  • Line 33: [Object.groupBy(array, groupingFunction)] groups the elements of an array based on the result of a sorting function—much more readable than the manual construction using reduce() (compare the two constructions: lines 24–29 and line 33);
  • the result of Object.groupBy is an object without a prototype ([Object: null prototype])—a detail visible at runtime, which avoids certain pitfalls related to properties inherited from Object.prototype (such as toString, hasOwnProperty...) if a category were to bear that name;
  • line 40: [Map.groupBy] works identically but returns a Map rather than a literal object—essential whenever the grouping keys are not strings (in this case, booleans);
  • [Array.fromAsync(asyncIterable)] constructs an array from an asynchronous source—an async function\* generator, for example—without having to write a manual for loop yourself to accumulate the results.
npx tsx whats-new/groupBy-and-fromAsync.ts

Execution result:

with reduce : {
  passed: [
    { name: 'Ana', grade: 15 },
    { name: 'Nora', grade: 12 },
    { name: 'Zoé', grade: 17 }
  ],
  failed: [ { name: 'Léo', grade: 8 }, { name: 'Théo', grade: 6 } ]
}
with Object.groupBy : [Object: null prototype] {
  passed: [
    { name: 'Ana', grade: 15 },
    { name: 'Nora', grade: 12 },
    { name: 'Zoé', grade: 17 }
  ],
  failed: [ { name: 'Léo', grade: 8 }, { name: 'Théo', grade: 6 } ]
}
passed = [
  { name: 'Ana', grade: 15 },
  { name: 'Nora', grade: 12 },
  { name: 'Zoé', grade: 17 }
]
failed = [ { name: 'Léo', grade: 8 }, { name: 'Théo', grade: 6 } ]
with Map.groupBy, key [true] (passed) = [
  { name: 'Ana', grade: 15 },
  { name: 'Nora', grade: 12 },
  { name: 'Zoé', grade: 17 }
]
with Map.groupBy, key [false] (failed) = [ { name: 'Léo', grade: 8 }, { name: 'Théo', grade: 6 } ]
--- Array.fromAsync ---
pages = [ 'page 1', 'page 2', 'page 3' ]

docs.title: 3.11.2. Summary Table
docs.text:
Let’s summarize, by version of ECMAScript, all the new features presented in this course since the “Basics” chapter:

  • [ES2020]: optional chaining ?., null coalescing ??, BigInt, Promise.allSettled, String.matchAll;
  • [ES2021]: logical assignment ||=/&&=/??=, numeric separators 1_000_000, Promise.any, String.replaceAll;
  • [ES2022]: private fields and methods #name, static initialization blocks, Object.hasOwn, Array.at, top-level await, Error with cause;
  • [ES2023]: findLast/findLastIndex, immutable methods toSorted/toReversed/toSpliced/with;
  • [ES2024]: Object.groupBy/Map.groupBy, Array.fromAsync, Promise.withResolvers, String.isWellFormed/toWellFormed.

The following chapters describe the new features of ECMAScript 2026, as well as [Temporal], the modern replacement for the Date object.

docs.title: 3.12. New Features in ECMAScript 2026
docs.text: ECMAScript 2026 (the 17th edition of the language) was officially finalized by TC39 in 2026. According to the official text of the specification (https://tc39.es/ecma262/2026/), this edition added: Math.sumPrecise to add a set of numbers while minimizing precision loss; Iterator.concat to chain iterators; Array.fromAsync (already introduced in the previous chapter); Error.isError to reliably identify error objects; methods on Map.prototype and WeakMap.prototype to provide a default value during a read operation; methods on Uint8Array for hexadecimal and Base64 conversions; a context parameter for the revivers of JSON.parse; and JSON.rawJSON for fine-tuning the output of JSON.stringify.

docs.title: 3.12.1. ⚠️ An important warning before you begin
docs.text:
Stage 4 of TC39 guarantees that a feature’s behavior will no longer change, but does not guarantee its immediate availability in all JavaScript engines. While preparing this chapter, one concrete example clearly demonstrated this: [Math.sumPrecise] causes the error “TypeError: Math.sumPrecise is not a function,” even on recent versions of Node.js. This is not a bug in this course: V8 (the engine used by Node and Chrome) simply has not yet implemented this feature—unlike Firefox, Safari, and Bun, which already have it (source: official issue ticket for the TypeScript repository, github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues/63427).

That’s why each script in this chapter uses typeof to check for itself whether the feature it demonstrates is available before using it, and displays a clear message if it isn’t—rather than crashing abruptly. This is a best practice in itself when using very recent language features.

Important: All the scripts in this chapter have actually been run in the development environment for this course (Node.js 26.7.0); some of them display the message “not available,” which is an actual result and not an assumption. On your machine, with a different version of Node.js, some of these scripts may display an actual result rather than this message—feel free to compare.

The following scripts are located in the [ecmascript-2026] folder:

docs.title: 3.12.2. [01-math-sumPrecise] script
docs.text:
'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW ECMAScript 2026] Math.sumPrecise()
// ========================================================================
// [update] at the time this script is written, V8 (hence node and Chrome)
// does NOT YET implement Math.sumPrecise, whereas Firefox, Safari and Bun
// already have it. This is a concrete example of the gap that can exist between
// "the feature has entered the official language specification"
// and "all the JavaScript engines have actually implemented it": TC39 Stage 4
// (reached on 07/28/2025 for this feature) guarantees that the
// behaviour will no longer change, but does NOT guarantee an immediate
// availability everywhere. See ecmascript-2026/README.md for the details and the
// sources.
// To check for yourself whether YOUR node already has this feature:
//   node -e "console.log(typeof Math.sumPrecise)"

// adding floating-point numbers with + accumulates rounding errors,
// because each number is represented in binary imprecisely
const numbers: number[] = [0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.1];

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 1) the old way, with reduce(): the result is not exact
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
const sumWithReduce = numbers.reduce((accumulator, value) => accumulator + value, 0);
console.log("sum with reduce =", sumWithReduce);
// we expect exactly 1.9, but the result often contains spurious decimals
// (e.g.: 1.9000000000000001) because of rounding errors that accumulate over the additions

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 2) Math.sumPrecise(): adds all the numbers exactly
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// unlike a loop of successive additions, the algorithm used internally
// avoids accumulating the intermediate rounding errors
if (typeof Math.sumPrecise === "function") {
  const preciseSum = Math.sumPrecise(numbers);
  console.log("sum with Math.sumPrecise =", preciseSum);
} else {
  // here we avoid a brutal crash (TypeError) to remain educational:
  // this message will be displayed as long as your JavaScript engine has not yet
  // implemented this feature, although it is already finalized in the spec
  console.log("Math.sumPrecise is not yet available on this JavaScript engine",
    "(see the comment at the top of this file)");
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// why it is useful: financial, accounting, scientific calculations -
// anywhere a small repeated rounding error can become a real bug
// (e.g.: an invoice total that never comes out right to the cent)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------

npx tsx ecmascript-2026/01-math-sumPrecise.ts

Execution result:

sum with reduce = 1.9000000000000004
Math.sumPrecise is not yet available on this JavaScript engine (see the comment at the top of this file)

docs.title: 3.12.3. script [02-iterator-concat]
docs.text:
[Iterator.concat] concatenates multiple iterables (array, Set, generator, etc.) into a single lazy iterator: the elements are generated only as needed, without constructing a complete intermediate collection—unlike the spread operator [...a, ...b], which copies everything immediately into memory.

'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW ECMAScript 2026] Iterator.concat()
// ========================================================================
// [Node 26+ - officially listed in the node 26.0.0 release notes:
// see https://nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v26.0.0 - so normally already
// available if you are on node 26. If this is not the case, check with:
//   node -e "console.log(typeof Iterator.concat)"
// see also ecmascript-2026/README.md for the case of the other new features of
// this folder, which do not all have the same level of availability]

// we sometimes have several data sources to go through one after the other
// (for example: several arrays, or an array then a Set, ...)
const firstWave: string[] = ["Ana", "Léo"];
const secondWave: Set<string> = new Set(["Nora", "Théo"]);
const thirdWave: string[] = ["Zoé"];

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 1) the old way: everything had to be gathered in a new array
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
const allGuestsArray: string[] = [...firstWave, ...secondWave, ...thirdWave];
console.log("with spread :", allGuestsArray);
// drawback: this creates a new array IN MEMORY with all the elements copied,
// even if we only need the first 2 (e.g.: for a paginated display)

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 2) Iterator.concat(): chains the iterables without copying them first
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Iterator.concat accepts any kind of iterable (array, Set, Map, generator...)
// and returns a "lazy" iterator: the elements are only produced as they are needed
if (typeof Iterator.concat === "function") {
  const allGuests = Iterator.concat(firstWave, secondWave, thirdWave);

  console.log("-----------------------");
  for (const guest of allGuests) {
    console.log("guest =", guest);
  }

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // advantage of laziness: we can stop along the way
  // without having paid the cost of building a complete collection in advance
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  const firstThree = Iterator.concat(firstWave, secondWave, thirdWave)
    .take(3)
    .toArray();
  console.log("first three guests =", firstThree);
} else {
  console.log("Iterator.concat is not available on this JavaScript engine",
    "(see the comment at the top of this file)");
}

npx tsx ecmascript-2026/02-iterator-concat.ts

Execution result:

with spread : [ 'Ana', 'Léo', 'Nora', 'Théo', 'Zoé' ]
-----------------------
guest = Ana
guest = Léo
guest = Nora
guest = Théo
guest = Zoé
first three guests = [ 'Ana', 'Léo', 'Nora' ]

docs.title: 3.12.4. script [03-error-isError]
docs.text:
[Error.isError] reliably detects whether a value is an error, even when it comes from another JavaScript "realm" (an isolated execution context—an iframe, a worker, or the Node.js vm module): Each realm has its own Error class, which causes instanceof Error to fail, as the script demonstrates in practice:

'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW ECMAScript 2026] Error.isError()
// ========================================================================
// [availability status to check for yourself: see ecmascript-2026/README.md.
// Some ES2026 new features (like Math.sumPrecise) are still missing
// from V8 despite having reached Stage 4 - it is not impossible that this is also the case
// here. Check with: node -e "console.log(typeof Error.isError)"]

// until now, to know whether a value is an error, we used [instanceof Error]
// (cf. exceptions/excep-03.ts) - this works well... except in some tricky cases

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 1) the [instanceof] trap with several JavaScript "realms"
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// a "realm" is an isolated JavaScript execution context: for example,
// an iframe in a browser, a worker, or node's [vm] module which allows
// executing code in a separate context. Each realm has ITS OWN [Error] class,
// distinct from the one of the main realm.
import vm from 'node:vm';

// we execute "new Error('from elsewhere')" in a separate realm
const errorFromAnotherRealm: unknown = vm.runInNewContext("new Error('from elsewhere')");

console.log("errorFromAnotherRealm =", errorFromAnotherRealm);
// [instanceof Error] fails here: it is NOT the same [Error] class as ours,
// even though the object IS, conceptually, an error
console.log("errorFromAnotherRealm instanceof Error :", errorFromAnotherRealm instanceof Error);

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 2) Error.isError(): reliable detection, even between different realms
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
if (typeof Error.isError === "function") {
  console.log("Error.isError(errorFromAnotherRealm) :", Error.isError(errorFromAnotherRealm));

  // for comparison, on a "normal" error (same realm), both ways of doing it
  // give the same result
  const normalError = new Error("classic error");
  console.log("normalError instanceof Error :", normalError instanceof Error);
  console.log("Error.isError(normalError) :", Error.isError(normalError));

  // and on a value that is clearly not an error
  console.log("Error.isError('abc') :", Error.isError("abc"));
  console.log("Error.isError(null) :", Error.isError(null));
} else {
  console.log("Error.isError is not available on this JavaScript engine",
    "(see the comment at the top of this file) - but the [instanceof] trap",
    "demonstrated above is quite real and already observable");
}

npx tsx ecmascript-2026/03-error-isError.ts

Execution result:

errorFromAnotherRealm = Error: from elsewhere
    at evalmachine.<anonymous>:1:1
    at Script.runInContext (node:vm:150:12)
    at Script.runInNewContext (node:vm:155:17)
    at Object.runInNewContext (node:vm:311:38)
    at <anonymous> (c:\Data\st-2026\GitHub Pages\fr_FR2\downloads\typescript-sept-2026\ecmascript-2026\03-error-isError.ts:23:43)
    at ModuleJob.run (node:internal/modules/esm/module_job:569:25)
    at async node:internal/modules/esm/loader:650:26
    at async asyncRunEntryPointWithESMLoader (node:internal/modules/run_main:101:5)
errorFromAnotherRealm instanceof Error : false
Error.isError(errorFromAnotherRealm) : true
normalError instanceof Error : true
Error.isError(normalError) : true
Error.isError('abc') : false

This script illustrates an interesting point even without Error.isError available: the line errorFromAnotherRealm instanceof Error : false clearly shows the actual pitfall that Error.isError is supposed to resolve—yet the object is, conceptually, a true error.

docs.title: 3.12.5. script [04-map-weakmap-getOrInsert]
docs.text:
[Map.prototype.getOrInsert]/[getOrInsertComputed] address a very common need: “if the key already exists, take its value; otherwise, create a default value and store it,” all in a single line rather than a verbose if (!map.has(key)) { map.set(...) }. The same principle applies to WeakMap.

'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW ECMAScript 2026] Map.prototype.getOrInsert / getOrInsertComputed
// ========================================================================
// [Node 26+ - officially listed in the node 26.0.0 release notes:
// see https://nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v26.0.0 - so normally already
// available if you are on node 26. If this is not the case, check with:
//   node -e "console.log(typeof Map.prototype.getOrInsert)"
// see also ecmascript-2026/README.md for the case of the other new features of
// this folder, which do not all have the same level of availability]

// a very frequent need: "if the key already exists in the Map, take its value;
// otherwise, create a default value, store it, then use it"

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 1) the old way: if/has() then set() - verbose, and easy to get wrong
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
const registrationsByWorkshop = new Map<string, string[]>();

function registerOldWay(workshop: string, participant: string): void {
  if (!registrationsByWorkshop.has(workshop)) {
    registrationsByWorkshop.set(workshop, []);
  }
  registrationsByWorkshop.get(workshop)!.push(participant);
  // the "!" is needed here: TypeScript cannot know, at this precise spot,
  // that the .get() following a .set() just before will necessarily succeed
}
registerOldWay("cooking", "Ana");
registerOldWay("cooking", "Léo");
console.log("with the old way :", registrationsByWorkshop);

if (typeof Map.prototype.getOrInsert !== "function") {
  console.log("Map.prototype.getOrInsert is not available on this JavaScript engine",
    "(see the comment at the top of this file) - only part 1) above could be executed");
} else {
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 2) Map.prototype.getOrInsert(): the same thing, in a single line
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  const registrations2 = new Map<string, string[]>();

  const register = (workshop: string, participant: string): void => {
    // returns the existing array for [workshop], or initializes it to [] if it does not exist yet
    registrations2.getOrInsert(workshop, []).push(participant);
  }
  register("pottery", "Nora");
  register("pottery", "Théo");
  console.log("with getOrInsert :", registrations2);

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 3) getOrInsertComputed(): the default value is computed ONLY if needed
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // with getOrInsert(key, value), the default [value] is ALWAYS evaluated,
  // even when the key already exists and we do not need it (here it does not
  // matter for an empty array [], but it can for an expensive calculation)
  const counters = new Map<string, number>();

  const increment = (key: string): void => {
    // the callback is called ONLY if the key does not exist yet in the Map
    const value = counters.getOrInsertComputed(key, () => {
      console.log(`[computing the initial value for "${key}"]`);
      return 0;
    });
    counters.set(key, value + 1);
  }
  increment("visits");
  increment("visits"); // here, the callback will NOT be executed again
  increment("clicks");
  console.log("counters =", counters);

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 4) WeakMap.prototype.getOrInsert / getOrInsertComputed: same principle,
  // to associate additional data with objects without preventing their
  // cleanup by the garbage collector
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  interface Metadata {
    views: number;
  }
  const metadataByObject = new WeakMap<object, Metadata>();

  const recordAView = (object: object): void => {
    const metadata = metadataByObject.getOrInsertComputed(object, () => ({ views: 0 }));
    metadata.views++;
  }
  const article = { title: "Discovering the WeakMap" };
  recordAView(article);
  recordAView(article);
  console.log("metadata of the article =", metadataByObject.get(article));
}

npx tsx ecmascript-2026/04-map-weakmap-getOrInsert.ts

Execution result:

with the old way : Map(1) { 'cooking' => [ 'Ana', 'Léo' ] }
with getOrInsert : Map(1) { 'pottery' => [ 'Nora', 'Théo' ] }
[computing the initial value for "visits"]
[computing the initial value for "clicks"]
counters = Map(2) { 'visits' => 2, 'clicks' => 1 }
metadata of the article = { views: 2 }

docs.title: 3.12.6. script [05-uint8array-base64-hex]
docs.text:
Uint8Array (a raw byte array) now includes new methods for converting to and from base64 and hexadecimal—formats commonly used to transmit binary data in JSON or URL—without relying on a third-party package:

'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW ECMAScript 2026] Uint8Array: base64 and hexadecimal conversion
// ========================================================================
// [availability status to check for yourself: see ecmascript-2026/README.md.
// Some ES2026 new features (like Math.sumPrecise) are still missing
// from V8 despite having reached Stage 4 - it is not impossible that this is also the case
// here. Check with: node -e "console.log(typeof Uint8Array.prototype.toBase64)"]

// [Uint8Array] is a typed array that stores raw bytes (values 0-255) -
// for example the content of a file, an image, or data received over the network

// before 2026, to encode these bytes in base64 (the format used for example
// in "data:" URLs, or to transmit binary data in JSON),
// you had to go through roundabout functions or third-party packages (buffer on the node side,
// btoa/atob on the browser side - imperfect and not originally designed for that)

const bytes = new Uint8Array([72, 101, 108, 108, 111]); // "Hello" in ASCII codes

if (typeof bytes.toBase64 !== "function") {
  console.log("Uint8Array.prototype.toBase64 is not available on this JavaScript engine",
    "(see the comment at the top of this file)");
} else {
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 1) base64 encoding
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  const inBase64 = bytes.toBase64();
  console.log("bytes in base64 =", inBase64);

  // decoding: rebuilding a Uint8Array from a base64 string
  const recoveredBytes = Uint8Array.fromBase64(inBase64);
  console.log("recovered bytes =", recoveredBytes);
  console.log("identical to the original :", bytes.toString() === recoveredBytes.toString());

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 2) hexadecimal encoding
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  const inHexadecimal = bytes.toHex();
  console.log("bytes in hexadecimal =", inHexadecimal);

  const bytesFromHex = Uint8Array.fromHex(inHexadecimal);
  console.log("bytes from hex =", bytesFromHex);

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 3) filling an existing Uint8Array, from a given offset
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // useful to assemble several pieces in the same buffer, without intermediate
  // allocations
  const buffer = new Uint8Array(10);
  const writeResult = buffer.setFromHex("48656c6c6f"); // "Hello" in hexadecimal
  console.log("buffer after setFromHex =", buffer);
  console.log("characters read / written =", writeResult);
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// why it is useful: transmitting binary data in text formats
// (JSON, URL, HTTP headers...), without depending on a third-party package or on hacks
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------

npx tsx ecmascript-2026/05-uint8array-base64-hex.ts

Execution result:

bytes in base64 = SGVsbG8=
recovered bytes = Uint8Array(5) [ 72, 101, 108, 108, 111 ]
identical to the original : true
bytes in hexadecimal = 48656c6c6f
bytes from hex = Uint8Array(5) [ 72, 101, 108, 108, 111 ]
buffer after setFromHex = Uint8Array(10) [
  72, 101, 108, 108, 111,
   0,   0,   0,   0,   0
]
characters read / written = { read: 10, written: 5 }

docs.title: 3.12.7. script [06-json-rawJSON-and-reviver]
docs.text:
This last script differs from the previous ones: [JSON.rawJSON]/[isRawJSON], as well as the new "context" parameter in the JSON.parse reviver, already work with Node 22 (the outputs in this chapter were obtained with Node 26):

'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW ECMAScript 2026] JSON.rawJSON / JSON.isRawJSON, and the reviver context
// ========================================================================
// [these two new features already work with node 22, unlike the other
// scripts of this folder which require node 24 - see ecmascript-2026/README.md]

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 1) the problem: JSON.stringify loses precision on large integers
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// a classic JavaScript number (type [number]) cannot represent
// exactly the integers beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (cf. basics/basics-09.ts)
// yet many APIs (databases, social networks, ...) send
// 17-19 digit numeric identifiers in their JSON
const databaseColumnIdentifier = "9007199254740993123"; // too large for a [number]

interface DataRecord {
  id: unknown; // unknown here because it will be either a RawJSON, or a normal value
  name: string;
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 2) JSON.rawJSON(): inserts a "raw" number into a JSON.stringify,
//    without ever passing it through the [number] type (hence without loss of precision)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
const record: DataRecord = {
  id: JSON.rawJSON(databaseColumnIdentifier),
  name: "temperature-sensor-3"
};

const jsonText = JSON.stringify(record);
console.log("jsonText =", jsonText);
// the identifier appears as is in the produced text, digit for digit,
// whereas an id: Number(databaseColumnIdentifier) would have been rounded

// JSON.isRawJSON() makes it possible to check whether a value was created by JSON.rawJSON
console.log("JSON.isRawJSON(record.id) =", JSON.isRawJSON(record.id));

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 3) the JSON.parse reviver now receives a 3rd parameter [context]
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// before 2026, the reviver only received (key, value): impossible to know
// what the EXACT JSON text this value came from was (useful precisely
// to retrieve a large number without loss, by keeping it as text)
const reReadObject = JSON.parse(jsonText, (key, value, context) => {
  // [context.source] gives the raw JSON text corresponding to this value,
  // before any conversion to a JavaScript type - undefined for objects/arrays
  if (context?.source !== undefined) {
    console.log(`key="${key}", converted value=${value}, original JSON text="${context.source}"`);
  }
  return value;
});
console.log("reReadObject =", reReadObject);
  • [JSON.rawJSON(text)] inserts a “raw” number into JSON.stringify without ever converting it to the number type—useful for very large numeric identifiers (beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, see basics-09), which would otherwise lose precision;
  • the third parameter, context, of the reviver function provides access, via context.source, to the raw JSON text of the value currently being processed—before any conversion to a JavaScript type.
npx tsx ecmascript-2026/06-json-rawJSON-and-reviver.ts

Execution result:

jsonText = {"id":9007199254740993123,"name":"temperature-sensor-3"}
JSON.isRawJSON(record.id) = true
key="id", converted value=9007199254740993000, original JSON text="9007199254740993123"
key="name", converted value=temperature-sensor-3, original JSON text=""temperature-sensor-3""
reReadObject = { id: 9007199254740993000, name: 'temperature-sensor-3' }

We can clearly see the benefit of JSON.rawJSON: the resulting JSON text preserves the identifier digit by digit (9007199254740993123), whereas a simple id: Number(...) would have rounded it—as demonstrated by the value returned by JSON.parse (9007199254740993000), which was indeed converted to the number type and lost precision.

docs.title: 3.13. Temporal: the modern replacement for Date
docs.text: [Temporal] is a new global namespace intended to replace the old Date object, which has long been considered flawed: mutability, months numbered 0 through 11, lack of true time zone handling, and ambiguous string parsing. Date has not been removed from the language—existing code continues to work—but Temporal is now the recommended approach for any new code that manipulates dates, times, and durations.

docs.title: 3.13.1. ⚠️ Exact status regarding ECMAScript 2026
docs.text:
The Temporal proposal reached Stage 4 of TC39 in March 2026, and numerous articles have presented it as part of ECMAScript 2026. However, the official section of the specification summarizing the content of ECMAScript 2026 (cited in the previous chapter) does not explicitly mention it—the matter remains to be clarified. In practical terms, Temporal is natively available in Node.js 26 and up-to-date browsers, making this chapter relevant right now.

The following scripts are located in the [temporal] folder:

docs.title: 3.13.2. [01-plainDate-plainTime-plainDateTime] script
docs.text:
This script demonstrates [Temporal.PlainDate] (a date without time or time zone), [Temporal.PlainTime] (a time without date), and [Temporal.PlainDateTime] (date + time, without time zone):

'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW ECMAScript 2026] Temporal: PlainDate, PlainTime, PlainDateTime
// ========================================================================
// [requires Node 26+ - see temporal/README.md]

// [Temporal] is a brand new namespace, designed to replace [Date],
// which suffered from several flaws: mutability, months numbered from 0 to 11
// (January = 0!), no real time zone handling, and a
// single object supposed to represent at the same time a date, a time AND an instant.
// Temporal clearly separates these notions into several types.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 1) Temporal.PlainDate: a date WITHOUT time or time zone
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// useful for: a birthday, a due date, a public holiday...
// notions that have no "precise moment in the day"
const birthday = Temporal.PlainDate.from("2026-08-24");
console.log("birthday =", birthday.toString());
console.log("year =", birthday.year, ", month =", birthday.month, ", day =", birthday.day);
// unlike the old Date, the month is numbered normally: 8 = August (not 7!)
console.log("day of the week (1=Monday..7=Sunday) =", birthday.dayOfWeek);
console.log("number of days in this month =", birthday.daysInMonth);

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 2) immutability: add() and subtract() return a NEW object
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// with the old Date, date.setDate(date.getDate() + 7) modifies the object in place -
// a classic source of bugs when this object is shared elsewhere in the code
const inOneWeek = birthday.add({ days: 7 });
console.log("birthday (unchanged) =", birthday.toString());
console.log("inOneWeek (new object) =", inOneWeek.toString());

// arithmetic on months: automatically handles the number of days of the following month
const endOfJanuary = Temporal.PlainDate.from("2026-01-31");
const oneMonthLater = endOfJanuary.add({ months: 1 });
console.log("endOfJanuary =", endOfJanuary.toString(), ", +1 month =", oneMonthLater.toString());
// -> "2026-02-28" and not a weird overflow into March, unlike the old Date

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 3) comparing two dates
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
const backToSchool = Temporal.PlainDate.from("2026-09-01");
console.log("birthday before back to school :", Temporal.PlainDate.compare(birthday, backToSchool) < 0);
console.log("equality :", birthday.equals("2026-08-24"));

// duration between two dates
const duration = birthday.until(backToSchool);
console.log("duration until back to school =", duration.toString());

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 4) Temporal.PlainTime: a time WITHOUT date or time zone
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// useful for: "the class starts at 2:30 pm", regardless of the day
const classTime = Temporal.PlainTime.from("14:30:00");
console.log("classTime =", classTime.toString());
const endOfClass = classTime.add({ hours: 1, minutes: 30 });
console.log("endOfClass =", endOfClass.toString());

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 5) Temporal.PlainDateTime: date + time, but WITHOUT time zone
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// useful for: a "civil" appointment without worrying about the time zone (e.g.: a form
// that just displays "08/24/2026 14:30" without specifying where)
const appointment = Temporal.PlainDateTime.from("2026-08-24T14:30:00");
console.log("appointment =", appointment.toString());
// we can extract the date part and the time part separately
console.log("date part =", appointment.toPlainDate().toString());
console.log("time part =", appointment.toPlainTime().toString());
  • Unlike the old Date object, the month in Temporal.PlainDate is numbered normally: 8 refers to August, not July;
  • [immutability]: add() and subtract() always return a new object—the original is never modified, unlike Date.prototype.setDate;
  • arithmetic operations on months automatically handle different month lengths (31 January + 1 month does indeed result in 28 February, not an overflow into March);
  • Temporal.PlainDate.compare(...) and .until(...) allow you to compare two dates and calculate the duration between them.

docs.title: 3.13.3. script [02-zonedDateTime]
docs.text:
[Temporal.ZonedDateTime] is the type most similar to the old Date: it combines date, time, and time zone in a reliable and explicit way:

'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW ECMAScript 2026] Temporal.ZonedDateTime: the real replacement for Date
// ========================================================================
// [requires Node 26+ - see temporal/README.md]

// [Temporal.ZonedDateTime] is the type closest to the old [Date]:
// it combines a date, a time AND a time zone - but in a reliable
// and explicit way, whereas [Date] handled this in a confusing and implicit way.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 1) creating a ZonedDateTime, with an EXPLICIT time zone
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// unlike "new Date('2026-08-24T14:30:00')" which is ambiguous (local time?
// UTC? it depends on the format and the JS engine!), here the time zone is mandatory
const parisMeeting = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from("2026-08-24T14:30:00[Europe/Paris]");
console.log("parisMeeting =", parisMeeting.toString());
console.log("time zone =", parisMeeting.timeZoneId, ", offset =", parisMeeting.offset);

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 2) converting the same meeting to another time zone
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// withTimeZone() does NOT change the real instant, only the way it is displayed -
// useful to show the time of the same event to participants all over the world
const newYorkMeeting = parisMeeting.withTimeZone("America/New_York");
console.log("same meeting, seen from New York =", newYorkMeeting.toString());
const tokyoMeeting = parisMeeting.withTimeZone("Asia/Tokyo");
console.log("same meeting, seen from Tokyo =", tokyoMeeting.toString());

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 3) arithmetic automatically handles daylight saving time changes (DST)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// this is THE classic trap of the old Date: adding "24 hours" does not always
// correspond to adding "1 day" during a summer/winter time change
const beforeTimeChange = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from("2026-10-24T20:00:00[Europe/Paris]");
// we add one "calendar" day: Temporal understands that the time change must be skipped
const oneDayLater = beforeTimeChange.add({ days: 1 });
console.log("before =", beforeTimeChange.toString());
console.log("+ 1 calendar day =", oneDayLater.toString());
// we add exactly 24 hours: this is NOT necessarily the same local time
// if a summer/winter time change took place in between
const twentyFourHoursLater = beforeTimeChange.add({ hours: 24 });
console.log("+ exactly 24 hours =", twentyFourHoursLater.toString());

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 4) the current time, in the system's time zone
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
const now = Temporal.Now.zonedDateTimeISO();
console.log("now =", now.toString());
console.log("system time zone =", Temporal.Now.timeZoneId());

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 5) comparison and duration between two ZonedDateTimes in different time zones
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
const planeDeparture = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from("2026-12-20T22:00:00[Europe/Paris]");
const planeArrival = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from("2026-12-21T11:30:00[Asia/Tokyo]");
// Temporal compares the real instants, regardless of the time zone displayed on each side
const flightDuration = planeDeparture.until(planeArrival);
console.log("flight duration =", flightDuration.toString());
  • unlike new Date('2026-08-24T14:30:00'), whose interpretation (local time or UTC) depends on the exact format of the string, Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from(...) requires an explicit time zone, enclosed in square brackets;
  • withTimeZone(...) converts the display of the same actual time to another time zone without changing the time itself—useful for displaying a meeting time to participants in multiple countries;
  • the arithmetic correctly handles daylight saving time changes: adding “1 calendar day” is not always the same as adding “exactly 24 hours”—a classic pitfall of the old Date function.

docs.title: 3.13.4. script [03-duration-and-instant]
docs.text:
[Temporal.Duration] represents a period of time (not a specific moment); [Temporal.Instant] represents a specific, universal point in time—the direct replacement for new Date(...).getTime():

'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW ECMAScript 2026] Temporal.Duration and Temporal.Instant
// ========================================================================
// [requires Node 26+ - see temporal/README.md]

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 1) Temporal.Duration: represents a SPAN of time (not a precise moment)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// before, a duration had to be cobbled together "by hand" in milliseconds -
// not very readable, and with no distinction between calendar units (months, years)
// and fixed units (hours, minutes, seconds)
const tripDuration = Temporal.Duration.from({ hours: 2, minutes: 45 });
console.log("tripDuration =", tripDuration.toString());
console.log("hours =", tripDuration.hours, ", minutes =", tripDuration.minutes);

// a duration can also be created from its ISO 8601 notation
const worksDuration = Temporal.Duration.from("P3M2W"); // 3 months and 2 weeks
console.log("worksDuration =", worksDuration.toString());

// total() converts a whole duration into a single unit
console.log("tripDuration in minutes =", tripDuration.total("minutes"));

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 2) adding a duration to a date or a time
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
const departure = Temporal.PlainTime.from("08:15:00");
const arrival = departure.add(tripDuration);
console.log("departure =", departure.toString(), ", arrival =", arrival.toString());

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 3) Temporal.Instant: a PRECISE and UNIVERSAL point in time
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// unlike PlainDateTime or ZonedDateTime (which have a notion of calendar
// and time zone), Instant just represents "an instant", like a timestamp -
// it is the direct replacement for "new Date(something).getTime()"
const now = Temporal.Now.instant();
console.log("now (Instant) =", now.toString());
console.log("epoch in milliseconds =", now.epochMilliseconds);

// an Instant can be converted to a ZonedDateTime in any time zone,
// since a precise instant corresponds to a different local time depending on the time zone
const nowInParis = now.toZonedDateTimeISO("Europe/Paris");
const nowInSydney = now.toZonedDateTimeISO("Australia/Sydney");
console.log("now in Paris =", nowInParis.toString());
console.log("now in Sydney =", nowInSydney.toString());

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 4) duration between two instants, and comparison
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
const start = Temporal.Instant.from("2026-08-24T09:00:00Z");
const end = Temporal.Instant.from("2026-08-24T17:30:00Z");
console.log("duration of the working day =", start.until(end).toString());
console.log("start before end :", Temporal.Instant.compare(start, end) < 0);
  • A Duration can be constructed from an object ({ hours: 2, minutes: 45 }) or a string in the ISO 8601 format (e.g., "P3M2W" for 3 months and 2 weeks);
  • total(unit) converts a whole duration into a single unit (for example, minutes);
  • The same Instant can be converted to ZonedDateTime in any time zone—a specific instant corresponds to a different local time depending on your location.

docs.title: 3.13.5. script [04-comparison-with-Date]
docs.text:
This script addresses, one by one, the historical flaws in Date mentioned in the introduction and shows how Temporal corrects them:

'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW ECMAScript 2026] Temporal vs Date: the classic traps fixed
// ========================================================================
// [requires Node 26+ - see temporal/README.md]

// [Date] is not removed from the language (existing code keeps working),
// but [Temporal] is now the recommended API for any new code.
// this script illustrates, one by one, the historical flaws of [Date].

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// trap no. 1: months numbered from 0 to 11 in Date (January = 0!)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
const augustDate = new Date(2026, 7, 24); // 7 = August?! very confusing for a beginner
console.log("[Date] displayed month =", augustDate.getMonth(), "(but it really is the month of August)");

const augustPlainDate = Temporal.PlainDate.from({ year: 2026, month: 8, day: 24 });
console.log("[Temporal] displayed month =", augustPlainDate.month, "(8 = August, as everyone expects)");

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// trap no. 2: Date is mutable - a shared object can be modified by mistake
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
function addOneWeekDate(date: Date): Date {
  date.setDate(date.getDate() + 7); // modifies the object received as parameter!
  return date;
}
const originalDate = new Date(2026, 7, 24);
const dateWithOneMoreWeek = addOneWeekDate(originalDate);
// trap: originalDate has also been modified, whereas this was not necessarily intended
console.log("[Date] originalDate after the call =", originalDate.toDateString(), "(modified!)");
console.log("[Date] dateWithOneMoreWeek =", dateWithOneMoreWeek.toDateString());

function addOneWeekTemporal(date: Temporal.PlainDate): Temporal.PlainDate {
  return date.add({ days: 7 }); // returns a NEW object, modifies nothing
}
const originalPlainDate = Temporal.PlainDate.from({ year: 2026, month: 8, day: 24 });
const plainDateWithOneMoreWeek = addOneWeekTemporal(originalPlainDate);
console.log("[Temporal] originalPlainDate after the call =", originalPlainDate.toString(), "(unchanged)");
console.log("[Temporal] plainDateWithOneMoreWeek =", plainDateWithOneMoreWeek.toString());

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// trap no. 3: parsing a character string with Date is ambiguous
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// depending on the format of the string, "new Date(...)" interprets it sometimes as local time,
// sometimes as UTC - a frequent trap in production
console.log("[Date] new Date('2026-08-24') =", new Date("2026-08-24").toString(), "(interpreted as UTC)");
console.log("[Date] new Date('2026-08-24 00:00:00') =", new Date("2026-08-24 00:00:00").toString(), "(interpreted as local time)");
// -> the two lines above can display different times, for the "same" date!

// with Temporal, the behaviour is always explicit and unambiguous:
// a PlainDate has no time at all, a ZonedDateTime requires a precise time zone
console.log("[Temporal] PlainDate.from('2026-08-24') =", Temporal.PlainDate.from("2026-08-24").toString());

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// trap no. 4: Date cannot natively compute a "clean" duration
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
const date1 = new Date(2026, 0, 1);
const date2 = new Date(2026, 7, 24);
const millisecondsBetweenTheTwo = date2.getTime() - date1.getTime();
const daysBetweenTheTwo = millisecondsBetweenTheTwo / (1000 * 60 * 60 * 24);
console.log("[Date] days between the two dates (manual calculation) =", daysBetweenTheTwo);

const p1 = Temporal.PlainDate.from({ year: 2026, month: 1, day: 1 });
const p2 = Temporal.PlainDate.from({ year: 2026, month: 8, day: 24 });
console.log("[Temporal] duration between the two dates =", p1.until(p2).toString());

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// in summary: Temporal is immutable, without time zone ambiguity, with
// separate types for each use (date only, time only, precise instant,
// date+time+zone...), and reliable arithmetic even around summer time
// changes and months of different lengths.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  • [trap no. 1]: The months in Date are numbered from 0 to 11 (although new Date(2026, 7, 24) does indeed refer to August)—a common source of confusion for beginners;
  • [trap no. 2]: Date is mutable—modifying a Date object passed as a function parameter also modifies the original, which can be surprising; Temporal.PlainDate.add() always returns a new object;
  • [trap no. 3]: Parsing a string using new Date(...) is ambiguous depending on its exact format (local time or UTC); Temporal is always explicit;
  • [trap no. 4]: Date cannot natively calculate a “clean” duration between two dates (you must subtract timestamps in milliseconds and divide manually); Temporal.PlainDate.until(...) does this directly.

docs.title: 5. The HTTP Functions of TypeScript
docs.text: Here we present two ways to make HTTP requests in TypeScript: the [fetch] function, which has been native to Node since version 18, and the third-party library [axios]. The scripts for this chapter are located in the [http] folder of the project.

docs.title: 5.1. Choosing HTTP Tools
docs.text:
In 2019, fetch had not yet been implemented by node.js, and the original document recommended the node-fetch package. Since Node 18 (2022), [fetch] has been a native global function, standardized by the WHATWG Fetch standard—no longer needs to be imported.

[axios] remains an interesting library, however: compatible with both node.js and browsers, it offers a slightly richer API (interceptors, automatic JSON serialization, standardized error handling). We present both, using the same example, to show that the coding approach is similar.

docs.title: 5.2. The Tax Calculation Server
docs.text:
This chapter, like the following ones, refers to the NestJS server installed earlier. The test architecture is as follows:

In [A-B], JavaScript code executed by [node.js] will send requests to the web application [C] via [1]. The web application will send back jSON responses (4). The client-side JavaScript code can be organized into layers [UI, business, dao] (UI: User Interface). We will do this later. To run the following scripts, your NestJS server must be running.

docs.title: 5.3. [fetch-01] script
docs.text:
This script uses [fetch] to initialize a JSON session with the tax calculation server:

'use strict';

// [2026 update] in 2019, you had to install the [node-fetch] package to have
// the [fetch] function on the node side. Since Node 18 (2022), [fetch] is a native global
// function, standardized by the "WHATWG Fetch standard": no need to import it anymore.
// imports
import qs from 'qs';
import { sprintf } from 'sprintf-js';
import moment from 'moment';


// base URL of the tax-calculation server
const baseUrl: string = 'http://localhost:3000/main.php?';
// init session
async function initSession(): Promise<any> {
  // [2026 update] the native [fetch] does not know the [timeout] option.
  // to limit the waiting time, we give it a [signal] produced by
  // [AbortSignal.timeout(ms)] (available since Node 17.3): after this delay,
  // the request is automatically cancelled and [fetch] throws an error.
  const options: RequestInit = {
    method: "GET",
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000)
  };
  // execution of the HTTP request [get /main.php?action=init-session&type=json]
  let fetchStart: moment.Moment | undefined;
  try {
    // asynchronous request - [fetch] returns a promise
    fetchStart = moment(Date.now());
    const response = await fetch(baseUrl + qs.stringify({
      action: 'init-session',
      type: 'json'
    }), options);
    // [response] is the whole HTTP response of the server (HTTP headers + the response itself)
    // we display this response to see its structure
    console.log(sprintf("fetch response formatted as json,=%j, %s", response, time(fetchStart)));
    console.log("fetch response in javascript=", response);
    // we can access the HTTP headers
    console.log("response headers=", response.headers);
    // if the response is of type application / json, the server's json response is obtained with the asynchronous function [response.json()]
    // in this case the calling code gets a [Promise] object
    // [await] makes it possible to get the server's [json] response rather than its promise
    const jsonStart = moment(Date.now());
    const object = await response.json();
    console.log(sprintf("json response=%j, type=%s, %s", object, typeof (object), time(jsonStart)));
    return object;
    // if the response is of type text / plain, the server's text response is obtained with [response.text()]
    // in this case the calling code gets a [Promise] object
    // [await] makes it possible to get the server's [text] response rather than its promise
    // const text = await response.text();
    // console.log("text response=", text);
    // return text;
  } catch (error: any) {
    // we are here because the server sent an error code [404 Not Found, ...] with an empty body - we display the error to see its structure
    // or because the [fetch] client threw an exception (network unreachable, ...)
    // we display the structure of the error
    console.log(sprintf("fetch error in json=%j, %s", error, time(fetchStart)));
    console.log("fetch error in javascript=", typeof (error), error);
    // we throw the error msg received
    throw error.message;
  }
}

// the main function executes the asynchronous function [initSession]
async function main(): Promise<void> {
  try {
    console.log("HTTP request to the server in progress ---------------------------------------------");
    const response = await initSession();
    console.log("success ---------------------------------------------");
    console.log("response=", response, typeof (response))
  } catch (error) {
    console.log("error ---------------------------------------------");
    console.log("error=", error, typeof (error));
  }
}

// test
main();

// utility displaying time and duration
function time(start?: moment.Moment): string {
  // time of the current moment
  const now = moment(Date.now());
  // time formatting
  let result = "time=" + now.format("HH:mm:ss:SSS");
  // should a duration be calculated?
  if (start) {
    const duration = now.valueOf() - start.valueOf();
    const milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    const seconds = Math.floor(duration / 1000);
    // time + duration formatting
    result = result + sprintf(", duration= %s second(s) and %s milliseconds", seconds, milliseconds);
  }
  // result
  return result;
}
  • lines 3–5: [2026 update] — comment noting that fetch is now native, unlike in 2019;
  • line 13: this line is important. It specifies the header for the URL that the script will query. This will be supplemented by any parameters. Here, we used the configuration defined in the section “Installing a NestJS server”;
  • line 22: AbortSignal.timeout(2000) — replaces the timeout option in node-fetch (which does not exist in native fetch): if the request takes longer than 2 seconds, it is automatically canceled;
  • line 29: fetch(URL, options) — the syntax remains that of standard fetch: a URL, and an options object (method, cancellation signal, etc.);
  • lines 30–31: a jSON session is initiated;
  • line 36: the entire server response is displayed;
  • line 38: the response headers are displayed;
  • line 43: await response.json() — extracts the JSON body from the response; this is itself an asynchronous operation (the response may be a stream still being received);
  • line 52: fetch only throws an exception if the HTTP request failed (network unreachable, timeout, etc.). If a response is received, even with an error code (400, 500, etc.), fetch does not throw an exception: the response is normally available, line 38.
npx tsx http/fetch-01.ts

Execution result:

  • Lines 3–22: the entire server response;
  • line 4: the 200 status code means that the server was able to process the requested URL. This is shown on line 21. We have already used this URL with the Postman client;
  • lines 23–32: the response headers. They provide information about the response that follows. For example, on line 29, the server indicates that this response is 84 characters long;
  • line 28: the server sent a session cookie. This allows a client to maintain a memory space on the server called a session. This is managed by the web server. After receiving this session cookie—which is actually the client’s identifier with the server—the client must send it back with every new request. Note the format of this session cookie. We will retrieve it shortly in a TypeScript client.
  • line 33: the server’s jSON response;

docs.title: 5.4. script [fetch-02]
docs.text:
This script reuses fetch-01 while removing all demonstration details that are unnecessary for everyday use:

'use strict';

// [2026 update] [fetch] is now a native global function of node
// (since Node 18): no need to import the [node-fetch] package anymore as in 2019.
// imports
import qs from 'qs';

// base URL of the tax-calculation server
const baseUrl: string = 'http://localhost:3000/main.php?';
// init session
async function initSession(): Promise<any> {
  // options of the HHTP request [get /main.php?action=init-session&type=json]
  // [AbortSignal.timeout(ms)] replaces the [timeout] option which does not exist on native fetch
  const options: RequestInit = {
    method: "GET",
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000)
  };
  // execution of the HTTP request [get /main.php?action=init-session&type=json]
  const response = await fetch(baseUrl + qs.stringify({
    action: 'init-session',
    type: 'json'
  }), options);
  // result received in jSON
  return await response.json();
}

// the main function executes the asynchronous function [initSession]
async function main(): Promise<void> {
  try {
    console.log("HTTP request to the server in progress ---------------------------------------------");
    const response = await initSession();
    console.log("success ---------------------------------------------");
    console.log("response=", response)
  } catch (error: any) {
    console.log("error ---------------------------------------------");
    console.log("error=", error.message);
  }
}

// test
main();

docs.title: 5.5. script [axios-01]
docs.text:
Same example, with [axios]:

'use strict';
import axios, { AxiosInstance, AxiosRequestConfig } from 'axios';

// axios default configuration
axios.defaults.timeout = 2000;
axios.defaults.baseURL = 'http://localhost:3000/';

// init session
async function initSession(axios: AxiosInstance): Promise<any> {
  // options of the HHTP request [get /main.php?action=init-session&type=json]
  const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
    // [TypeScript update] axios.request() accepts, as far as typing is concerned, only one
    // configuration argument: the URL must therefore be in [options.url]
    // rather than as a separate 1st parameter of request()
    url: 'main.php',
    method: "GET",
    // URL parameters
    params: {
      action: 'init-session',
      type: 'x'
    }
  };
  // execution of the HTTP request [get /main.php?action=init-session&type=json]
  try {
    // asynchronous request
    const response = await axios.request(options);
    // response is the whole HTTP response of the server (HTTP headers + the response itself)
    // we display this response to see its structure
    // console.log("axios response=", response);
    // the server's response is in [response.data]
    return response.data;
  } catch (error: any) {
    // we are here because the server sent an error code [404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error, ...]
    // the [error] parameter is an exception instance - it can take various forms
    // we display it to see its structure
    // console.log("axios error=", typeof (error), error);
    if (error.response) {
      // the server reported an error in the HTTP status but it also sent a response
      // which is then found in [error.response.data]
      // we know that the server sends jSON responses with the structure {action, status, response}
      // and that in case of error, the error msg is in [response]
      return error.response.data;
    } else {
      // we throw the error
      throw error;
    }
  }
}

// the main function executes the asynchronous function [initSession]
async function main(): Promise<void> {
  try {
    console.log("HTTP request to the server in progress ---------------------------------------------");
    const response = await initSession(axios);
    console.log("success ---------------------------------------------");
    console.log("response=", response, typeof (response))
  } catch (error: any) {
    console.log("error ---------------------------------------------");
    console.log("error=", error.message);
  }
}

// test
main();
  • The URL query is constructed from the information in lines 6, 15, 19, and 20;
  • line 26: axios.request(options) — unlike fetch, the URL and the options are grouped into a single configuration object (line 11);
  • line 37: error.response — if the server responded (even with an error code), Axios places this response in error.response, which is accessible in the catch block — unlike fetch, Axios always throws an exception whenever the status code is not a success (2xx);
  • line 31: the successful response is in response.data — axios automatically extracts JSON; there’s no need for a separate await response.json() as with fetch.
npx tsx http/axios-01.ts

Execution result:

HTTP request to the server in progress ---------------------------------------------
success ---------------------------------------------
response= {
  action: 'init-session',
  status: 700,
  response: 'session started with type [json]'
} object

docs.title: 5.6. [axios-03] script — authentication
docs.text:
This script chains two requests: init-session, followed by authenticate-user in **[POST], with a body encoded by the **[qs] library:

'use strict';
import axios, { AxiosInstance, AxiosRequestConfig } from 'axios';
import qs from 'qs'

// axios configuration
axios.defaults.timeout = 2000;
axios.defaults.baseURL = 'http://localhost:3000/';


// init session
async function initSession(axios: AxiosInstance): Promise<any> {
  // options of the HHTP request [get /main.php?action=init-session&type=json]
  const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
    // [TypeScript update] URL included in [options.url] (the typed axios.request() accepts only one argument)
    url: 'main.php',
    method: "GET",
    // URL parameters
    params: {
      action: 'init-session',
      type: 'json'
    }
  };
  try {
    // execution of the HTTP request [get /main.php?action=init-session&type=json]
    const response = await axios.request(options);
    // the server's response is in [response.data]
    return response.data;
  } catch (error: any) {
    // server response
    if (error.response) {
      // the jSON response is in [error.response.data]
      return error.response.data;
    } else {
      // we rethrow the error
      throw error;
    }
  }
}

async function authenticateUser(axios: AxiosInstance, user: string, password: string): Promise<any> {
  // options of the HHTP request [post /main.php?action=authenticate-user]
  const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
    // [TypeScript update] URL included in [options.url]
    url: 'main.php',
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      'Content-type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded',
    },
    // POST body
    data: qs.stringify({
      user: user,
      password: password
    }),
    // URL parameters
    params: {
      action: 'authenticate-user'
    }
  };
  try {
    // execution of the HTTP request [post /main.php?action=authenticate-user]
    const response = await axios.request(options);
    // the server's response is in [response.data]
    return response.data;
  } catch (error: any) {
    // server response
    if (error.response) {
      // the jSON response is in [error.response.data]
      return error.response.data;
    } else {
      // we rethrow the error
      throw error;
    }
  }
}

// the main function executes the asynchronous functions one by one
async function main(): Promise<void> {
  try {
    // init-session
    console.log("init-session action in progress ---------------------------------------------");
    const response1 = await initSession(axios);
    console.log("success ---------------------------------------------");
    console.log("response=", response1);
    // authenticate-user
    console.log("authenticate-user action in progress ---------------------------------------------");
    const response2 = await authenticateUser(axios, 'admin', 'admin');
    console.log("success ---------------------------------------------");
    console.log("response=", response2)
  } catch (error) {
    console.log("error ---------------------------------------------");
    console.log("error=", error);
  }
}

// test
main();
  • lines 42–53: The POST request sends its parameters (user, password), encoded as application/x-www-form-urlencoded, via qs.stringify(...) in options.data;
  • lines 55–57: the URL ([post /main.php?action=authenticate-user]) also has a parameter;
  • both functions are executed sequentially in main (awaited one after the other) (lines 81, 86): the second can only make sense if the first succeeded, since it depends on the session cookie set by init-session.
npx tsx http/axios-03.ts

Execution result:

init-session action in progress ---------------------------------------------
success ---------------------------------------------
response= {
  action: 'init-session',
  status: 700,
  response: 'session started with type [json]'
}
authenticate-user action in progress ---------------------------------------------
success ---------------------------------------------
response= {
  action: 'authenticate-user',
  status: 103,
  response: [ 'no session in progress. Start with action [init-session]' ]
}
  • Lines 10–14: The action [authenticate-user] failed. The reason is as follows:
    • The action [init-session] did not send the session cookie to the server. This is the client’s identifier with the server. Because it did not send this identifier, the client is unknown to the server. In its response, the server included a session cookie. This tells the client: “Here is your identifier for your future requests”;
    • but the action [authenticate-user] also failed to send the session cookie to the server. This is because [init-session] did not take the time to store it. The server therefore does not recognize the client and does not know that it previously initiated a jSON session, and it informs the client of this;

The solution to this problem is to manage the session cookie sent by the server:

  • The very first request made to the server must store the session cookie sent by the server;
  • subsequent requests must retrieve this session cookie and send it to the server to authenticate;

docs.title: 5.7. Script [axios-04] — session cookie management
docs.text:
The code is the same as before but adds a function, [getRemoteData], to manage the session cookie:

'use strict';
import axios, { AxiosInstance, AxiosRequestConfig, AxiosResponse } from 'axios';
import qs from 'qs'

// axios configuration
axios.defaults.timeout = 2000;
axios.defaults.baseURL = 'http://localhost:3000/';

// session cookie
const sessionCookieName: string = "connect.sid";
let sessionCookie: string = '';

// init session
async function initSession(axios: AxiosInstance): Promise<any> {
  // options of the HHTP request [get /main.php?action=init-session&type=json]
  const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
    // [TypeScript update] URL included in [options.url]
    url: 'main.php',
    method: "GET",
    // URL parameters
    params: {
      action: 'init-session',
      type: 'json'
    }
  };
  // execution of the HTTP request
  return await getRemoteData(axios, options);
}

async function authenticateUser(axios: AxiosInstance, user: string, password: string): Promise<any> {
  // options of the HHTP request [post /main.php?action=authenticate-user]
  const options: AxiosRequestConfig = {
    // [TypeScript update] URL included in [options.url]
    url: 'main.php',
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      'Content-type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded',
    },
    // POST body
    data: qs.stringify({
      user: user,
      password: password
    }),
    // URL parameters
    params: {
      action: 'authenticate-user'
    }
  };
  // execution of the HTTP request
  return await getRemoteData(axios, options);
}

async function getRemoteData(axios: AxiosInstance, options: AxiosRequestConfig): Promise<any> {
  // for the session cookie
  if (!options.headers) {
    options.headers = {} as any;
  }
  (options.headers as any).Cookie = sessionCookie;
  // execution of the HTTP request
  let response: AxiosResponse;
  try {
    // asynchronous request
    response = await axios.request(options);
  } catch (error: any) {
    // the [error] parameter is an exception instance - it can take various forms
    if (error.response) {
      // the server's response is in [error.response]
      response = error.response;
    } else {
      // we rethrow the error
      throw error;
    }
  }
  // response is the whole HTTP response of the server (HTTP headers + the response itself)
  // we retrieve the session cookie if it exists
  const setCookie = response.headers['set-cookie'];
  if (setCookie) {
    // setCookie is an array
    // we look for the session cookie in this array
    let found = false;
    let i = 0;
    while (!found && i < setCookie.length) {
      // we look for the session cookie
      const results = RegExp('^(' + sessionCookieName + '.+?);').exec(setCookie[i]);
      if (results) {
        // we store the session cookie
        // eslint-disable-next-line require-atomic-updates
        sessionCookie = results[1];
        // found it
        found = true;
      } else {
        // next element
        i++;
      }
    }
  }
  // the server's response is in [response.data]
  return response.data;
}


// the main function executes the asynchronous functions one by one
async function main(): Promise<void> {
  try {
    // init-session
    console.log("init-session action in progress ----------------");
    const response1 = await initSession(axios);
    console.log("success --------------------------");
    console.log("response=", response1);
    // authenticate-user
    console.log("authenticate-user action in progress ---------");
    const response2 = await authenticateUser(axios, 'admin', 'admin');
    console.log("success -------------------");
    console.log("response=", response2)
  } catch (error: any) {
    console.log("error ------------------");
    console.log("error=", error.message);
  }
}

// test
main();

This script factors initSession and authenticateUser around a common function, [getRemoteData], which explicitly handles the session cookie (here connect.sid, see line 10)—which is essential because the server associates authentication and simulations with an HTTP session:

  • line 10: the name of the session cookie being searched for. It depends on the web server used. The NestJS server used in this course uses a session cookie named [connect.sid];
  • line 53: the [getRemoteData] function handles sending requests and receiving the server’s response. It also manages the session cookie. It takes two parameters:
    • the [AxiosInstance] object, which handles the general mechanics of HTTP Axios requests. This object and others are obtained through the import in line 2;
    • the [AxiosRequestConfig] object, which defines the options for a specific request;
  • Lines 54–58: [options.headers] sets the header for the HTTP request that will be sent to the server. If a session cookie exists, it must be included in this header. Line 58 performs this task. Upon completion of the first request, [getRemoteData] will store this cookie in the global variable defined on line 11. During the first request, its value will be an empty string. For subsequent requests, it will be the character string of the session cookie sent by the server in response to the first request.
  • Line 63: The HTTP request is executed;
  • line 76: the response header is checked to see if there is a “set-cookie” line. This line is present only if the client’s previous request did not include a “Cookie” line in its headers. When the server receives a HTTP request from the client that includes the ‘Cookie’ line, it no longer sends the session cookie because it knows the client already has it. It is up to the client to resend it with each new request. This is what happens on line 58;
  • line 77: if the server sent the header [Set-Cookie], then its contents must be retrieved. This header may contain multiple cookies in the form [cookie_name=value]. Lines 77–95 will be executed only once during the script’s execution. As mentioned, the server does not send the session cookie in response to requests that have been authenticated with that same session cookie;
  • line 84: we explicitly search for the cookie whose name was stored on line 10;
  • line 88: if it is found, it is stored in the global variable defined on line 11;

This mechanism ensures that:

  • the session cookie is retrieved from the response to the first HTTP request;
  • it is then systematically sent to the server with each new request, allowing the server to recognize its client;

The code is executed:

npx tsx http/axios-04.ts

success --------------------------
response= {
  action: 'init-session',
  status: 700,
  response: 'session started with type [json]'
}
authenticate-user action in progress ---------
success -------------------
response= {
  action: 'authenticate-user',
  status: 200,
  response: 'Authentication successful [admin, admin]'
}

docs.title: 5.8. script [fetch-03] — canceling requests
docs.text:
[NEW since 2019] This script illustrates two uses of the mechanism for canceling fetch requests, available natively since Node 18:

'use strict';
// ========================================================================
// [NEW since 2019] native fetch + cancellation of an HTTP request
// ========================================================================

// [fetch] is global since Node 18: no need for the [node-fetch] package
// used in 2019 in fetch-01.js/fetch-02.js (see the [2026 update] comments
// added in these two files)

// base URL of the tax-calculation server (see http/README.md)
// as for axios-01.js, this script assumes that the course's PHP server is running
// locally: without it, the requests fail with "fetch failed", which is normal
const baseUrl: string = 'http://localhost:3000/main.php';

// example 1: request with a maximum delay thanks to AbortSignal.timeout()
async function requestWithMaximumDelay(): Promise<void> {
  console.log("--- request with AbortSignal.timeout ---");
  try {
    const response = await fetch(baseUrl + '?action=init-session&type=json', {
      // beyond 2 seconds, the request is cancelled automatically
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000)
    });
    const data = await response.json();
    console.log("response =", data);
  } catch (error: any) {
    // if the delay is exceeded,
    // [error.name] is "TimeoutError" or "AbortError" depending on the case
    console.log("error.name =", error.name, ", message =", error.message);
  }
}

// example 2: manual cancellation of a request, for example because
// the user changed their mind (e.g.: they retype in a search field)
async function manuallyCancellableRequest(): Promise<void> {
  console.log("--- manually cancelled request ---");
  const controller = new AbortController();

  // we schedule a "business" cancellation after 500 ms
  // (in a real application, this would be for example a click on a "cancel" button)
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log("manual cancellation triggered");
    controller.abort();
  }, 10);

  try {
    const response = await fetch(baseUrl + '?action=init-session&type=json', {
      signal: controller.signal
    });
    const data = await response.json();
    console.log("response =", data);
  } catch (error: any) {
    console.log("error.name =", error.name, ", message =", error.message);
  }
}

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  await requestWithMaximumDelay();
  await manuallyCancellableRequest();
}

main();
  • [AbortSignal.timeout(ms)]: automatically cancels the request if it exceeds the specified timeout—a pattern already seen in the fetch-01 script;
  • [AbortController]: allows for manual cancellation, triggered by any application event (here, a setTimeout simulating, for example, a click on a “Cancel” button, or new text entered into a search field that invalidates the previous request).
npx tsx http/fetch-03.ts

Execution result:

--- request with AbortSignal.timeout ---
response = {
  action: 'init-session',
  status: 700,
  response: 'session started with type [json]'
}
--- manually cancelled request ---
manual cancellation triggered
error.name = AbortError , message = This operation was aborted
  • Lines 2–6: The first request completed normally;
  • lines 8–9: the second request was canceled due to the very short timeout (10 ms) set for the request (line 43 of the code);
